196Pre-specified statistical analysis plan
Master
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident
Use itWrite the plan before data collection. Run the analysis after the database is locked.
WhyA pre-specified statistical analysis plan protects your integrity and your viva. It forces every test to be chosen for a reason, before the data can tempt you. It also becomes the analysis section of your thesis.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a biostatistician with two decades of experience in clinical research who routinely explains statistical reasoning to clinicians. You are rigorous about assumptions and openly critical of common misuse, such as testing for normality in tiny samples or reporting p values without effect sizes.
My context
Design: [prospective cohort / RCT / cross-sectional / diagnostic accuracy / before-after]
Total sample size, and per group if applicable: [N; n1, n2]
Primary objective: [state]
Secondary objectives: [list]
Software: [SPSS / R / Stata / GraphPad / Jamovi / Python]
My statistical comfort level: [beginner / intermediate / advanced]
My variables, each with name, type and role (example format: "FEV1 % predicted, continuous, baseline and 12 weeks, primary outcome"): [LIST ALL VARIABLES]
Task
1. Variable dictionary: type, expected distribution, unit, and how to summarise it in Table 1.
2. Data cleaning: implausible-value checks, range limits, duplicate detection, a documented correction log.
3. Missing data: how to quantify it, likely mechanisms, the threshold at which complete-case analysis becomes unsafe, and a practical alternative at my sample size.
4. Assumption checking for each planned comparison, and what to do when an assumption fails.
5. Test selection: a table mapping each objective to the exact test, the reason, and the non-parametric alternative.
6. Effect measures with confidence intervals for every comparison.
7. Adjusted analysis: covariates and their justification, how many my events or sample can support (events per variable), and a multicollinearity check.
8. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses, labelled exploratory.
9. Multiplicity: whether correction is needed, and the method.
10. Runnable, commented syntax in my software for every analysis.
11. Reporting templates: decimals, p values (including very small ones) and CI placement.
12. Table 1, the main results table, and two figures that best show the primary finding.
13. The five statistical mistakes most likely in this design, and how to avoid each.
Rules
Use clearly marked placeholders instead of any numeric result, because this is a plan, not an analysis. If my sample is too small for something I asked for, say so and tell me what I can legitimately claim instead. If my design cannot support a causal claim, give the correct associational phrasing. Explain every recommendation in plain clinical language first, then in statistical terms.
Output
Thirteen numbered sections, with tables for the variable dictionary and the test map, and code blocks for syntax.
Tweak
End with the 5 criticisms a reviewer would make of this plan, and how to pre-empt each.
How to get more out of it
  • Lock and date this plan before you unblind or begin analysis. Attach it to your thesis appendix.
  • Run the syntax on 10 dummy rows first. Errors are easier to fix before the real data arrives.
  • Never let the model interpret your actual results without checking the raw output yourself.
  • → NEXT #198 Run my analysis on the real dataset, safely
197Sample size with every assumption shown
Master
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident
Use itWhile writing the protocol, before IEC submission.
WhyThe sample size is the most-questioned number in any synopsis. AI calculators make arithmetic errors, and the inputs matter more than the formula. This prompt shows every assumption and step so you can defend it and verify it in OpenEpi or G*Power.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a biostatistician who has calculated and defended sample sizes for hundreds of postgraduate protocols. You show every formula, every input and every step, and you say where each input must come from.
My context
Design: [cross-sectional / case-control / cohort / RCT / diagnostic accuracy / correlation]
Primary outcome and its type: [proportion / mean / correlation / sensitivity / time-to-event]
Primary objective or hypothesis: [paste]
Expected value(s) from literature or pilot data, with source: [e.g. prevalence 18% (Author, year); means 42 ± 9 vs 36 ± 9]
Precision or effect size I want to detect: [e.g. absolute margin of error 5%; difference of 6 units]
Alpha, power and sidedness: [e.g. 0.05, 80%, two-sided]
Expected dropout or non-response: [e.g. 10%]
Group ratio if comparing groups: [e.g. 1:1]
Eligible patients per month and months available: [N, X]
Task
1. Name the correct formula for my design and outcome, and explain why it fits.
2. Define every term in the formula.
3. Substitute my inputs and show the step-by-step calculation.
4. Apply the dropout adjustment and round up correctly.
5. Check feasibility: the months needed at my recruitment rate.
6. Show a sensitivity table: how the sample size changes if the key assumption is 20% better or worse.
7. Tell me exactly which inputs to enter in OpenEpi or G*Power to verify the result.
8. Write the sample-size paragraph for my protocol, including the source of each input.
Rules
Mark every input I did not supply as [INSERT FROM PUBLISHED SOURCE — VERIFY], because an assumption without a source is the first thing a committee rejects. Show your arithmetic so errors are visible. Do not choose an effect size to make the sample fit my patient numbers; if the study isn't feasible, say so.
Output
The formula and terms, the worked calculation, the feasibility check, the sensitivity table, the verification instructions, then the paragraph.
Tweak
End with the 3 committee questions about this sample size and short answers.
How to get more out of it
  • Never submit the AI number alone. Verify it in OpenEpi or G*Power and report the verified figure.
  • The expected value must come from a real study similar to yours, cited in your protocol.
  • If the number is unfeasible, change the design or outcome. Don't massage the effect size.
  • → NEXT #202 Sample size to estimate a proportion (prevalence)
198Run my analysis on the real dataset, safely
Master
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident
Use itAfter your dataset is cleaned and locked, in ChatGPT's data analysis mode, Julius AI or a similar tool that runs code.
WhyAI data tools can run a full analysis in minutes, and can also silently mis-code a variable or pick the wrong test. This prompt makes the tool follow your pre-specified plan, show its code and checks, and flag anything uncertain, so you can verify every number.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a careful biostatistician analysing a clinical thesis dataset. You follow the pre-specified plan exactly, show every step and every assumption check, and never proceed on a guess about coding.
My context
Uploaded file: [file name] with [N] rows and [K] columns
Codebook (variable, meaning, codes, units): [PASTE CODEBOOK HERE]
My pre-specified analysis plan: [PASTE SAP OR THE KEY TESTS HERE]
Primary outcome and exposure: [brief]
Task
1. Load the data and report rows, columns, variable types, missing values per variable, and any values outside the codebook's valid range. Stop and ask me before fixing anything.
2. Produce Table 1 (baseline characteristics) by group, with the summary statistic appropriate to each variable.
3. Run the primary analysis exactly as planned: show the assumption checks, the test used, the effect estimate with 95% CI and the exact p value.
4. Run the secondary analyses in the plan, labelled as such.
5. Produce the figures specified in the plan.
6. Show all code used, so I can re-run it.
7. List every decision you had to make that the plan did not specify.
Rules
Do not recode, drop or impute any data without asking me first, because silent data changes are the most dangerous AI analysis error. Follow my plan; if a planned test is inappropriate for the data, stop and explain rather than switching tests. Report numbers exactly as computed, without rounding before the final table.
Output
A data-check report, then Table 1, then results for each objective (test, estimate, CI, p), then the figures, the code and the decision log.
Tweak
Finish with the 3 numbers I should verify by hand or in a second tool before I trust the analysis.
How to get more out of it
  • Upload de-identified data only: study IDs, no names, no hospital numbers.
  • Re-run the key analysis in SPSS, Jamovi or R. If the numbers differ, find out why before writing.
  • Save the code and outputs with the date. They are your audit trail.
  • → NEXT #200 Interpret my software output correctly
199Multivariable regression: plan, run and interpret
Master
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen your objective involves adjusting for confounders or finding independent predictors.
WhyRegression is where theses most often overreach: too many variables for the events, stepwise selection, and adjusted odds ratios interpreted as causes. This prompt keeps the model honest and interpretable.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a biostatistician who teaches regression modelling to clinicians and reviews models for medical journals. You care about events per variable, sensible variable selection and plain-language interpretation.
My context
Outcome and its type: [binary / continuous / time-to-event / count]
Exposure of interest, if any: [variable]
Candidate covariates, with why each matters: [list]
Sample size and number of outcome events: [N, events]
Purpose of the model: [adjust for confounding / identify predictors / build a prediction score]
Software: [SPSS / R / Stata / Jamovi]
Task
1. Choose the right model (linear, logistic, Cox, Poisson or negative binomial) and justify it.
2. Calculate the number of parameters my events can support, and prioritise covariates accordingly.
3. Recommend how to select variables for my purpose (clinical reasoning or a causal diagram, not automatic stepwise), and how to handle continuous variables.
4. List the assumption checks and diagnostics for my model (linearity, proportional hazards, multicollinearity, influential points, goodness of fit).
5. Give runnable, commented syntax.
6. Show how to present results: a table of crude and adjusted estimates with 95% CIs, and a plain-language interpretation of each.
7. Explain what the model can and cannot conclude.
Rules
Warn me clearly if I have too few events for my covariates, because an overfitted model produces unstable estimates that examiners and reviewers will question. Interpret adjusted estimates as associations unless the design is randomised. Use placeholders instead of invented results.
Output
Numbered sections, a covariate-priority table, code blocks, and a results-table template.
Tweak
Finish with the 3 regression mistakes a viva examiner looks for, and how my plan avoids them.
How to get more out of it
  • Report crude and adjusted estimates side by side. Readers need to see what adjustment changed.
  • Avoid "independent predictor" language unless your purpose really is prediction, and validate if it is.
  • If the events are few, a simpler model with fewer, well-chosen covariates is more credible.
  • → NEXT #200 Interpret my software output correctly
200Interpret my software output correctly
Master
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident
Use itWhen SPSS, R, Jamovi or Stata output is in front of you and you need to understand and report it.
WhyStatistical output is full of numbers you don't need, and a few you absolutely do. Misreading which p value or estimate matters is common and costly. This prompt identifies the right numbers, explains them in clinical language and writes the result sentence.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a biostatistics tutor who explains software output line by line to clinicians and writes results exactly as journals expect.
My context
Software and test run: [e.g. SPSS independent-samples t-test]
My objective for this analysis: [paste]
Variable names and what they mean: [brief]
Sample size I expected in this analysis: [n per group]
What I expected to find, before running it: [brief]
The output (copy as text or upload a screenshot): [PASTE OUTPUT HERE]
Task
1. Identify which parts of the output answer my objective, and which to ignore.
2. Check that the right test was run for my variables, and that its assumptions appear to be met (e.g. Levene's test, expected counts).
3. Extract the key numbers: group summaries, effect estimate, 95% CI, test statistic, degrees of freedom and exact p value.
4. Explain the result in plain clinical language, then in statistical language.
5. Write the result sentence for my results section in journal style.
6. Flag anything suspicious: impossible values, suspiciously large effects, wrong n, or a mismatch with my expectations.
7. Say whether the result answers my objective fully, or whether another analysis is needed.
Rules
Use only the numbers in the output I pasted, reproduced exactly, because transcription errors in results are indistinguishable from fabrication. If the output is from the wrong test, say so and name the right one rather than interpreting it.
Output
A short "what to read" guide, the extracted-numbers table, the two explanations, the result sentence, then the flags.
Tweak
End with the one follow-up analysis or check this output suggests I should run.
How to get more out of it
  • Always check that n in the output matches the n you expect. Missing data silently drops cases.
  • Paste the output as text where possible. Screenshots can be misread.
  • Keep a results log: output file, date, and the sentence you wrote from it.
  • → NEXT #226 Report p values and CIs the way journals want
201Statistics viva drill for my thesis defence
Master
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident (final year)
Use itIn the weeks before your thesis defence or final viva.
WhyExaminers love statistics questions because most residents can't explain why they used a test. A drill based on your own thesis, one question at a time, with feedback, turns "my statistician did it" into confident answers.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a strict but fair biostatistics examiner on an MD/MS thesis viva panel. You ask questions one at a time, starting simple and escalating, and you give frank feedback after each answer.
My context
Thesis title and design: [paste]
Sample size and how it was calculated: [brief]
Tests used for each objective: [list]
Key results (estimates, CIs, p values): [paste]
Limitations I already know about: [list]
My weakest statistics topics, in my own view: [list]
Task
1. Ask me one statistics question at a time about my own thesis, starting with basics (variable types, why this test) and escalating (assumptions, power, confounding, multiplicity, clinical versus statistical significance).
2. After each of my answers: score it out of 10, give the ideal answer in 3–5 points, and name the gap in my reasoning.
3. Include at least 2 "trap" questions examiners commonly use (e.g. "what does p = 0.04 mean?", "was your study powered for this?").
4. After 12 questions, summarise my weak areas and give a 3-day revision plan targeted at them, with one resource type for each (textbook chapter, video, practice set).
Rules
Ask only one question per turn and wait for my answer, because the value is in answering under pressure. Base questions on my actual thesis details; where you need a detail I have not given, ask for it instead of assuming.
Output
Conversational: one question per turn, feedback in a short structured block, then the summary and plan at the end.
Tweak
Finish with the 5 statistical statements from my thesis I should be able to explain word for word.
How to get more out of it
  • Answer aloud before typing. The viva is spoken, not written.
  • Re-run the drill after revising your weak areas and compare scores.
  • Ask a friend to read the questions to you for a realistic rehearsal.
  • → NEXT #239 Explain any statistics term for the viva
202Sample size to estimate a proportion (prevalence)
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident / MBBS Student
Use itFor descriptive studies estimating a prevalence or proportion with a chosen precision.
Persona
You are a biostatistician who teaches precision-based sample-size calculation.
My context
Expected proportion (with source): [e.g. 30% (Author, year)]
Desired precision: [absolute margin, e.g. ±5%, or relative, e.g. 20% of p]
Confidence level: [95%]
Population size, if finite and small: [N or "large"]
Expected non-response: [e.g. 10%]
Task
1. Give the formula n = Z²·p(1−p)/d² and define each term.
2. Calculate step by step with my inputs, and apply the finite-population correction if relevant.
3. Adjust for non-response and round up.
4. Show how n changes with d = 3%, 5% and 7%.
5. Write the protocol sentence and list the OpenEpi inputs for verification.
Rules
Make clear whether the precision is absolute or relative, because confusing them changes n several-fold. Mark any unsourced input as [VERIFY FROM PUBLISHED SOURCE].
Output
The formula, the working, a small sensitivity table, then the sentence and verification inputs.
Pro tipIf no prior estimate exists, p = 50% gives the maximum (most conservative) sample size. Justify it in the protocol.
Try it withPrevalence of depression in haemodialysis patients, expected 40%, ±7% absolute precision.
→ NEXT #197 Sample size with every assumption shown
203Sample size to compare two means
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident
Use itWhen your primary outcome is continuous and you compare two groups.
Persona
You are a biostatistician who explains power-based sample sizes clearly.
My context
Expected mean and SD in each group (with source): [e.g. 45 ± 10 vs 38 ± 10]
Minimum clinically important difference: [value and why]
Alpha, power and sidedness: [0.05, 80%, two-sided]
Group ratio and dropout: [1:1, 10%]
Task
1. State the formula for comparing two independent means and define each term.
2. Calculate step by step, adjust for dropout and round up.
3. Show the effect of a smaller difference or larger SD in a sensitivity table.
4. Give the G*Power settings to verify.
5. Write the protocol sentence.
Rules
Base the difference on clinical importance, not on what makes the sample small, because committees ask "why this difference?". Mark unsourced SDs as [VERIFY FROM PUBLISHED SOURCE].
Output
Formula, working, sensitivity table, verification settings, sentence.
Pro tipIf you measure the outcome before and after in the same patients, ask for the paired calculation instead. It usually needs fewer patients.
Try it withMean post-operative pain score (VAS) 4.5 ± 1.8 vs 3.5 ± 1.8 with two analgesic regimens.
→ NEXT #197 Sample size with every assumption shown
204Sample size to compare two proportions
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident
Use itWhen your primary outcome is binary and you compare two groups (trial or cohort).
Persona
You are a biostatistician who calculates sample sizes for trials and cohorts.
My context
Expected proportion in each group (with source): [e.g. 30% vs 15%]
Alpha, power and sidedness: [0.05, 80%, two-sided]
Group ratio and dropout: [e.g. 1:1, 10%]
Continuity correction wanted?: [yes / no / unsure]
Task
1. State the formula for two independent proportions and define each term.
2. Calculate step by step, with and without continuity correction if relevant.
3. Adjust for dropout and round up.
4. Show a sensitivity table for smaller differences.
5. Give the OpenEpi or G*Power inputs and the protocol sentence.
Rules
Express the expected difference as both absolute and relative change, because committees look for a clinically meaningful difference. Mark unsourced proportions as [VERIFY FROM PUBLISHED SOURCE].
Output
Formula, working, sensitivity table, verification inputs, sentence.
Pro tipSmall absolute differences in rare outcomes need very large samples. Check feasibility before you commit.
Try it withSurgical-site infection 12% with standard care versus 5% with a new protocol.

205Sample size for a diagnostic accuracy study
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident
Use itWhen your primary objective is the sensitivity and/or specificity of a test.
Persona
You are a diagnostic-research statistician familiar with Buderer's method.
My context
Expected sensitivity and specificity (with source): [e.g. Se 85%, Sp 80%]
Desired precision (half-width of 95% CI): [e.g. ±7%]
Prevalence of the target condition in my study population: [e.g. 30%]
Dropout or indeterminate results: [e.g. 5%]
Task
1. Calculate the number of diseased participants needed for sensitivity and the number of non-diseased needed for specificity.
2. Convert each to a total sample size using the prevalence.
3. Take the larger total, adjust for losses and round up.
4. Explain why prevalence matters so much.
5. Write the protocol sentence and the verification approach.
Rules
Show both calculations, because many theses calculate only for sensitivity and are underpowered for specificity. Mark unsourced inputs as [VERIFY FROM PUBLISHED SOURCE].
Output
Both calculations, the total, the prevalence explanation, then the sentence.
Pro tipIf prevalence in your population is low, consider enriching with known cases, and report it as a limitation.
Try it withLung ultrasound for pneumonia: expected Se 90%, Sp 85%, prevalence 40%, precision ±7%.

206Sample size for a correlation study
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident
Use itWhen your primary objective is a correlation between two continuous variables.
Persona
You are a biostatistician who calculates sample sizes for correlation and agreement studies.
My context
Expected correlation coefficient (with source): [e.g. r = 0.35]
Alpha, power and sidedness: [0.05, 80%, two-sided]
Dropout: [e.g. 10%]
Task
1. Explain the Fisher z-transformation approach in plain language.
2. Calculate the sample size step by step.
3. Adjust for dropout and round up.
4. Show n for r = 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5.
5. Warn if my real question is agreement (e.g. two methods measuring the same thing), which needs a different approach.
Rules
Mark unsourced expected correlations as [VERIFY FROM PUBLISHED SOURCE], because correlation strength drives the sample size dramatically.
Output
Explanation, working, sensitivity table, then the agreement warning if relevant.
Pro tipA statistically significant weak correlation (r = 0.2) is rarely clinically useful. Plan for a meaningful r.
Try it withCorrelation between serum ferritin and HbA1c in type 2 diabetes, expected r = 0.3.

207Sample size for a case-control study
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident
Use itWhen your design compares cases and controls for an exposure.
Persona
You are an epidemiologist who calculates case-control sample sizes, including matched designs.
My context
Expected exposure prevalence in controls (with source): [e.g. 20%]
Odds ratio worth detecting: [e.g. 2.0]
Controls per case: [1 / 2 / 3]
Matched or unmatched: [brief]
Alpha, power: [0.05, 80%]
Task
1. Calculate the number of cases and controls step by step for an unmatched design.
2. Explain how matching and more controls per case change the requirement.
3. Show how n changes for OR = 1.5, 2.0 and 2.5.
4. Give OpenEpi inputs to verify.
5. Write the protocol sentence.
Rules
Explain why going beyond 4 controls per case gives little additional power. Mark unsourced inputs as [VERIFY FROM PUBLISHED SOURCE].
Output
Working, a sensitivity table, verification inputs, then the sentence.
Pro tipIf cases are scarce, adding controls per case is the cheapest way to gain power.

208Is my sample big enough for regression?
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident
Use itWhen you plan a multivariable model and need to know how many variables it can support.
Persona
You are a biostatistician who reviews regression plans for overfitting.
My context
Outcome type and expected number of outcome events (or N for continuous outcomes): [brief]
Candidate predictors, and how many parameters each uses (categorical variables use several): [list]
Purpose: [adjustment / prediction]
Task
1. Count the parameters my candidate list uses.
2. Apply events-per-variable reasoning and explain why the 10-per-variable rule is only a rough guide.
3. Tell me the maximum parameters my study can support.
4. Suggest how to prioritise or combine variables.
5. Mention formal approaches for prediction models, and mark their details [CONFIRM WITH STATISTICIAN].
Rules
Count events, not total patients, for binary and time-to-event outcomes, because that is the most common error in thesis regression plans.

A parameter count table, the calculation, then the recommendations.

209Which statistical test? A decision table
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident / MBBS Student
Use itWhen you are unsure which test fits each objective.
Persona
You are a biostatistics teacher known for clear, correct test-selection advice.
My context
My objectives: [PASTE OBJECTIVES HERE]
For each: outcome variable and type, comparison groups (number, independent or paired), sample size: [brief]
Task
1. For each objective, name the parametric test, the non-parametric alternative, and when to use which.
2. Name the effect measure to report with each test.
3. Name the assumptions to check.
4. Put everything in one decision table.
Rules
Base the parametric versus non-parametric choice on the variable's distribution and sample size, not on a normality test alone, because normality tests are unreliable in small and very large samples.
Output
A decision table (objective, outcome type, groups, test, alternative, effect measure, assumptions).

210Is my data normally distributed? Decide sensibly
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident
Use itBefore choosing between parametric and non-parametric methods.
Persona
You are a biostatistician who teaches sensible distribution checks rather than blind reliance on normality tests.
My context
Variable and what it measures: [brief]
Sample size per group: [n]
Summary statistics (mean, SD, median, IQR, min, max): [paste]
Histogram or Q-Q plot description, or the Shapiro-Wilk result: [paste]
Task
1. Assess the distribution from the summaries (e.g. SD large relative to the mean for a positive-only variable suggests skew) and the plot.
2. Explain what the normality test does and does not tell me at my sample size.
3. Recommend how to summarise the variable (mean ± SD or median with IQR) and which test family to use.
4. Mention transformation (e.g. log) as an option, with its trade-offs.
Rules
Combine clinical knowledge of the variable with the data, because a normality test alone is underpowered in small samples and oversensitive in large ones.
Output
The assessment, the explanation, the recommendation, then the transformation note.
Pro tipHospital-stay length, CRP and most lab counts are usually skewed. Expect medians.

211Choose and report the right non-parametric test
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident
Use itWhen your data is skewed or ordinal and parametric tests don't fit.
Persona
You are a biostatistician who explains non-parametric methods in plain language.
My context
Outcome and its type: [skewed continuous / ordinal]
Groups and whether independent or paired: [brief]
Sample sizes: [n per group]
Task
1. Name the right test (Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Kruskal-Wallis, Friedman) and why.
2. Explain what it actually tests in plain language.
3. Tell me which summary and effect measure to report (median, IQR, Hodges-Lehmann estimate or rank-biserial correlation).
4. Give the post-hoc approach if there are more than 2 groups.
5. Show the reporting sentence template.
Rules
Avoid saying the test compares medians unless the distributions have similar shapes, because that is a common reporting error.
Output
The test choice, explanation, reporting guidance, then the template.
Pro tipReport the median and IQR per group alongside the p value. A p value alone tells readers nothing about the size of the difference.

212Chi-square, Fisher's exact or something else?
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident / MBBS Student

Persona
You are a biostatistics tutor who explains categorical-data tests precisely.
My context
Variables and categories: [brief]
Table layout and cell counts (paste the cross-table if you have it): [PASTE TABLE]
Are the groups independent or paired?: [brief]
Task
1. Decide between chi-square, chi-square with continuity correction, Fisher's exact, chi-square for trend and McNemar, based on my table and design.
2. Explain the expected-count rule and check it on my table.
3. Name the effect measure to report (risk difference, relative risk or odds ratio with 95% CI).
4. Show the reporting sentence template.

Base the expected-count check on expected, not observed, counts, because that distinction is commonly confused.

The decision, the expected-count check, the effect measure, then the template.

213Before-after or matched data: paired analysis

1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident

You are a biostatistician who catches residents analysing paired data as independent groups.
My context
What is measured and when: [brief]
Outcome type: [continuous / binary / ordinal]
Sample size: [n pairs]
Task
1. Confirm whether the data is truly paired, and why that matters.
2. Name the test: paired t-test, Wilcoxon signed-rank or McNemar.
3. Name the effect measure: mean difference with 95% CI, median difference, or discordant-pair odds ratio.
4. Explain the assumption checks (e.g. distribution of the differences).

214Outcomes measured three or more times
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident

Persona

My context
Outcome and time points: [brief]
Groups (if comparing): [brief]
Sample size and missing follow-ups: [brief]
Software: [SPSS / R / Jamovi]
Task
1. Explain why running separate t-tests at each time point is wrong.
2. Compare repeated-measures ANOVA, a linear mixed model and the Friedman test for my data.
3. Recommend one, with its assumptions and how it handles missing time points.
4. Give the software steps or syntax.
5. Show how to present the results (a line graph with error bars, and a table).

Recommend a mixed model if follow-ups are missing, and explain why, because repeated-measures ANOVA drops every patient with any missing time point.

215Correlation or agreement? Methods comparison done right
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident
Use itWhen comparing two methods of measuring the same thing, or relating two variables.
Persona
You are a measurement statistician who explains why correlation is not agreement.
My context
The two measurements and what they measure: [brief]
Purpose: [do they agree? / are they related?]
Sample size: [n]
Task
1. Tell me whether my question is about association (correlation) or agreement (interchangeability).
2. For association: choose Pearson or Spearman and explain why.
3. For agreement: explain the Bland-Altman analysis (bias, limits of agreement) and ICC, and when to use each.
4. Define in advance what limits of agreement would be clinically acceptable.

216ROC curve, AUC and the best cut-off
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident
Use itWhen your study evaluates a continuous marker or score for diagnosis or prognosis.
Persona
You are a diagnostic statistician who explains ROC analysis honestly, including its limits.
My context
Marker or score: [brief]
Outcome (reference standard): [brief]
Sample size and number with the outcome: [brief]
Software: [SPSS / MedCalc / R / Jamovi]
Task
1. Explain what the ROC curve and AUC represent in plain language.

5. Show the reporting template.
Rules
Report the AUC with its 95% CI, and call a data-derived cut-off exploratory unless it is validated, because optimistic cut-offs are a common reviewer criticism.
Output
Explanation, steps, cut-off guidance, then the template.
Pro tipCompare your marker's AUC with an existing score's AUC in the same patients. It makes the result meaningful.
Try it withSerum lactate for predicting 28-day mortality in sepsis.

217Time-to-event analysis: Kaplan-Meier and Cox
Standard
1.7 Sample size & statistics · PG Resident

You are a biostatistician who teaches survival analysis to clinicians clearly.
My context
Event and time origin: [brief]
Follow-up duration and how censoring occurs: [brief]
Groups and covariates: [brief]
Number of events: [n]
Software: [SPSS / R / Stata]
Task
1. Define time zero, the event and censoring for my study.
2. Explain Kaplan-Meier curves and the log-rank test for group comparison.
3. Explain the Cox model, the hazard ratio, and the proportional-hazards check.
4. Say how many covariates my events can support.
5. Give software steps and a reporting template (median survival, HR with 95% CI, number at risk under the curve).
Rules
Warn me if informative censoring is likely (e.g. sicker patients lost to follow-up), because it biases survival estimates.

My context

Why values are missing, as far as I know: [brief]
Sample size: [N]

1. Classify the likely mechanism for each variable (MCAR, MAR or MNAR) in plain language.
2. Recommend an approach for each: complete-case analysis, multiple imputation or sensitivity analysis.

4. Warn against single mean imputation and last observation carried forward.
5. Give software steps if imputation is needed.
Rules
Recommend reporting missingness transparently even when it is small, because silent exclusion is an examiner favourite.

226Report p values and CIs the way journals want

Section 1.8
1.8

Results, tables & figures

Results report what you found, in past tense, with no interpretation. Every number must match the output, and every table must earn its place.

25prompts
3Master
14Standard
8Quick
How to use this section

Use it after analysis, to turn software output into clean tables, figures and past-tense results.

Start with the Master prompts (#241–243) for the full workflow; use the Standard prompts (#244–257) for one task at a time; reach for the Quick prompts (#258–265) when you have two minutes. Tap any title below to jump to it, and follow → NEXT to move to the next step.

  1. #241Write the Results chapter from my analysis output

  6. #246Report secondary outcomes without clutter

  9. #249Build the chart step by step in my software
  10. #250Format my table to journal standard
  11. #251Titles, legends and footnotes for my tables and figures
  12. #252Remove interpretation from my results
  13. #253Stop repeating my tables in the text
  14. #254Report a non-significant result honestly
  15. #255Report diagnostic accuracy results (STARD)
  16. #256Present regression results clearly

241Write the Results chapter from my analysis output
Master
1.8 Results, tables & figures · PG Resident
Use itAfter your analysis is complete and verified, before writing the discussion.
WhyThe results chapter is where transcription errors, interpretation creep and text that repeats the tables creep in. Writing it from your verified numbers in a fixed order (flow, baseline, primary, secondary) keeps it accurate, readable and defensible.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a medical journal editor who writes and edits results sections. You report findings in past tense, in a logical order, with effect estimates and confidence intervals, and you never interpret in the results.
My context
Design and reporting guideline: [e.g. prospective cohort, STROBE]
Participant flow numbers (screened, eligible, enrolled, lost, analysed): [numbers]
Table 1 baseline characteristics (paste the table): [PASTE TABLE]
Primary outcome result with effect estimate, 95% CI and p: [paste exactly]
Secondary outcome results: [paste exactly]
Tables and figures I have, with numbers and titles: [list]
Target length: [e.g. 800–1,200 words for a thesis; 500–700 for a journal]
Task
1. Open with participant flow, referring to the flow diagram.
2. Describe baseline characteristics briefly, highlighting only clinically important features and referring to Table 1.
3. Report the primary outcome with its effect estimate, 95% CI and exact p value.
4. Report secondary outcomes in the order of the objectives.
5. Report any pre-specified subgroup or sensitivity analyses, labelled as such.
6. Refer to each table and figure at the right point, and highlight rather than repeat their contents.
7. After the draft, list every number used with its source (table or output), for cross-checking.
Rules
Use only the numbers I pasted, reproduced exactly, because a single mistyped number undermines the credibility of the whole chapter. No interpretation, no comparison with literature and no causal words. Report non-significant results with their estimates and CIs, never as "no effect". Qualify "significant" as statistically significant.
Output
The results text with sub-headings by objective, then the number-source table.
Tweak
End with the 3 results an examiner will look at first, and whether my text presents each one clearly.
How to get more out of it
  • Write results before the discussion. It stops you writing results to fit your story.
  • Check every number in the text against its table. Mismatches are the commonest results error.
  • If the text simply repeats a table, cut the text to the key finding and refer to the table.
  • → NEXT #243 Consistency audit: text, tables, figures and abstract
242Plan every table and figure in my results
Master
1.8 Results, tables & figures · PG Resident
Use itAfter analysis and before writing, to decide how your results will be displayed.
WhyExaminers and reviewers read tables and figures first. A planned set, where each item answers an objective and nothing is duplicated, makes results easy to follow. A random pile of SPSS outputs and pie charts makes them hard work.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a scientific data-visualisation editor for a medical journal. You match each result to the display that shows it most honestly and clearly, and you follow journal conventions for tables and figures.
My context
Objectives: [PASTE OBJECTIVES]
Results for each objective (brief, with the variable types): [PASTE SUMMARY]
Number of tables and figures allowed (thesis or journal): [e.g. no limit / 4 tables + 2 figures]
Software I'll use for figures: [Excel / GraphPad / R / SPSS]
My university's or journal's figure requirements, if any: [e.g. 300 dpi, greyscale, maximum width]
Task
1. Propose the complete set: which results go in tables, which in figures, and which only in text.
2. For each table: title, rows, columns, summary format, footnotes and abbreviations.
3. For each figure: chart type and why (bar with error bars, box plot, forest plot, Kaplan-Meier, ROC, scatter with fit line, flow diagram), axes, units, labels and legend.
4. Flag displays to avoid for my data (pie charts, 3D charts, dynamite plots for skewed data, dual axes).
5. Give step-by-step instructions to create each figure in my software.
6. Number everything in order of mention in the text.
7. Say which displays could go in an appendix instead of the main chapter.
Rules
Choose displays that show the distribution or uncertainty (CIs, IQRs) rather than hiding it, because misleading displays are a frequent examiner criticism. Use placeholders instead of values.
Output
A display plan table (number, type, objective served, content), then table templates, figure specifications, the "avoid" list and the software steps.
Tweak
End with the single figure that best tells the story of my thesis, and why.
How to get more out of it
  • One figure that shows your primary result clearly is worth more than ten decorative charts.
  • Keep fonts, colours and decimal places consistent across all tables and figures.
  • Make every table understandable on its own, with a full title and footnotes.
  • → NEXT #249 Build the chart step by step in my software
243Consistency audit: text, tables, figures and abstract
Master
1.8 Results, tables & figures · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen the thesis or manuscript is drafted, before submission.
WhyInconsistent numbers between the abstract, text, tables and figures are among the most common reasons reviewers lose trust in a paper, and examiners spot them fast. A systematic audit catches them all at once.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a meticulous statistical reviewer for a medical journal who cross-checks every number in a manuscript for consistency and plausibility.
My context
Abstract: [PASTE ABSTRACT]
Results text: [PASTE RESULTS TEXT]
Tables (as text): [PASTE TABLES]
Figure legends and any numbers shown in figures: [PASTE LEGENDS]
Total N and group sizes: [numbers]
Missing data per key variable: [brief]
Version of the document and date: [e.g. draft 3, 12 May]
Task
1. Extract every number from each section and match it across sections.
2. Flag any number that differs between sections.
3. Check internal arithmetic: percentages match their numerators and denominators, subgroup counts sum to totals, means lie within their ranges, and CIs contain their point estimates.
4. Check that p values are consistent with the CIs (a 95% CI excluding the null should go with p < 0.05).
5. Check that the denominators change sensibly where there is missing data, and that the missing data is reported somewhere.
6. Check that every table and figure is cited in the text, in order.
7. Check that the abstract's conclusion matches the primary result as reported in the results text.
Rules
Report discrepancies without deciding which value is right, because only the original source output can settle that. Do not alter any numbers yourself.
Output
A discrepancy table (number, location A, location B, issue), then the arithmetic and consistency check results, then the citation-order check and the abstract check.
Tweak
Finish with the 3 discrepancies most likely to be noticed by an examiner or reviewer, to fix first.
How to get more out of it
  • Fix discrepancies from the original output, never by adjusting the text to match a table.
  • Re-run this audit after every major revision. New inconsistencies appear with each edit.
  • Ask a colleague to check 10 random numbers against the raw output as an independent check.
  • → NEXT #241 Write the Results chapter from my analysis output
244Describe Table 1 in two short paragraphs
Standard
1.8 Results, tables & figures · PG Resident
Use itWhen writing the baseline characteristics paragraph of your results.
Persona
You are a journal editor who keeps baseline descriptions short and informative.
My context
Table 1 (paste as text): [PASTE TABLE]
Design (randomised or observational): [brief]
Groups: [brief]
Target: [thesis / journal]
Task
1. Write 2 short paragraphs describing the study population: key demographics, key clinical features, and notable differences between groups.
2. Highlight only clinically important features, not every row.
3. For an RCT, describe balance without p values; for observational studies, note the differences that may confound results.
Rules
Reproduce numbers exactly and refer to Table 1 rather than repeating it, because text that repeats a table wastes the reader's time.
Output
The two paragraphs.
Pro tipReaders use Table 1 to judge whether your results apply to their patients. Make the setting and severity clear.
Try it withTable 1 of a 200-patient sepsis cohort comparing survivors and non-survivors.

245Report the primary outcome properly
Standard
1.8 Results, tables & figures · PG Resident
Use itFor the most important paragraph of your results.
Persona

My context

Task
1. Write the primary-outcome paragraph: summaries in each group, the effect estimate with 95% CI and p value, and the adjusted estimate if applicable.
2. Refer to the relevant table or figure.

Rules
Report the estimate and CI before the p value, and use past tense without interpretation, because readers need the size and precision of the effect, not just significance.

Pro tipGive absolute numbers as well as relative measures, e.g. "18/100 vs 30/100 (RR 0.60, 95% CI …)".

246Report secondary outcomes without clutter
Standard
1.8 Results, tables & figures · PG Resident
Use itWhen you have several secondary outcomes to report.
Persona
You are an editor who reports multiple outcomes clearly and briefly.
My context
Secondary objectives: [list]
Results for each (estimates, CIs, p values): [PASTE RESULTS]
Table where they are shown: [e.g. Table 3]
Which analyses were pre-specified and which were added later: [brief]
Task
1. Report each secondary outcome in the order of the objectives, in 1–2 sentences each.
2. Group related outcomes where sensible.
3. Refer to the table rather than repeating every number.
4. Label exploratory analyses clearly, and keep them after the pre-specified ones.
Rules
Report non-significant secondary outcomes as fully as significant ones, because selective reporting is a form of bias that examiners recognise.
Output
The paragraphs.
Pro tipIf a secondary outcome surprised you, report it plainly here. The interpretation belongs in the discussion.
Try it withSecondary outcomes: ICU stay, ventilator days, AKI incidence, and 90-day mortality.

Section 1.9
1.9

Discussion, conclusion & limitations

The discussion is where good data gets ruined by overclaiming, and it is the only section where your scientific judgement is visible. Structure it deliberately.

How to use this section

Use it with your final results and key papers in hand, to write a discussion that doesn't overclaim.

266Write the discussion: ten paragraphs, no overclaiming
Master
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itAfter results are final. This is the section examiners and reviewers read most closely.
WhyThe discussion is where good data gets ruined by overclaiming, and it is the only section where your scientific judgement is visible. A fixed structure (answer, compare, explain, implications, strengths, limitations, future, conclusion) keeps it honest and complete.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a journal editor and senior academic who has written and revised hundreds of discussion sections and rejected many more. You are ruthless about over-interpretation, unsupported causal language, and limitation sections that hide the real weaknesses.
My context
Design: [state] · Sample size: [state]
Primary objective: [state]
Primary result with effect estimate and CI: [paste exactly as computed]
Secondary results: [paste, with numbers]
Findings that surprised me or contradicted my hypothesis: [state]
Findings that were not significant: [state]
Known limitations: [list]
Setting: [Indian tertiary / rural / private, etc.] · Target: [thesis / journal name]
I have uploaded the [N] most relevant published papers. Use only these, plus anything you retrieve through live search with a verifiable PMID or DOI.
Task
Draft a discussion of about [800–1,200] words:
1. Paragraph 1: answer the research question in 1–3 sentences with the principal finding and its numbers. No literature.
2. Paragraphs 2–4: for each key comparison, state what the prior study found, whether mine agrees or differs, and the likely reason (population, setting, definitions, measurement, sample size, follow-up). End every comparison with an interpretive sentence.
3. Paragraph 5: the most plausible mechanism, marked clearly where speculative.
4. Paragraph 6: clinical implications: who could act on this and how; say plainly if it is not yet practice-changing.
5. Paragraph 7: strengths, without inflation.
6. Paragraph 8: limitations in order of threat to the conclusion, each with the likely direction of bias.
7. Paragraph 9: specific, doable future research, not "further studies are needed".
8. Paragraph 10: a 2–3 sentence conclusion that does not exceed the data.
Rules
Use associational language unless my design is randomised; "caused", "led to", "resulted in" and "prevented" are banned otherwise, because causal overreach is the most common reviewer criticism. Qualify every "significant" as statistical or clinical. Never call a non-significant result a "trend". Where a comparison needs a source I have not supplied, write [CITATION NEEDED — FIND SOURCE]. Introduce no result that is not in my results section.
Output
The discussion in paragraphs with no sub-headings unless my target requires them, within the word range.
Tweak
Then list separately the three sentences a hostile reviewer would attack first, and how to rewrite each one defensively.
How to get more out of it
  • Give the model your actual numbers. A discussion written around vague findings reads exactly as vague as it was written.
  • The hostile-reviewer list is worth more than the draft. Act on it before submission.
  • If the draft sounds more confident than you feel about your own data, the draft is wrong, not your instinct.
  • → NEXT #267 Limitations that are honest, ranked and specific
267Limitations that are honest, ranked and specific
Master
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itWhen writing the limitations paragraph, and before your viva.
WhyExaminers judge your scientific maturity by your limitations. A generic list ("small sample, single centre") signals you didn't think. Limitations ranked by threat, each with the direction of bias and what you did to reduce it, signal that you did.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a clinical epidemiologist and journal reviewer who evaluates limitation sections for honesty and insight. You expect each limitation to state how it could have changed the result.
My context
Design and setting: [paste]
How participants were selected and how many declined or were lost: [brief with numbers]
How the exposure and outcome were measured, and by whom: [brief]
Confounders measured and not measured: [lists]
Sample size, and whether the study was powered for each reported outcome: [brief]
Primary result: [estimate with CI]
Limitations I have thought of: [list]
Task
1. Identify all important limitations under selection, information (measurement), confounding, sample size or precision, and generalisability.
2. Rank them by how much they threaten my main conclusion.
3. For each, state the likely direction of bias (towards or away from the null, or unpredictable) and whether it could explain my result entirely.
4. For each, state what I did in the design or analysis to reduce it, if anything.
5. Write the limitations paragraph (180–250 words) in ranked order, honest but not self-defeating.
6. Separately, list 2 limitations I should acknowledge in the viva even if they are not in the thesis text.
Rules
Be specific to my study, because generic limitations suggest you haven't understood your own design. Don't invent limitations my design doesn't have, and don't hide real ones behind softer wording. Keep numbers exactly as I gave them.
Output
A ranked limitation table (limitation, type, direction of bias, mitigation, impact), then the paragraph, then the viva list.
Tweak
End with a one-line statement of how confident a reader should be in my primary conclusion, given these limitations.
How to get more out of it
  • Start with the limitation that matters most, not the most comfortable one.
  • "Single-centre" is only a limitation if you explain why your centre might differ from others.
  • Pair each limitation with what the next study should do differently. It leads naturally into future research.
  • → NEXT #268 Hostile-reviewer attack on my discussion
268Hostile-reviewer attack on my discussion
Master
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen your discussion is drafted, before your guide or a journal sees it.
WhyThe kindest thing you can do for your discussion is let someone attack it first. A structured hostile review finds overclaims, missing comparisons and weak logic, and it hands you defensive rewrites you can use on paper and at the viva.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are Reviewer 2: a senior, sceptical peer reviewer for a high-impact clinical journal. You are fair but relentless, and you target over-interpretation, selective comparisons and conclusions that outrun the data.
My context
Design, sample size and primary result: [brief with numbers]
Target: [thesis / journal name and its readership]
My results section: [PASTE RESULTS]
My discussion: [PASTE DISCUSSION]
Task
1. Write a reviewer report on the discussion with major comments (threats to validity or interpretation) and minor comments (wording, clarity, missing references), each quoting the text it refers to.
2. Identify every sentence that claims more than the results show, and every causal claim unsupported by the design.
3. Identify comparisons with literature that seem selective, where only agreeing studies are cited, and say what kind of study is missing.
4. Identify results reported in the discussion that do not appear in the results.
5. Identify important limitations the discussion leaves out or understates.
6. For each major comment, write a defensive rewrite of the relevant text and a one-line response I could use in a reply to reviewers or at the viva.
Rules
Quote the exact text for every criticism, because unquoted criticism cannot be acted on. Rewrites must not add new data or references; use [CITE] slots where a reference is needed. Keep my numbers unchanged.
Output
The reviewer report (major, then minor), then a table (quoted sentence, problem, rewrite, one-line response).
Tweak
End with an overall verdict (accept, minor revision, major revision) with the single change that would most improve the discussion.
How to get more out of it
  • Run this before your guide reads the draft. Their time is better spent on judgement than on catching overclaims.
  • Keep the responses. They are ready-made answers for viva questions about your interpretation.
  • Run it again after revising. The major comments should turn into minor ones.
  • → NEXT #278 Scan my discussion for overclaiming
269Conclusion, recommendations and summary chapter
Master
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itFor the final chapters of your thesis: summary, conclusion and recommendations.
WhyMany Indian theses end with separate summary, conclusion and recommendations chapters, and examiners read them first when time is short. They must match the objectives exactly and claim no more than the data shows.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a senior examiner for MD/MS theses who reads the summary and conclusion first to judge whether the student understood their study. You insist that every conclusion maps to an objective and every recommendation is proportionate to the evidence.
My context
Thesis title: [paste]
Objectives (numbered): [PASTE OBJECTIVES]
Key results for each objective (with numbers): [PASTE RESULTS]
Main limitations: [list]
My university's required end chapters and word limits: [e.g. Summary 500 words, Conclusion, Recommendations]
Design and setting: [brief]
Task
1. Write the summary chapter: background (2 lines), aims, methods (design, setting, sample, key measurements), key results by objective with numbers, and the conclusion, within the word limit.
2. Write the conclusion: one numbered statement per objective, each answering it directly and in associational terms where appropriate.
3. Write recommendations in 3 groups: for clinical practice (only if justified), for the department or health system, and for future research, each specific and feasible.
4. Build a check table showing each objective, its conclusion statement and the result that supports it.
5. Flag any result that is important but not captured by any conclusion.
Rules
Every conclusion must answer an objective using a result I gave, because conclusions without matching results are a classic examiner criticism. Recommendations for practice must be proportionate: a single-centre observational study can suggest or support, not establish. Keep numbers exactly as supplied.
Output
The summary, the numbered conclusions, the grouped recommendations, then the check table.
Tweak
End with the one conclusion statement most likely to be challenged at the viva, and a safer wording for it.
How to get more out of it
  • Read your conclusion and your objectives side by side. They should mirror each other.
  • Future-research recommendations should name the design, population and outcome.
  • Keep the summary free of any number that doesn't appear in your results chapter.
  • → NEXT #283 The "Summary" chapter of an Indian thesis
270The first paragraph of the discussion
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itTo open your discussion.
Persona
You are a journal editor who wants the discussion to open with the answer, not with background.
My context
Primary objective: [paste]
Primary result with numbers: [paste]
Most important secondary result: [paste]
Design: [brief]
Task
1. Write the opening paragraph (60–100 words) stating the answer to the research question with the key numbers.
2. Add one sentence on the most important secondary finding.
3. Give an alternative version for a journal article of 50 words or fewer.
Rules
No literature, no background and no interpretation in this paragraph, and use associational language for observational designs, because the first sentence is read as your main claim.
Output
The two versions.
Pro tipIf you can't state your main finding in one sentence, your results section needs work first.
Try it withPrimary: in-hospital mortality 18% vs 27% between early and late mobilisation groups (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.45–0.99).

271Compare one finding with the literature
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itFor each key comparison paragraph in your discussion.
Persona
You are a clinical academic who writes comparison paragraphs that interpret rather than list.
My context
My finding with numbers: [paste]
Comparable studies I have read, with design, setting, population and result: [PASTE DETAILS OR UPLOAD PAPERS]
Task
1. Compare my finding with each study: agree, partly agree or differ.
2. For differences, give the most likely explanations (population, setting, definitions, measurement, timing, sample size).
3. Write a paragraph of 120–180 words that compares and interprets, ending with what the comparison means.
Rules
Use only the studies I supplied, citing each with its reference number, because comparisons with unseen or invented studies are academic misconduct. Present disagreeing studies too, not only supporting ones.
Output
A comparison table, then the paragraph.
Pro tipOne paragraph per key finding is a good discipline. Don't mix three findings in one paragraph.
Try it withMy finding: prevalence of sarcopenia 38% in COPD; three studies reported 15%, 25% and 40%.

272Why my result differs from previous studies
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itWhen your result disagrees with published findings and you must explain it.
Persona
You are an epidemiologist skilled at explaining discrepancies between studies without special pleading.
My context
My study: design, population, setting, definitions, sample size and result: [brief]
The study or studies I differ from, with the same details: [brief]
Task
1. Compare the studies systematically on each methodological dimension.
2. Rank the plausible explanations for the difference.
3. Consider chance (sample size, CI overlap) explicitly.
4. Write a discussion paragraph presenting the difference and the most likely explanations, without dismissing either result.
Rules
Don't claim my study is "better" without a specific methodological reason, and consider that my own study might be the outlier, because examiners respect balanced reasoning.
Output
The comparison table, the ranked explanations, then the paragraph.
Pro tipOverlapping confidence intervals often mean the "difference" isn't really a difference. Check that first.
Try it withMy study found no association between vitamin D and TB outcome; two earlier studies found one.
→ NEXT #271 Compare one finding with the literature
273The mechanism paragraph, clearly labelled as speculation
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itWhen your discussion needs a biological or clinical explanation for your finding.
Persona
You are a clinician-scientist who explains mechanisms carefully and labels speculation clearly.
My context
My finding: [paste]
Relevant physiology or mechanisms I know of, with sources: [PASTE NOTES WITH CITATIONS]
Task
1. Suggest the 2–3 most plausible mechanisms for my finding.
2. For each, say how strong the supporting evidence is (established, plausible, speculative).
3. Write a paragraph of 100–150 words presenting them with hedged language.
4. Suggest what study could test the leading mechanism.
Rules
Mark every mechanistic claim needing support as [CITE], and phrase speculation as speculation ("may", "could", "one possible explanation"), because mechanisms presented as fact are a common overreach.
Output
The mechanism list with evidence strength, then the paragraph, then the testing suggestion.
Pro tipKeep this paragraph short. Examiners value an honest "the mechanism is unclear" over a confident guess.
Try it withFinding: low serum magnesium associated with higher ICU mortality.
→ NEXT #274 Clinical implications without overreach
274Clinical implications without overreach
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itFor the implications paragraph of your discussion.
Persona
You are a guideline-panel member who judges how far a single study can change practice.
My context
Main findings: [paste]
Design, sample size and setting: [brief]
Who could use the findings (clinicians, administrators, programmes): [list]
Task
1. State what the findings could mean for practice, and for whom.
2. Distinguish what can be acted on now, what needs confirmation, and what is hypothesis-generating.
3. Write the implications paragraph (100–150 words).
4. Flag any implication that overreaches the design.
Rules
Use proportionate verbs (suggests, supports, may inform) for single-centre observational results, because "should be adopted" claims are rarely justified by one study.
Output
The three-level classification, the paragraph, then the overreach flags.
Pro tipName the specific clinical decision your findings touch, e.g. "whether to repeat lactate at 6 hours".
Try it withFinding: a bedside frailty score predicted post-operative delirium in elderly surgical patients.
→ NEXT #275 Strengths without inflation
275Strengths without inflation
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itFor the strengths paragraph of your discussion.
Persona
You are a sceptical reviewer who dislikes inflated strength statements.
My context
Design features: [e.g. prospective, consecutive recruitment, blinded outcome assessment, validated tools, low loss to follow-up]
Anything unique about my setting or population: [brief]
Task
1. Identify genuine methodological strengths and explain why each matters for validity.
2. Remove claims that are not real strengths (e.g. "first study in India" unless verified, or "large sample" when it isn't).
3. Write the strengths paragraph (80–120 words).
Rules
Tie each strength to a bias it reduces, because a strength without a reason is just a claim. Do not claim novelty unless I confirm it has been checked; write [VERIFY NOVELTY] instead.
Output
A strengths table (feature, bias reduced), the removed claims, then the paragraph.
Pro tip"Prospective, consecutive recruitment with complete follow-up" is a real strength. Say it plainly.
Try it withA prospective cohort of 180 patients with 97% follow-up and blinded outcome assessment.
→ NEXT #267 Limitations that are honest, ranked and specific
276Future research that someone could actually do
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itInstead of writing "further studies are needed".
Persona
You are a research funder who only backs specific, feasible next studies.
My context
My findings and limitations: [brief]
Open questions my study raised: [list]
My setting and the resources a follow-up study could realistically use: [brief]
Task
1. Propose 3–4 specific future studies, each with design, population, setting, outcome and why it follows from my findings.
2. Rank them by importance and feasibility, and say which one could be a thesis for a junior resident in my department.
3. Write the future-research paragraph (80–120 words).
Rules
Make each proposal specific enough to become someone's thesis topic, because vague calls for research add nothing.
Output
A proposal table, then the paragraph.
Pro tipLink each future study to one of your limitations. It shows you understand what your study couldn't answer.
Try it withMy cross-sectional study found an association between sleep apnoea and poor asthma control.
→ NEXT #277 A conclusion that doesn't exceed the data
277A conclusion that doesn't exceed the data
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itFor the final paragraph of your discussion or abstract.
Persona
You are a journal editor who rewrites overreaching conclusions every day.
My context
Primary objective: [paste]
Primary result: [paste]
Design and setting: [brief]
My current conclusion: [paste]
Target: [thesis / journal abstract / poster]
Task
1. Check my conclusion against the result and design, and list every overreach.
2. Rewrite it in 2–3 sentences: what was found, in whom, and what it suggests.
3. Write a one-sentence version for the abstract.
Rules
Match the strength of language to the design and precision of the result, because the conclusion is the most-quoted sentence of any study.
Output
The overreach list, the rewritten conclusion, then the abstract sentence.
Pro tipYour conclusion should answer your primary objective in the same words the objective used.
Try it withCurrent: "Early antibiotics save lives in sepsis." Design: retrospective cohort.
→ NEXT #269 Conclusion, recommendations and summary chapter
278Scan my discussion for overclaiming
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itAs a final check on any discussion or conclusion.
Persona
You are a research-integrity editor who scans manuscripts for spin.
My context
My design: [design]
My primary result: [estimate, CI, p]
My discussion text: [PASTE DISCUSSION]
Task
1. Flag causal language used with an observational design.
2. Flag spin: "trend towards", "marginally significant", emphasis on secondary results over a null primary result, and extrapolation beyond the population.
3. Flag unqualified "significant".
4. Give a corrected version of each flagged sentence.
Rules
Keep the meaning where it is justified and change only the overreaching wording, because the goal is accuracy, not timidity.
Output
A table (sentence, type of spin, corrected sentence), then a count by type.
Pro tipSearch your text for "caus", "effect", "impact", "prevent", "led to", "due to". Most overclaims hide there.
Try it withA discussion claiming a supplement "improved outcomes" based on a before-after study.
→ NEXT #268 Hostile-reviewer attack on my discussion
279Who do my results apply to?
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itFor the generalisability part of your limitations or implications.
Persona
You are an epidemiologist who thinks carefully about external validity.
My context
Setting and how patients reached my hospital: [brief]
Population characteristics (severity, age, comorbidity, socio-economic profile): [brief]
Exclusions: [list]
Proportion of screened patients who were enrolled: [numbers]
Task
1. Describe the population my results apply to most directly.
2. Identify populations to whom they may not apply, and why.
3. Discuss referral bias for a tertiary centre, if relevant, and the likely direction of its effect on my estimates.
4. Write a generalisability paragraph (80–120 words).
Rules
Base the assessment on my actual setting and exclusions, because generic statements about "single-centre studies" add nothing.
Output
Headed notes, then the paragraph.
Pro tipTertiary-centre patients are usually sicker. Say whether that makes your estimates higher or lower than in district practice.
Try it withICU cohort at a referral hospital receiving transfers from 6 districts.
→ NEXT #267 Limitations that are honest, ranked and specific
280Discuss a surprising result
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itWhen a result contradicts your hypothesis or expectations.
Persona
You are a thoughtful senior researcher who treats surprising results as information, not embarrassment.
My context
What I expected, and why: [brief]
What I found, with numbers: [paste]
Possible issues with my data or methods: [brief]
Task
1. List the explanations in order: chance, bias, confounding, measurement error, and a genuine effect.
2. Evaluate each against my study details.
3. Suggest a check I can still run (e.g. a sensitivity analysis) if appropriate.
4. Write a paragraph (100–150 words) presenting the finding honestly.
Rules
Don't explain away the finding, and don't overstate it, because examiners respect a balanced treatment of surprises.
Output
The explanations table, the check, then the paragraph.
Pro tipSurprising findings often make the best future-research questions. Say so.
Try it withExpected obesity to worsen ARDS outcomes; found lower mortality in obese patients.
→ NEXT #266 Write the discussion: ten paragraphs, no overclaiming
281Discuss a non-significant primary result
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itWhen your primary outcome was not statistically significant.
Persona
You are a statistician-editor who helps authors write honest, publishable null-result discussions.
My context
Primary result (estimate, 95% CI, p): [paste]
Sample size and whether it met the calculated target: [brief]
Expected effect used for the sample size: [brief]
Task
1. Interpret the CI: what effect sizes are ruled out, and what remain plausible.
2. Discuss power: whether the study could have detected a clinically important effect.
3. Compare with the literature honestly.
4. Write the opening paragraph of the discussion for this result.
Rules
Don't call the result a trend or imply a hidden effect, and don't call it proof of no effect, because both misrepresent a null result.
Output
The CI interpretation, the power note, then the paragraph.
Pro tip"Our study was unable to demonstrate…" is better than "there was no difference".
Try it withRR 0.85 (95% CI 0.62–1.17), p = 0.32, sample of 180 against a target of 200.
→ NEXT #266 Write the discussion: ten paragraphs, no overclaiming
282Check the structure of my discussion
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itWhen your discussion is drafted and feels disorganised.
Persona
You are a thesis-writing coach who maps discussions against a standard structure.
My context
My discussion: [PASTE DISCUSSION]
My primary result: [paste]
Target structure, if my guide or journal prescribes one: [brief]
Task
1. Map each paragraph to a structural element: principal findings, comparison, explanation, mechanism, implications, strengths, limitations, future research or conclusion.
2. Identify missing, repeated or misplaced elements.
3. Suggest a reordering.
4. Check that the first paragraph states the principal finding and the last states a proportionate conclusion.
Rules
Suggest structural changes only, keeping my text as it is, because the content and voice must remain mine.
Output
A paragraph map table, the problems, then the suggested order.
Pro tipIf your discussion opens with background, move it. The first paragraph must answer the question.
Try it withA discussion that opens with 2 paragraphs of epidemiology before mentioning the results.
→ NEXT #266 Write the discussion: ten paragraphs, no overclaiming
283The "Summary" chapter of an Indian thesis
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itWhen your university requires a separate summary chapter.
Persona
You are an MD/MS thesis examiner who reads the summary first.
My context
Title and objectives: [paste]
Methods in brief: [paste]
Key results by objective, with numbers: [paste]
Conclusion: [paste]
Word or page limit: [e.g. 500 words]
Task
1. Write the summary within the limit, with short paragraphs for background, aims, methods, results and conclusion.
2. Keep results in the order of the objectives, with the key numbers.
3. Check that every number appears in my results chapter.
Rules
Add no information that isn't elsewhere in the thesis, because the summary must be a faithful miniature of it.

The summary with its word count, then the number check.
Pro tipWrite the summary last and read it aloud. If it doesn't flow, your thesis argument doesn't either.

284What my findings mean for Indian practice
Standard

Use itFor a paragraph relating your results to Indian clinical practice, programmes or policy.
Persona
You are a public-health physician familiar with Indian health programmes and resource settings.
My context
My findings: [brief]
Relevant national programmes, guidelines or practices I know of: [list with sources]
Resource context of typical Indian hospitals for this condition: [brief]
Task
1. Relate the findings to current Indian practice and resource realities.
2. Identify which national programme or guideline, if any, the findings are relevant to.
3. Discuss feasibility of acting on the findings in district and primary settings.
4. Write the paragraph (100–150 words).
Rules
Mention a programme or guideline only if I listed it or you mark it [VERIFY PROGRAMME / GUIDELINE], because misnamed programmes undermine credibility.
Output
Headed notes, then the paragraph.
Pro tipExaminers in India value this paragraph. It shows you thought beyond your own hospital.
Try it withFinding: low-cost bedside ultrasound detected pneumonia as accurately as X-ray in children.

285Cut my discussion to the word limit
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itWhen your discussion is over the limit for your thesis or target journal.
Persona
You are a journal editor who cuts discussions without losing substance.
My context
My discussion: [PASTE DISCUSSION]
Current and target word count: [e.g. 1,900 → 1,200]
Parts I must keep: [list]
Task
1. Identify repetition of results, background that belongs in the introduction, over-long literature summaries and redundant limitations.
2. Produce the trimmed discussion at or under the target.
3. List what was cut, so I can restore anything essential.
Rules
Keep all citations with their claims and all numbers unchanged, because trimming must not alter the evidence. Keep the standard structure intact.

The trimmed discussion with its word count, then the cut list.

286Practical recommendations from my thesis
Standard
1.9 Discussion, conclusion & limitations · PG Resident
Use itWhen your thesis format requires a recommendations section.
Persona
You are a health-policy adviser who writes recommendations that are proportionate to the evidence.
My context
Key findings: [brief]
Design strength and limitations: [brief]
Stakeholders: [clinicians, hospital, programme, researchers]
My university's format for this section, if any: [brief]
Task
1. Write 4–6 recommendations grouped by stakeholder.
2. Grade each by the strength of support from my study (strong, moderate or preliminary).
3. Make each specific and feasible, with who should act, how, and what it would cost in effort.

Section 1.10
1.10

Protocol, ethics & synopsis

The protocol is the document you will be held to for three years, and the IEC is the gate you must pass first. Decide everything in advance.
