Master
1.13 Conference abstracts, posters & oral papers · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itBefore a conference abstract deadline, once your results (or interim results) are verified.
WhyConference abstracts are judged in minutes by reviewers scoring dozens of submissions. A clear question, a stated design, real numbers and a proportionate conclusion, within the exact limit and format, is what gets accepted, and often what gets you into the award session.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a scientific committee member for national and international medical conferences who scores hundreds of abstracts each year. You know what reviewers reward and what gets rejected.
My context
Conference name and its abstract rules (word or character limit, headings, whether the title and authors count, category options): [PASTE RULES]
Study design, setting and period: [brief]
Sample size and participant flow: [numbers]
Primary result with estimate, CI and p: [paste exactly]
Key secondary results: [paste]
Whether the data is final or interim: [final / interim with n so far]
Task
1. Draft the abstract in the conference's exact format and headings, within the limit, stating the count used (words or characters, as the conference counts them).
2. Background: the problem and the gap in 2 sentences. Methods: design, setting, participants, key measurements and analysis. Results: the numbers that answer the objective. Conclusion: proportionate, and linked to practice or research.
3. Write 3 title options within any title limit.
4. Recommend the best category, and whether to opt for oral, poster or award consideration.
5. Score the draft against typical reviewer criteria (importance, methods, clarity of results, validity of the conclusion, presentation) and revise the weakest part.
Rules
Use only my numbers, reproduced exactly; label interim data as interim, because presenting interim results as final is misconduct. No references unless the conference allows them. No "results will be presented" placeholders, because reviewers reject abstracts without results.
Output
The final abstract with its count, the titles, the category advice, then the scoring table.
Tweak
End with the one sentence a reviewer is most likely to criticise, and a safer rewrite.
How to get more out of it
  • Check how the conference counts: words or characters, and whether spaces, title and authors are included.
  • Submit a day early. Portals slow down or crash near deadlines.
  • Keep the abstract text. The journal version later must not contradict it.
  • → NEXT #382 Research poster from my manuscript or thesis
382Research poster from my manuscript or thesis
Master
1.13 Conference abstracts, posters & oral papers · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itAfter abstract acceptance as a poster, 2–3 weeks before the conference.
WhyMost posters are shrunken papers that nobody reads. A good poster is read from two metres away in under a minute: one clear question, one clear answer, figures instead of paragraphs. This prompt turns your paper into that.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a scientific poster designer and conference judge who has evaluated hundreds of posters. You design for visual hierarchy, brevity and a clear take-home message.
My context
Accepted abstract: [PASTE ABSTRACT]
Key results, tables and figures available: [list]
Poster specifications (size, orientation, print or e-poster, template requirements): [paste]
Design tool: [PowerPoint / Canva / other]
Institution logo and branding requirements: [brief]
Whether I will stand by the poster or it will be viewed alone: [brief]
Task
1. Write a one-line take-home message to feature prominently.
2. Plan the panels: title, authors and affiliations, background (40 words), objective (1 line), methods (a small flow diagram or 4 bullets), results (2–3 figures or tables with one-line captions), conclusion (2–3 bullets), and references, acknowledgements and QR code.
3. Write the text for every panel, 500–800 words in total.
4. Specify the layout: columns, reading order, the central figure, font sizes (title, headings, body), colours and white space.
5. Convert any results table into a figure where that would be clearer.
6. Give step-by-step build instructions in my tool.
7. Write a 90-second walk-through script for when judges stop by.
Rules
Use only content and numbers from my abstract and results, keeping them identical to the abstract, because judges compare the poster with the abstract. Keep text sizes readable from 2 metres (body about 24–32 pt on an A0 poster; mark exact sizes [CHECK TEMPLATE]).
Output
The take-home message, a panel table with text, the layout specification, the build steps, then the walk-through script.
Tweak
End with a checklist to run on the printed or displayed poster before the session.
How to get more out of it
  • If your poster has more than 800 words, it has too many.
  • Put your main result graph in the centre, at eye level.
  • A QR code linking to the abstract or full paper lets interested readers go deeper.
  • → NEXT #388 90-second poster walk-through for judges
383Thesis → 8-minute oral paper, with slides and Q&A
Master
1.13 Conference abstracts, posters & oral papers · PG Resident
Use itWhen your abstract is accepted for oral or award-paper presentation.
WhyOral paper slots are short and strictly timed, and chairs cut off speakers who overrun. A timed slide plan, a spoken script and rehearsed answers turn a nervous 12-minute ramble into a confident 8-minute presentation that wins awards.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a conference presentation coach and award-session judge who has trained many residents for oral paper presentations.
My context
Abstract and key results: [PASTE]
Time allowed for the talk and for discussion: [e.g. 8 + 2 minutes]
Figures and tables available: [list]
Award session?: [yes / no]
My speaking pace and confidence: [brief]
What the audience will mostly be: [specialists / mixed / students]
Conference's slide requirements (template, aspect ratio, file format): [paste]
Task
1. Plan 8–10 slides with a time budget per slide: title; background and gap; objective; methods (one visual); participant flow; primary result (one clear figure); secondary results; limitations; conclusion and take-home.
2. For each slide, give the title as a message ("Early mobilisation halved delirium days"), the content (maximum 3 bullets or 1 figure), and speaker notes.
3. Write a spoken script at about 130 words per minute that fits the time exactly.
4. Prepare the 8 most likely audience and judge questions with 30-second answers.
5. Give a rehearsal plan for the week before, including one rehearsal in front of colleagues who ask hard questions.
6. List the technical checks for the day (file format, fonts embedded, videos, backup on a pen drive and email).
Rules
Keep every number identical to my abstract, and don't add results that aren't in it, because judges check. Keep slides visual: no paragraphs, and at least 24 pt text.
Output
A slide table (slide, title, content, time, notes), the script with its word count, the Q&A table, then the rehearsal plan.
Tweak
End with the opening 2 sentences and the closing 2 sentences to memorise word for word.
How to get more out of it
  • Rehearse with a timer at least 5 times. Most residents overrun by 30–50%.
  • Write slide titles as messages, not topics. The audience should get the story from the titles alone.
  • Have 2–3 backup slides for predictable questions.
  • → NEXT #390 Prepare for questions after my talk
384Choose the right conference for my work
Standard
1.13 Conference abstracts, posters & oral papers · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen deciding where to submit your abstract.
Persona
You are an academic mentor who guides residents on conference strategy.
My context
Specialty and the topic of my work: [brief]
Stage of the work: [final results / interim / case report]
Budget and travel constraints: [brief]
Goals: [award, networking, first presentation, international exposure]
Task
1. Describe the options: national specialty conferences, state or zonal meetings, international conferences and virtual meetings, and what each offers.
2. Explain how to find upcoming conferences and deadlines, and check that they are legitimate (predatory conferences exist too).
3. Explain the categories typically available (oral, poster, e-poster, award paper, case report sessions) and eligibility, e.g. age or membership requirements for awards.
4. Build a comparison table from the conferences I find.
Rules
Don't name specific conferences, dates or fees from memory; mark anything named as [VERIFY ON THE OFFICIAL SITE], because dates and rules change every year.
Output
The options overview, the finding and legitimacy steps, the categories note, then the comparison template.
Pro tipStudent and resident award sessions at national specialty conferences are among the best first stages for your work.
Try it withMD Pulmonary Medicine resident with final thesis results, limited travel budget.

385Score my abstract like a conference reviewer
Standard
1.13 Conference abstracts, posters & oral papers · PG Resident
Use itBefore you submit a conference abstract.
Persona
You are a conference abstract reviewer who scores submissions on a standard rubric.
My context
My abstract: [PASTE ABSTRACT]
Conference and category: [brief]
Limit: [words or characters]
Task
1. Score it out of 5 on: importance of the question, clarity of the objective, appropriateness of the methods, completeness of the results (with numbers), validity of the conclusion, and clarity of writing.
2. Quote the text behind each score.
3. Say whether it would likely be accepted, and in which format (oral or poster).
4. Give the 3 most important revisions.
Rules
Be honest about the likely outcome, and quote rather than paraphrase, because encouraging but vague feedback won't improve the abstract.
Output
A scoring table, the verdict, then the revisions.
Pro tipAbstracts without numbers in the results are usually rejected. Check yours has them.
Try it withA 250-word abstract on ultrasound-guided versus landmark-guided central line insertion.

386Adapt my poster into an e-poster
Standard
1.13 Conference abstracts, posters & oral papers · PG Resident
Use itWhen the conference uses screen-displayed e-posters.
Persona
You are a digital poster designer who adapts print posters for screens.
My context
My poster content or file description: [PASTE OR DESCRIBE]
E-poster specification (aspect ratio, single or multiple slides, resolution, file type, interactivity allowed): [paste]
Task
1. Restructure the content for the format: a single 16:9 slide or a short slide set.
2. Reduce the text further for on-screen reading distance.
3. Suggest a reading flow and the use of any allowed interactivity (e.g. clickable panels).
4. Specify export settings.
Rules
Keep all numbers identical to the abstract; don't add new content, because e-posters are judged against the submitted abstract.
Output
The restructured layout plan, the reduced text, then the export settings.
Pro tipCheck your e-poster on a laptop from 1.5 metres before submitting. If you can't read it, neither can judges.

387Layout brief for Canva or PowerPoint
Standard
1.13 Conference abstracts, posters & oral papers · PG Resident
Use itWhen building the poster yourself.
Persona
You are a graphic designer who specialises in clean scientific posters.
My context
Poster size and orientation: [e.g. A0 portrait, 841 × 1189 mm]
Panels and approximate text length for each: [list]
Figures: [list]
Tool: [Canva / PowerPoint]
Task
1. Give the page set-up for my tool (custom size, margins, grid).
2. Suggest a 3-column grid and the placement of each panel.
3. Give a font system (one sans-serif family, sizes for title, headings, body and captions) and a colour palette of 2–3 colours plus neutrals that is colour-blind safe.
4. Describe alignment, spacing and how to place figures so they print sharply.
5. Give print-export settings.
Rules
Recommend readable, conservative choices, and mark exact template or institutional branding rules as [CHECK TEMPLATE], because conferences often mandate them.
Output
Numbered set-up and design steps, a font and colour table, then export settings.
Pro tipLeave about 25% of the poster as white space. Crowded posters are skipped.

1.13 Conference abstracts, posters & oral papers · PG Resident
Use itThe week before your poster session.
Persona
You are a poster-session judge who knows what makes a presenter memorable.
My context
My poster content (panel text or summary): [PASTE]
Time judges typically spend: [e.g. 2–3 minutes]
Task
1. Write a 90-second script: the hook, the question, what I did, the key result (pointing to the figure), what it means, and one limitation.
2. Write a 30-second version for passers-by.
3. List 6 questions judges ask at posters, with short answers from my content.
4. Give body-language and positioning tips.
Rules
Use only what is on my poster, with numbers identical to it, because judges look at the poster while you talk.

The two scripts with timing, the Q&A table, then the tips.

1.13 Conference abstracts, posters & oral papers · PG Resident
Use itWhen you need slides quickly for a 5–10 minute talk.
Persona
You are a presentation designer for medical conferences.
My context
Abstract and results: [PASTE]
Time limit: [minutes]
Slide template requirements: [brief]
Audience: [specialists / mixed]
Task
1. Recommend the number of slides (about one per minute).
2. For each slide, give a message title, a content suggestion (figure, table or a maximum of 3 bullets), and speaker notes.
3. Suggest the design: font sizes, contrast and one accent colour.
4. List slides to put in the backup section.

390Prepare for questions after my talk
Standard
1.13 Conference abstracts, posters & oral papers · PG Resident
Use itIn the days before your oral or poster presentation.
Persona
You are a session chair who has asked and heard thousands of conference questions.
My context
My abstract and key slides: [PASTE]
Known limitations: [list]
Audience: [specialists / mixed / award judges]
Task
1. List 12 likely questions: methodology, sample size, bias, generalisability, clinical relevance, "what next", and one hostile question.
2. Write a 30-second answer for each, grounded in my study.
3. Give a technique for questions I can't answer (acknowledge, offer a reasoned view, and follow up).
4. Suggest 2 backup slides that answer the most likely questions.
Rules
Base answers on my data only; where I lack the information, script an honest "we didn't measure that", because bluffing in front of experts is obvious.
Output
A Q&A table, the technique, then the backup-slide suggestions.
Pro tipRepeat the question before answering. It buys you thinking time and helps the audience hear it.
Try it withOral paper on a retrospective cohort of snakebite outcomes.

391Prepare for an award-paper session
Standard
1.13 Conference abstracts, posters & oral papers · PG Resident
Use itWhen your paper is selected for a best-paper or young-investigator award session.
Persona
You are an award-session judge at national medical conferences.
My context
Abstract and presentation plan: [PASTE]
Award rules and judging criteria, if published: [paste]
Time limits: [brief]
Task
1. Map the typical judging criteria (originality, methodological rigour, clinical relevance, clarity, time management and handling of questions) to my presentation, and identify gaps.
2. Suggest changes to strengthen my weakest criterion.
3. Prepare answers to the judges' likely tough questions.
4. Give a checklist for the day: file formats, backup copies, arrival time, dress and timing.
Rules
Mark criteria that I haven't confirmed from the official rules as [CHECK AWARD RULES], because eligibility and criteria differ between conferences.
Output
A criteria-mapping table, the improvements, the Q&A, then the checklist.
Pro tipJudges remember speakers who finish on time and answer questions honestly.

Persona
You are a grants officer who reviews travel-grant applications.
My context
Conference, dates and the type of presentation accepted: [brief]
Estimated costs (registration, travel, stay): [amounts]
Funding body and its criteria: [paste]

Task

2. Build a cost table with justification.

Standard
1.13 Conference abstracts, posters & oral papers · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itAfter the conference, while feedback is fresh.
Persona
You are a publication mentor who helps residents turn presentations into papers.
My context
My abstract and presentation: [PASTE]
Questions and feedback received at the conference: [brief]
Whether the abstract was published in a journal supplement: [yes / no]
Task
1. List the feedback that should shape the paper.
2. Explain how a published conference abstract affects journal submission (it is usually acceptable, but must be disclosed), marked [CHECK TARGET JOURNAL POLICY].
3. Make a plan for writing the full paper within 6 weeks.
4. Draft the disclosure sentence about the prior presentation.
Rules
Keep results consistent with the presented abstract, or explain any differences (e.g. final versus interim data), because inconsistency raises questions about data integrity.
Output
The feedback list, the policy note, the 6-week plan, then the disclosure sentence.
Pro tipConference momentum fades in weeks. Start the paper the week you return.

394Record a presentation for a virtual or hybrid conference
Standard
1.13 Conference abstracts, posters & oral papers · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen the conference asks for a pre-recorded talk or you present online.
Persona
You are a medical educator who produces clear, professional recorded talks on a modest budget.
My context
Talk length and format required (video file, live online, slide upload): [paste]
Slides ready?: [yes / no]
Equipment available: [laptop, phone, microphone, quiet room]
Task
1. Give a set-up checklist: camera at eye level, lighting in front of me, a quiet room, microphone choice, and a plain background.
2. Explain how to record in PowerPoint, Zoom or similar tools, including slide-by-slide recording to make editing easier.
3. Adapt my script for the camera: shorter sentences, and a visual cue every 30 seconds.
4. Give export settings and the file-naming convention the conference requires.
5. Plan for live Q&A online: internet backup, and mute and unmute etiquette.
Rules
Mark platform-specific steps as [MAY DIFFER BY VERSION], because recording menus change often. Keep the talk within the time limit exactly, since recorded talks are often cut automatically.
Output
The set-up checklist, recording steps, script tips, export settings, then the Q&A plan.
Pro tipRecord one slide at a time. A mistake then costs 40 seconds, not the whole talk.

JobBest toolWhy

The ethics of AI in research
  • Disclose AI use as your institution and target journal require.
  • Don't submit AI text verbatim. Rewrite it in your own academic voice.
  • Verify every statistic, reference and data point against the primary source.
  • AI cannot replace your guide's approval, your IEC clearance or your clinical judgement.

This resource is for educational purposes. It does not replace your institutional research guidelines, ethics committee requirements, university thesis regulations or the advice of your supervisor and statistician. Verify all AI-generated content independently before using it in any submitted work. AI cannot be an author; disclose AI use per ICMJE and your target journal's policy.

Section 2.1
2.1

Seminar preparation

A seminar is judged by what the audience remembers the next morning. Build it around clear objectives, current evidence and a story, not a textbook chapter read aloud.

How to use this section

Use it one to two weeks before your seminar, to plan the objectives, the evidence and the flow.

401Mixed-audience seminar deck, clinically rigorous
Master
2.1 Seminar preparation · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen you have a departmental seminar on any topic and want a complete, evidence-based deck.
WhyDepartmental audiences are mixed: MBBS students, interns, residents and consultants in the same room. A deck pitched at resident level, with a short foundation recap for juniors and a controversies section for consultants, keeps everyone engaged, and cites real evidence rather than textbook generalities.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a senior academic in [SPECIALTY] who has delivered and moderated hundreds of departmental seminars. You are clinically rigorous, evidence-based and practical, and you never invent citations or statistics.
My context
Topic: [e.g. Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: from pathophysiology to ventilator management]
Audience: mixed (MBBS students, interns, junior residents, senior residents, consultants)
Time available: [e.g. 45 minutes + 15 minutes discussion]
Sources I have (guidelines, reviews, textbook chapters), uploaded or listed: [UPLOAD OR LIST]
Output format: [slide-by-slide text for PowerPoint / a .pptx file if your tool can create one]
Task
1. Pitch the core content at resident level, with a 1–2 slide foundation recap early, and advanced nuance for consultants.
2. Follow this structure, adapting as needed: title slide with a one-line clinical hook; why this matters (a representative case); foundation recap (definitions, classification); pathophysiology; clinical features and diagnostic approach (criteria or scores in tables); management, stepwise, first-line versus escalation; an evidence corner (landmark trials and current guidelines); controversies and grey zones; 3–5 key takeaways; references in Vancouver style.
3. For every slide give a message title, concise bullets (one idea per slide), a table where comparisons help, and speaker notes.
4. Mark what is exam-relevant for students and what is decision-changing for residents and consultants.
5. Suggest where a figure, flowchart or algorithm should go, and describe it.
Rules
Name trials and guidelines only from my sources or with [VERIFY] beside each, because misremembered trial names and years are the most embarrassing seminar error. Mark every drug dose as [VERIFY DOSE FROM CURRENT GUIDELINE]. Show me the slide-by-slide text for review before building any file.
Output
A slide table (number, title, bullets, visual, speaker notes, audience tag), then the reference list with [VERIFY] flags.
Tweak
End with the 5 questions a consultant is most likely to ask after this seminar, and short evidence-based answers.
How to get more out of it
  • Tuning levers: change the depth (resident ↔ consultant), the slide count (about 1 slide per minute) and the visual style.
  • Verify every trial and guideline in the evidence corner against the original source before presenting.
  • Rehearse the controversies section. It is where the discussion will go.
  • → NEXT #408 Learning objectives with Bloom's verbs
402From topic to seminar blueprint in one sitting
Master
2.1 Seminar preparation · PG Resident
Use itThe day your seminar topic is assigned, before you open any textbook.
WhyMost residents start a seminar by reading everything and end with 80 slides and no structure. Starting with objectives, a time budget and a storyline tells you exactly what to read and what to leave out.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a medical educator and senior faculty member who mentors residents on seminar preparation. You think backwards from what the audience must be able to do after the session.
My context
Topic as assigned: [e.g. Approach to hyponatraemia]
Specialty and my year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and its level: [brief]
Duration: [minutes]
Days until the seminar: [N]
Moderator's known expectations or style: [brief or "unknown"]
Task
1. Clarify the scope: what is in, what is out, and how to phrase the final seminar title.
2. Write 4–6 learning objectives using Bloom's verbs (explain, differentiate, apply, choose).
3. Build a storyline: an opening case, 5–7 content blocks mapped to the objectives, and a closing return to the case.
4. Create a time budget per block that fits the duration.
5. For each block, list the must-read sources by type (current guideline, recent review, textbook chapter) with [VERIFY LATEST EDITION].
6. Make a day-by-day preparation plan for the days I have, including a rehearsal.
7. Predict the moderator's 5 likely questions.
Rules
Keep the content proportional to the time, about one slide per minute, and cut anything not tied to an objective, because overlong seminars lose the audience in the middle. Name no specific papers from memory; describe the source type and mark it [FIND AND VERIFY].
Output
Scope note, objectives, storyline table (block, objective, minutes, key points), the source list, the preparation plan, then the predicted questions.
Tweak
End with the single case vignette to open with, 60 words, de-identified and realistic for Indian practice.
How to get more out of it
  • Show the objectives and storyline to your moderator a week before. It avoids a last-minute restructure.
  • Read the guideline first, the review second and the textbook last.
  • Keep the opening case alive: return to it in every block.
  • → NEXT #401 Mixed-audience seminar deck, clinically rigorous
403Evidence pack: guidelines and trials, verified from my sources
Master
2.1 Seminar preparation · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen your seminar needs an evidence corner and you have gathered the guidelines and key papers.
WhyThe evidence section is where seminars go wrong: trials cited with the wrong year, outcomes overstated, or guidelines quoted from memory. Building it strictly from uploaded sources, with quotes, makes it accurate and defensible when a consultant challenges it.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are an evidence-based medicine specialist who prepares evidence summaries for clinical guideline panels. You quote the source for every claim and state the certainty of evidence clearly.
My context
Seminar topic and the clinical questions it must answer: [list 3–5 questions]
Guidelines uploaded (name, organisation, year): [UPLOAD / LIST]
Key trials and meta-analyses uploaded: [UPLOAD / LIST]
Setting to apply the evidence to: [e.g. Indian tertiary and district hospitals]
Audience and how much time the evidence section gets: [e.g. residents and consultants, 8 minutes]
My specialty and year: [brief]
Task
1. For each clinical question, summarise what the uploaded guidelines recommend, with the strength or grade, quoting the recommendation wording.
2. Build a trials table: trial, year, design, population, intervention versus comparator, primary outcome and result with CI, and the key limitation.
3. Identify where guidelines disagree with each other, and why.
4. Identify where the evidence does not apply well to Indian settings (population, resources, drug availability).
5. Write 3 evidence-corner slides with speaker notes.
6. List any major trial or guideline the audience will expect that is missing from my uploads, marked [FIND AND UPLOAD], so I can add it before the seminar.
Rules
Use only the uploaded documents; for anything else write [NOT IN MY SOURCES — VERIFY], because a single wrong trial detail can discredit the whole seminar. Reproduce effect sizes exactly. State certainty levels as the guideline states them.
Output
A recommendations table per question, the trials table, the disagreement notes, the applicability notes, then the slide text.
Tweak
End with the one piece of evidence I should read in full before presenting, because it is most likely to be questioned.
How to get more out of it
  • Upload the guideline PDFs themselves, not summaries of them.
  • Put the year on every trial and guideline on the slides. Consultants check it.
  • If two guidelines disagree, show both. That is where the best discussion happens.
  • → NEXT #421 Compare two or more guidelines
404Full speaker script for a 45-minute seminar
Master
2.1 Seminar preparation · PG Resident
Use itWhen your slides are ready and you want to rehearse to time.
WhyReading slides aloud is the commonest seminar failure. A script written for speaking, with timing, transitions and planned interaction, lets you rehearse properly, then speak from notes on the day.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a speaking coach for medical educators who writes natural, spoken scripts and trims them to the second.
My context
My slides (titles and bullets, or upload the file): [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Duration of the talk (excluding discussion): [e.g. 40 minutes]
Audience: [brief]
My speaking style and my nerves: [brief]
Points where I want audience interaction: [brief or "suggest"]
Parts of the content I find hardest to explain: [list]
Language mix the audience is comfortable with: [e.g. English with occasional Hindi]
Task
1. Write a spoken script per slide at about 130 words per minute, in conversational academic English.
2. Mark timing checkpoints (e.g. "by slide 10: 12 minutes").
3. Add a transition sentence between sections, so the story flows.
4. Insert 3–4 interaction moments: a question to the audience, a quick show of hands, or a case pause.
5. Mark the lines to memorise word for word (opening, key message, closing).
6. Flag slides whose script runs long, and suggest cuts.
7. For the hardest parts I listed, write a simpler explanation or an analogy I can use if the audience looks lost.
8. Write a 30-second emergency version of the conclusion in case time runs out.
Rules
Keep facts exactly as on my slides and add no new data, because the script must match what the audience sees. Script the interaction moments with a fallback answer in case nobody responds.
Output
A script table (slide, script, seconds, interaction), then the checkpoints and the memorise list.
Tweak
End with a 5-step rehearsal plan for the next 3 days.
How to get more out of it
  • Rehearse aloud with a timer. Silent reading always underestimates the time.
  • Don't read the script on the day. Speak from the checkpoints and the memorised lines.
  • Record one rehearsal on your phone. You'll hear your filler words immediately.
  • → NEXT #434 Feedback on my rehearsal script
405Case-based interactive seminar
Master
2.1 Seminar preparation · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen you want a seminar built around an unfolding case rather than a lecture.
WhyCase-based seminars keep the audience thinking instead of copying. Revealing a case in stages, with questions at each stage, teaches clinical reasoning and makes the content stick.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a clinician-educator who designs case-based learning sessions for residents, and who knows how to reveal information at the right pace.
My context
Topic: [TOPIC]
Learning objectives: [PASTE OR "suggest"]
Audience and number: [brief]
Duration: [minutes]
A real case I can adapt (de-identified), or "create a realistic one": [PASTE OR REQUEST]
Setting where the case takes place: [emergency / ward / OPD / district hospital]
Common mistakes residents make with this condition: [list or "suggest"]
Task
1. Build an unfolding case in 4–6 stages: presentation, examination, initial investigations, key result, management decision, and follow-up or complication.
2. At each stage, write 1–2 questions for the audience, the expected answers, and the teaching point to deliver.
3. Map each stage to a learning objective.
4. Add a short mini-lecture slide (3 bullets) after each stage to consolidate.
5. Close with a summary of the reasoning path, and take-home points.
6. Suggest how to run it: small groups, polls or calling on people.
7. Build at least one stage around a common mistake, so the audience can discover why it is wrong.
8. Give the timing for each stage so the whole case fits the duration.
Rules
Keep the case realistic for Indian practice and fully de-identified. Mark drug doses and guideline specifics as [VERIFY], because case-based sessions invite detailed questions.
Output
A stage table (stage, information revealed, questions, expected answers, teaching point, objective), the mini-lecture slides, then the facilitation guide.
Tweak
End with 2 variations of the case (a different age or comorbidity) for repeat sessions.
How to get more out of it
  • Reveal information on separate slides. Showing everything at once kills the reasoning.
  • Wait 10 seconds after asking a question. Silence is thinking time.
  • Keep a "parking lot" for tangent questions and answer them at the end.
  • → NEXT #435 Make my seminar interactive
406Mock moderator: grill me before the real seminar
Master
2.1 Seminar preparation · PG Resident
Use it2–3 days before your seminar, once the slides are final.
WhyThe dreaded part of a seminar is the moderator's questions. A realistic mock session, one question at a time with feedback, turns fear into preparation and shows you exactly which slides need strengthening.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a senior professor and seminar moderator known for probing questions on basics, recent evidence and practical application. You are strict but fair, and you give frank feedback.
My context
Seminar topic and my specialty and year: [brief]
My slide titles and key content: [PASTE]
Areas I feel weakest in: [list]
My moderator's known style or favourite themes: [brief or "unknown"]
Duration of the seminar and the discussion slot: [brief]
Task
1. Ask me one question at a time, mixing basic science, clinical application, recent evidence, Indian context and "what would you do" scenarios.
2. After each answer, score it out of 10, give the ideal answer in 3–5 points, and tell me which slide should cover it better.
3. Include 2 classic trap questions moderators use on this topic.
4. Mix difficulty: start with 3 basic questions, then 4 applied questions, then 3 advanced or evidence questions.
5. After 10 questions, summarise my weak areas and the slides to strengthen, and give me a one-day plan to fix them.
Rules
Ask only one question per turn and wait for my answer, because the value is in answering under pressure. Base questions on my topic and slides. Mark any fact in your ideal answers that depends on a guideline as [VERIFY].
Output
Conversational: one question per turn, feedback in a short structured block (score, ideal answer, gap, slide to fix), then the final summary with the weak areas ranked from most to least urgent.
Tweak
End with the 3 questions I should prepare backup slides for.
How to get more out of it
  • Answer aloud before typing. The seminar is spoken.
  • Add backup slides at the end of the deck for the questions you struggled with.
  • Ask a colleague to play the moderator with these questions for a real rehearsal.
  • → NEXT #404 Full speaker script for a 45-minute seminar
407Turn a new guideline into a seminar
Master
2.1 Seminar preparation · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen a new or updated clinical guideline is released and your department wants a session on it.
Why"What's new in the guideline" seminars are common and often done badly: a slide per recommendation, read aloud. The useful version shows what changed, why, what it means for practice here, and what remains uncertain.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a guideline methodologist and clinician who explains guideline updates to busy clinicians, focusing on what changes practice.
My context
The guideline (upload the full text or the recommendations section): [UPLOAD]
The previous version, if available: [UPLOAD OR "not available"]
Audience and duration: [brief]
Local practice for this condition in my hospital: [brief]
Drugs, tests or devices the guideline recommends that my hospital lacks: [list or "unsure"]
My specialty and year: [brief]
Task
1. List the key recommendations with their strength and certainty, quoting the exact wording and the section number.
2. Identify what is new or changed since the previous version, and the evidence cited for each change.
3. Classify each change as practice-changing, practice-confirming or minor.
4. Discuss applicability to Indian settings: resources, drug availability, cost and staffing.
5. Build a 20–30 minute slide plan: what changed, why, what to do on Monday, and uncertainties.
6. Write a one-page summary handout.
7. Suggest a simple audit the department could run to check adherence to the key recommendation.
8. Note which recommendations are conditional or based on low-certainty evidence, so the audience doesn't treat them as absolute.
Rules
Quote only from the uploaded guideline and mark anything else [VERIFY], because a misquoted recommendation can change patient care. Don't overstate the certainty of weak recommendations.
Output
The recommendations table, the changes table (old position, new position, evidence, classification), the applicability notes, the slide plan with timings, then the handout.
Tweak
End with the 3 recommendations most likely to be debated in the department, and why.
How to get more out of it
  • Lead with what changes practice. Nobody remembers the minor edits.
  • Bring the guideline's own algorithm figure if it has one, and credit it.
  • Invite a senior to comment on local applicability. It turns the seminar into a discussion.
  • → NEXT #420 The Indian perspective slide
408Learning objectives with Bloom's verbs
Standard
2.1 Seminar preparation · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itAt the very start of seminar preparation.
Persona
You are a medical educator trained in curriculum design who writes precise, measurable learning objectives.
My context
Topic: [TOPIC]
Audience level: [MBBS / interns / residents / mixed]
Duration: [minutes]
Task
1. Write 4–6 learning objectives, each starting with a Bloom's verb (define, explain, differentiate, interpret, apply, choose, justify).
2. Spread them across levels: recall, understanding and application.
3. Say which part of the seminar will deliver each objective.
4. Suggest one quick end-of-session check for each objective.
Rules
Avoid vague verbs such as "know", "understand" and "learn about", because they cannot be checked. Keep the number realistic for the time available.
Output
A numbered objectives list, a mapping table (objective, seminar block, check question).
Pro tipPut the objectives on slide 2 and return to them on the last slide. Moderators notice.
Try it withTopic: approach to a patient with haemoptysis, for MD Medicine residents, 40 minutes.

Pro tipPut the checkpoint times in small text in your speaker notes, not on the slides.

Sources I am using: [UPLOAD / LIST]

2. Link each step to a symptom, sign, investigation finding or treatment target.
3. Describe a flowchart or diagram for each slide.

Sources: [UPLOAD / LIST]
Task
1. Build a stepwise algorithm: initial assessment, first-line tests, branch points with decision criteria, and further tests.
2. Mark "can't-miss" diagnoses and red flags at the right points.
3. Describe the algorithm as a flowchart (boxes and arrows) for a slide.
4. Add a resource-limited variant for district hospitals.
5. Write speaker notes walking through one example patient.
Rules
Mark cut-off values and test choices that depend on a guideline as [VERIFY FROM SOURCE], because algorithms are often photographed and reused.
Output
The flowchart description, a branch table (decision point, criterion, next step), the resource-limited variant, then the notes.
Pro tipWalk the audience through the algorithm with a real case. Algorithms alone are hard to follow.

Seminar structure planned: [PASTE OUTLINE]
Task
1. Write 12 questions to ask NotebookLM, one or two per section of my outline.
2. Write a customisation instruction for an Audio Overview that focuses on my learning objectives.
3. Explain how to check each answer using NotebookLM's citations.
4. Suggest how to turn the answers into slide bullets.
Rules
Phrase every question so the answer must come from my sources, because NotebookLM is reliable only when grounded in them.
Output
The question list by section, the audio instruction, then the verification and conversion steps.
Pro tipListen to the Audio Overview on your commute the day before. It's surprisingly good revision.
Try it with8 sources on heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.

433What have I missed?
Standard
2.1 Seminar preparation · PG Resident
Use itWhen your slides are drafted and you want a completeness check.
Persona
You are a senior moderator who spots missing topics in seminars instantly.
My context
Topic and objectives: [PASTE]
My slide titles and bullets: [PASTE]
Audience: [brief]
Task
1. Compare my content against what a complete seminar on this topic should cover for this audience.
2. List the important gaps and suggest where each should go.
3. List content that is excessive or off-topic.
4. Check that each objective is covered.
Rules
Prioritise gaps by importance for the audience, not completeness for its own sake, because adding everything makes seminars overlong.

A gaps table (gap, importance, where to add), then the excess list and the objective check.

My context
My script or rehearsal transcript: [PASTE]
Timing achieved versus allowed: [e.g. 52 minutes versus 40 allowed]
Feedback I've already received: [brief]
Task
1. Identify sections that run long, repeat themselves or wander.
2. Identify jargon and sentences that are hard to follow when spoken.
3. Identify missing transitions and weak openings or closings.
4. Suggest specific cuts to hit the time, with the time saved by each.

My context

Audience size and setting: [e.g. 30 people, seminar room with a projector]

My context

439Pro-con debate seminar
Standard
2.1 Seminar preparation · PG Resident / Faculty

Persona

My context
Motion: [e.g. "All patients with sepsis should receive early vasopressors"]
My side: [pro / con]
Time per speaker and format: [brief]
Sources: [UPLOAD / LIST]
Task
1. Build my strongest case: 3–4 arguments, each with the best evidence from my sources.
2. Anticipate the opponent's strongest arguments and prepare rebuttals.
3. Write an opening statement and a closing statement.
4. Suggest 2 slides per argument.
Rules
Use honest evidence even on my side, and acknowledge the limitations of my sources, because misrepresenting evidence loses a medical audience's trust.
Output
The arguments table, the rebuttals, the statements, then the slide plan.
Pro tipConcede a minor point early. It makes your main arguments more credible.

Standard
2.1 Seminar preparation · PG Resident

My context
My slides (paste the text or upload the file): [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Topic, audience and duration: [brief]
Sources I used: [list]
Task
1. Check medical accuracy slide by slide, flagging any statement that needs verification or seems outdated.
2. Check clarity: overloaded slides, vague titles, missing labels and unreadable tables.
3. Check structure against the objectives and the time.
4. Give the 10 most important fixes, in priority order, with the slide number.
Rules
Flag doubtful facts as [VERIFY] rather than correcting them from memory, because I must confirm them against my sources. Quote the slide text for every comment.
Output
A slide-by-slide comment table, then the top 10 fixes.
Pro tipFix the accuracy flags first, then clarity, then design. Moderators forgive plain slides, not wrong ones.

441Build a seminar from our department's cases

Section 2.2
2.2

Journal club

A journal club is not a summary of a paper. It is a critical appraisal that ends with one question: should this change what we do for our patients?

60prompts
7Master
35Standard
18Quick
How to use this section

Use it the week you are assigned a paper: appraise it first, then build the presentation.

Start with the Master prompts (#461–467) for the full workflow; use the Standard prompts (#468–502) for one task at a time; reach for the Quick prompts (#503–520) when you have two minutes. Tap any title below to jump to it, and follow → NEXT to move to the next step.

461Journal club presentation: appraisal to bottom line
Master
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident
Use itThe week before you present, once your paper is chosen and you have the full text.
WhyMost journal clubs retell the abstract. A strong one summarises the question, appraises it with a validated checklist, states the real strengths and limitations, and ends with a clear clinical bottom line for your patients. That is what faculty remember.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a clinical epidemiologist who has moderated departmental journal clubs for 15 years and is known for spotting the flaw everyone else missed. You teach residents to appraise, not summarise.
My context
My level and specialty: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience: [residents and faculty / mixed]
Time for presentation and discussion: [e.g. 20 + 15 minutes]
Checklist my department prefers: [CASP / JBI / CONSORT-based / none]
[PASTE FULL TEXT OF THE PAPER OR UPLOAD THE PDF]
Task
1. Summarise the study in 5 lines: question (PICO), design, setting, sample, and main result with numbers.
2. Explain why the study was done: the gap it addressed and the prior evidence, as described by the authors.
3. Appraise it with the appropriate checklist for its design, item by item, quoting the paper for each judgement.
4. Identify the 3 genuine strengths and the 3 limitations that most threaten the conclusion, with the likely direction of bias.
5. Interpret the results in clinical terms: absolute risk difference, NNT or NNH where applicable, and the precision of the estimates.
6. Judge applicability to Indian patients and our hospital's resources.
7. State the clinical bottom line in 2 sentences: would this change our practice, and why or why not?
8. Build a 12–15 slide outline with message titles, bullets and one-line speaker notes.
Rules
Use only the paper I provided; where a detail is not reported, write [NOT REPORTED] rather than assuming, because the audience will check the paper. Calculate NNT only from numbers in the paper and show the arithmetic. Keep judgement and fact clearly separate.
Output
The 5-line summary, the appraisal table (item, judgement, quote), the strengths and limitations, the clinical interpretation, the bottom line, then the slide outline.
Tweak
End with the 3 questions faculty are most likely to ask me, with short answers grounded in the paper.
How to get more out of it
  • Read the methods section twice. The flaw is almost always there, not in the discussion.
  • Check the trial registry entry. Compare the registered primary outcome with the reported one.
  • Practise the bottom line aloud. It is the sentence the head of department will remember.
  • → NEXT #489 The faculty questions I'll face
462Choose the right paper for journal club
Master
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident
Use it2–3 weeks before your journal club, when you need to pick a paper.
WhyThe paper decides the journal club. A recent, practice-relevant paper with a clear design and a genuine debate makes a great session. An obscure or poorly designed paper makes for a long hour. This prompt helps you choose deliberately.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a senior faculty member who coordinates the department's journal club and knows which papers generate good learning and discussion.
My context
Specialty and my year: [brief]
Recent journal clubs in the department (so I don't repeat): [list]
Areas of practice that are debated in our unit: [list]
Candidate papers I have found (title, journal, year, design; paste abstracts if possible): [PASTE 3–6 CANDIDATES]
Departmental rules (e.g. published within the last 12 months, major journals only): [brief]
Task
1. Score each candidate on: relevance to our practice, recency, design quality, clarity of the question, potential for discussion, and teaching value for appraisal skills.
2. Flag any candidate that is a secondary analysis, a small pilot, or has an obvious fatal flaw that would make the session one-sided.
3. Recommend one paper and a backup, with reasons.
4. Suggest what to read alongside it: the accompanying editorial, the protocol, the trial registration and key prior studies (described by type, marked [FIND]).
5. Suggest the central debate question the journal club should resolve.
6. Explain how to confirm the paper's status (published version, corrections, retractions).
Rules
Judge only from the abstracts and details I pasted, and don't claim facts about papers I didn't provide, because a wrong claim about a paper's findings will surface during the session. Prefer papers whose full text I can access legally.
Output
A scoring table (paper, criterion scores, total, flags), the recommendation with a backup, the companion-reading list, then the debate question.
Tweak
End with a one-line pitch I can send to the coordinator to get the paper approved.
How to get more out of it
  • High-impact trials that challenge current practice make the best journal clubs.
  • Check whether the paper has an accompanying editorial. It is a free second opinion.
  • Avoid papers you can't obtain in full text. You can't appraise an abstract.
  • → NEXT #461 Journal club presentation: appraisal to bottom line
463Deep appraisal of a randomised controlled trial
Master
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen your journal-club paper is an RCT and you want to go beyond the checklist.
WhyRCTs look robust, but their flaws are subtle: inadequate concealment, unblinded outcome assessment, outcome switching, post-hoc subgroups and inappropriate analysis populations. A structured deep appraisal finds what a quick read misses.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a trial methodologist who appraises RCTs for guideline panels. You apply the Cochrane RoB 2 domains and the CONSORT checklist, and you explain statistics in clinical language.
My context
The trial (upload the full text, and supplementary material if available): [UPLOAD]
Trial registration number and protocol, if available: [PASTE OR "not found"]
Clinical question I care about: [one line]
My comfort level with statistics: [beginner / intermediate / advanced]
Task
1. Randomisation and allocation concealment: how they were done, and whether they were adequate (quote the methods).
2. Blinding: who was blinded, and whether the primary outcome could be influenced by knowing the allocation.
3. Baseline balance and any imbalances that matter clinically.
4. Deviations and missing data: losses, crossovers, and ITT versus per-protocol analysis.
5. Outcomes: primary outcome definition, whether it is patient-important or surrogate, composite components, and whether it matches the registration.
6. Statistics: sample-size assumptions versus observed rates, the effect estimate with CI, NNT, and multiplicity.
7. Subgroups: pre-specified or not, interaction tests, and credibility.
8. An overall RoB 2 judgement per domain, and the certainty of the conclusion.
Rules
Quote the paper for every judgement, and mark anything not reported as [NOT REPORTED], because unsupported criticism is easily dismissed in a journal club. Show the arithmetic for NNT and absolute differences. If I haven't provided the registry entry, say what to check there rather than assuming.
Output
Eight headed sections, a RoB 2 domain table (domain, judgement, quote), then a one-paragraph verdict.
Tweak
End with the single methodological issue most likely to change how the results should be interpreted.
How to get more out of it
  • Look for the CONSORT flow diagram first. Losses and exclusions tell you a lot.
  • A "significant" result on a surrogate outcome is not the same as a patient-important benefit.
  • Compare the event rate in the control group with the one assumed in the sample-size calculation. If it's lower, the trial was probably underpowered.
  • → NEXT #475 Absolute effects: ARR, RRR, NNT and NNH
464Appraise a cohort or case-control study
Master
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen your journal-club paper is observational.
WhyObservational studies drive many practice changes, and many false beliefs. Confounding, selection and measurement bias can create associations that vanish in trials. Appraising them properly is one of the most important skills a clinician can have.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are an epidemiologist who teaches the appraisal of observational research, with STROBE for reporting and ROBINS-I or Newcastle-Ottawa for bias.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
The study (upload the full text): [UPLOAD]
Design as stated by the authors: [cohort / case-control / cross-sectional]
Clinical question I care about: [one line]
Task
1. Confirm the real design and the direction of inquiry, and whether the authors' label is correct.
2. Selection: source population, how participants were identified, and whether selection could relate to both exposure and outcome.
3. Measurement: how the exposure and outcome were measured, and whether misclassification is differential.
4. Confounding: which confounders were measured and adjusted for, which important ones are missing, and whether the adjustment set is sensible (no mediators or colliders).
5. Analysis: model choice, events per variable, handling of missing data, and sensitivity analyses.
6. Causality: apply the Bradford Hill considerations briefly to the main association.
7. Interpretation: whether the authors' language matches the design (association versus causation).
8. An overall risk-of-bias judgement and a bottom line for practice.
Rules
Quote the paper for each judgement and mark anything missing as [NOT REPORTED], because journal-club audiences check claims against the text. Don't dismiss the study merely for being observational; judge how well it handled its own biases.
Output
Eight headed sections, a bias table (domain, concern, likely direction), then a one-paragraph verdict.
Tweak
End with the unmeasured confounder most likely to explain the result, and how a future study could address it.
How to get more out of it
  • Draw the causal diagram for the main association. Missing confounders become obvious.
  • Large effect sizes, dose-response relationships and consistency across studies strengthen a causal reading.
  • Watch for "healthy user" effects in drug studies. They are a classic trap.
  • → NEXT #479 Confounding in an observational paper
465Appraise a diagnostic accuracy study
Master
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen your journal-club paper evaluates a test, score or imaging method.
WhyDiagnostic studies are easily biased, through the wrong spectrum of patients, partial verification or unblinded reading, and the resulting accuracy figures often collapse in real practice. QUADAS-2 thinking protects you from adopting a test that won't perform.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a diagnostic-research methodologist who applies QUADAS-2 and STARD, and who explains sensitivity, specificity and likelihood ratios in bedside terms.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The study (upload the full text): [UPLOAD]
The clinical role I would use this test for: [replacement / triage / add-on]
Prevalence of the condition in my setting, if known: [estimate or "unknown"]
Task
1. Patient selection: consecutive or random, the case-control ("two-gate") design risk, and whether the spectrum matches my practice.
2. Index test: conduct, threshold (pre-specified or data-driven), and blinding to the reference standard.
3. Reference standard: whether it correctly classifies the condition, and blinding to the index test.
4. Flow and timing: the interval between tests, whether all patients received the same reference standard, and exclusions and indeterminate results.
5. Results: reconstruct the 2 × 2 table, then check the sensitivity, specificity, predictive values and likelihood ratios with 95% CIs.
6. Apply the results to my setting's prevalence: the post-test probabilities for a positive and a negative result.
7. A QUADAS-2 judgement per domain, with applicability concerns.
8. A bottom line: should we use this test, and for what role?
Rules
Quote the paper for judgements, and show the arithmetic for recalculated values and post-test probabilities, because the audience may check them. Mark any numbers not reported as [NOT REPORTED] instead of inferring them.
Output
Eight headed sections, the 2 × 2 table, the QUADAS-2 table, then the bottom line.
Tweak
End with the patient group in whom this test would most likely mislead, and why.
How to get more out of it
  • Likelihood ratios are more useful at the bedside than sensitivity and specificity. Teach them.
  • If the threshold was chosen after seeing the data, the accuracy is optimistic.
  • A test is only useful if it changes management. Ask what you would do differently with the result.
  • → NEXT #461 Journal club presentation: appraisal to bottom line
466Appraise a systematic review or meta-analysis
Master
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen your journal-club paper is a systematic review or meta-analysis.
WhyMeta-analyses sit at the top of the evidence pyramid, but only if they are done well. Poor searches, mixing of incompatible studies, low-quality inputs and ignored heterogeneity can produce confident, wrong answers. AMSTAR 2 and GRADE thinking separate robust reviews from misleading ones.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a systematic-review methodologist and GRADE-trained guideline developer who appraises reviews using AMSTAR 2 and explains forest plots clearly.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The review (upload the full text and supplements if available): [UPLOAD]
Clinical question I care about: [one line]
My comfort level with meta-analysis statistics: [beginner / intermediate / advanced]
Task
1. Question and protocol: a clear PICO, and whether it was registered (e.g. PROSPERO) before the review.
2. Search: databases, dates, grey literature, language limits, and whether it was comprehensive.
3. Selection and extraction: duplicate screening and extraction, and the list of excluded studies with reasons.
4. Risk of bias of the included studies: the tool used, and how the results were incorporated.
5. Synthesis: appropriateness of pooling, fixed versus random effects, heterogeneity (I², prediction interval), sensitivity and subgroup analyses.
6. Publication bias: funnel plot or tests, where appropriate.
7. Certainty of evidence: GRADE for the main outcomes, whether reported or as my estimate.
8. An AMSTAR 2 critical-domain judgement and a bottom line.
Rules
Quote the paper for each judgement, and mark missing items as [NOT REPORTED], because reporting gaps are themselves findings. Explain the forest plot using the review's own numbers, without recomputing the pooled estimates.
Output
Eight headed sections, the AMSTAR 2 table, a plain-language forest-plot explanation, then the bottom line.
Tweak
End with whether a new trial is still needed on this question, and why.
How to get more out of it
  • A meta-analysis of small, biased trials is still biased. Check the inputs before admiring the pooled result.
  • High I² means "these studies disagree". Find out why before trusting the average.
  • Look for the prediction interval. It shows the range of effects to expect in a new setting.
  • → NEXT #473 Explain a forest plot to the audience
467Decode the statistics in my paper
Master
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident
Use itWhen the paper's statistics are beyond your comfort level and the journal club is soon.
WhyFaculty often ask "what does this hazard ratio mean?" or "why this test?". Understanding the statistics in your own paper, in plain language, is the difference between a confident presenter and one who reads the numbers aloud.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a biostatistician who teaches clinicians to read the statistics in published papers, in plain language first and technical language second.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The paper (upload, or paste the methods and results): [UPLOAD / PASTE]
Statistical terms I don't understand in it: [list]
My statistics background: [beginner / intermediate]
Task
1. List every statistical method used, and explain in one line why it was chosen for this data.
2. Explain each key result in plain language: the effect measure, its CI, the p value, and what they mean together.
3. Explain the terms I listed with an example from this paper.
4. Convert relative measures to absolute ones where the data allows (ARR, NNT), showing the arithmetic.
5. Point out any statistical choice a reviewer might question (e.g. multiplicity, per-protocol analysis, stepwise selection).
6. Write 3 "if asked, say this" sentences about the statistics for my journal club.
7. Suggest one simple visual to explain the main result.
8. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Use only the numbers in the paper, and if something can't be calculated from the reported data, say so rather than estimating, because recalculated numbers will be checked by the audience.
Output
A methods table (method, purpose), the plain-language results, the glossary, the absolute measures, the questionable choices, then the scripted sentences.
Tweak
End with the one statistics question I'm most likely to be asked, and the ideal answer.
How to get more out of it
  • Always convert relative risk reductions into absolute numbers. It changes how impressive a result looks.
  • If a CI crosses the line of no effect, say "inconclusive", not "no effect".
  • Ask a statistician colleague to check your NNT arithmetic before the session.
  • → NEXT #461 Journal club presentation: appraisal to bottom line
468Five-line PICO summary of the paper
Standard
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident / MBBS Student
Use itAs your first step with any paper, and for the opening slide.
Persona
You are an evidence-based medicine tutor who summarises studies precisely.
My context
The paper or its abstract and methods: [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
My specialty: [brief]
Audience: [brief]
Task
1. Write the PICO(T): population with key inclusion features, intervention or exposure, comparator, primary outcome and time frame.
2. Add the design, the setting (country and number of centres) and the sample size.
3. State the main result with its effect estimate and CI.
4. Write the whole summary in 5 lines for a slide.
Rules
Use the paper's own definitions and numbers exactly, and write [NOT REPORTED] if something is missing, because the opening summary sets the audience's understanding of everything that follows.
Output
The PICO table, then the 5-line slide text.
Pro tipIf you can't write the PICO clearly, re-read the methods before going further.
Try it withA multicentre RCT of early versus delayed anticoagulation after ischaemic stroke with atrial fibrillation.

Standard
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident

Persona
You are a research-integrity reviewer who compares abstracts with full texts.
My context
The abstract: [PASTE ABSTRACT]
The results section and tables: [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Trial registration details, if available: [PASTE]
Task
1. Compare every number in the abstract with the results section and tables.
2. Check whether the abstract highlights secondary outcomes or subgroups over a non-significant primary outcome.
3. Check whether the abstract's conclusion matches the primary result.
4. Check whether harms reported in the paper appear in the abstract.
5. Summarise any spin found, with examples.
Rules
Quote both texts for every discrepancy, because accusations of spin must be demonstrated, not asserted.

A comparison table (item, abstract, full text, match), then the spin summary.

What I know about prior evidence and guidelines (with sources): [LIST]
Audience: [brief]

Represent the authors' rationale accurately, and mark any claim of mine that isn't from the paper or my sources as [VERIFY], because context slides are often where misquotation happens.

My context
The paper's methods section: [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Design: [design]
Task

Report the methods exactly as the paper states them, and flag missing essentials as [NOT REPORTED], because methods slides are where the audience looks for flaws.

My context
The paper's results section, tables and figures: [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Primary outcome: [state]
Task
1. Present the primary outcome with the event rates in each group, the effect estimate, the CI and the p value.
2. Present the 2–3 most important secondary outcomes and the main harms.

473Explain a forest plot to the audience
Standard

You are a statistics teacher who explains forest plots in plain language.
My context
A description of the forest plot, or the numbers in it: [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Outcome and effect measure: [e.g. risk ratio for mortality]
Task
1. Explain the anatomy: study rows, squares (weight), lines (CIs), the diamond (pooled estimate) and the line of no effect.
2. Interpret this specific plot: the direction, size and precision of the pooled effect, and the consistency across studies.
3. Explain the heterogeneity statistics shown.
4. Write a 1-minute spoken explanation for the journal club.

Use only the plot's reported numbers and don't recompute the pooled estimate, because recalculations from a figure are unreliable.

Standard

Persona
You are a biostatistician who explains time-to-event results clearly.
My context
A description of the Kaplan-Meier figure, and the reported HR, CI, p value and numbers at risk: [PASTE]
Task
1. Explain the axes, the censoring marks and the numbers at risk.
2. Explain when the curves separate, and what that implies clinically.
3. Explain the hazard ratio in plain language, and whether proportional hazards seem reasonable from the curves.

Standard
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident / MBBS Student
Use itFor every trial or cohort result you present.
Persona
You are an EBM tutor who converts relative results into absolute terms clinicians can use.
My context
Event counts or rates in each group, for benefits and harms: [PASTE NUMBERS FROM THE PAPER]
Follow-up duration: [time]
Task
1. Calculate the control event rate, the experimental event rate, ARR, RRR and NNT, with a CI for the NNT where possible.
2. Do the same for the main harm (ARI and NNH).
3. Interpret the benefit-harm balance in plain language.
4. Show how the NNT changes for a patient with a higher or lower baseline risk.
Rules
Show every formula and step, state the time frame of the NNT, and use only the paper's numbers, because NNT without a time frame is meaningless.

A calculation table, then the plain-language interpretation.

Standard
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident
Use itFor the core appraisal section of your journal club.
Persona

My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The paper (methods and results): [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Design: [design]
Task
1. Assess selection bias, performance bias, detection bias, attrition bias and reporting bias.
2. For each, give a judgement (low, some concern, high) and a quote from the paper.
3. Say whether any bias could plausibly explain the entire result.
4. Summarise the overall internal validity in 3 sentences.

Quote the paper for each judgement, and mark unreported items [NOT REPORTED], because judgements without evidence won't survive faculty questioning.

477Does this apply to our patients?

My context
The paper's population, setting, intervention delivery and exclusions: [PASTE]
Our patients and setting: [e.g. tertiary government hospital, high TB and malnutrition burden, limited ICU beds]
Task
1. Compare the study population with our patients: age, severity, comorbidities, ethnicity and socio-economic factors.
2. Compare the setting and resources: staffing, monitoring, drug and device availability, and cost.
3. Identify exclusions that remove patients we commonly see.
4. Judge whether the effect would likely be larger, smaller or similar here.
5. Write the applicability slide.
Rules
Base the comparison on the paper's reported characteristics and my description, and mark assumptions as [ASSUMPTION], because applicability judgements are opinion and should be labelled as such.

478Hunt for the hidden bias
Standard
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident
Use itWhen the paper looks clean and you want to find what others will miss.
Persona
You are a sceptical peer reviewer with a gift for spotting subtle bias.
My context
The full paper: [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Task
1. Look for subtle issues: run-in periods, enrichment, early stopping for benefit, composite outcomes driven by soft components, per-protocol-only analyses, changes to outcomes or sample size, imbalance in co-interventions, and industry involvement in analysis.
2. For each issue found, quote the paper and explain its likely effect.
3. Rank the issues by how much they could change the interpretation.
4. Suggest how to present the key issue in the journal club without being unfair.
Rules
Report only issues supported by the text, and say "none found" for categories that are clean, because inventing problems is as bad as missing them.

Standard

Persona

My context
Exposure, outcome and the variables adjusted for (from the methods and tables): [PASTE]
Task

2. Check which were measured and adjusted for, and which are missing.
3. Check for adjustment for mediators or colliders.

487The clinical bottom line
Standard
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itFor the final slide of your journal club.
Persona
You are a senior clinician who turns appraisals into clear, honest practice decisions.
My context
My appraisal summary (validity, results, applicability): [PASTE]

Output
The three one-liners, the bottom line, the patient groups, then the next steps.
Pro tipEnd with a question to the head of department: "Should we change our protocol?". It starts the real discussion.
Try it withAppraisal of a trial of restrictive versus liberal transfusion in upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

488Questions to drive the discussion
Standard
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident

Persona

My context

2. For each, write the key points a good answer would contain.

491Fill the CASP checklist for my paper
Standard
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident / MBBS Student

Persona
You are an EBM tutor familiar with the CASP checklists for each study design.
My context
Study design: [RCT / cohort / case-control / diagnostic / systematic review / qualitative]
The paper: [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Task
1. Identify the correct CASP checklist for the design.
2. Answer each checklist question with yes, no or can't tell, and a quote from the paper.
3. Summarise the overall appraisal in 3 sentences.
Rules
Base every answer on the paper's text and mark "can't tell" where it isn't reported, because the checklist is only valuable if it is honest.

492Certainty of evidence using GRADE
Standard
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen you want to rate how confident we can be in the paper's main finding.
Persona
You are a GRADE-trained guideline methodologist.
My context
The paper's design and main outcome result: [PASTE]
Its main limitations from my appraisal: [LIST]
Task
1. Start from the design's baseline certainty.
2. Assess each downgrading domain: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias.
3. Assess the upgrading domains for observational studies (large effect, dose-response, plausible confounding).
4. Give the final certainty (high, moderate, low or very low) with reasoning.
5. Write a GRADE-style sentence ("…probably reduces…").
Rules
Apply GRADE to a single study cautiously, and state that GRADE is designed for bodies of evidence, because rating one study alone overstates precision.
Output
A GRADE table (domain, judgement, reason), then the final rating and the sentence.
Pro tipGRADE-style wording, such as "probably" or "may", is an excellent way to phrase your bottom line.
Try it withA single large RCT with some risk of bias and a wide CI.

493Appraise a qualitative study
Standard
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen your journal-club paper uses interviews or focus groups.
Persona
You are a qualitative health researcher familiar with COREQ and the CASP qualitative checklist.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The paper: [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Task
1. Assess the fit of a qualitative approach for the question.
2. Assess sampling, data collection, the researchers' reflexivity, analysis method, saturation and rigour (e.g. member checking, triangulation).
3. Assess whether the findings are supported by quotes.
4. Discuss transferability to our setting.
5. Summarise the value of the findings for practice.
Rules
Judge qualitative research by its own standards of rigour, not by sample size or statistics, because applying quantitative criteria misjudges it.
Output
Headed appraisal sections, then the summary.
Pro tipQualitative studies explain the "why" behind poor adherence and patient behaviour. They make excellent journal clubs.
Try it withInterviews with patients about reasons for stopping TB treatment.

494Appraise an economic evaluation
Standard
2.2 Journal club · Faculty / Senior Resident
Use itWhen your paper is a cost-effectiveness or cost-utility analysis.
Persona
You are a health economist who explains economic evaluations to clinicians.
My context
The paper: [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Our health system context: [e.g. Indian public sector, PMJAY]
Task
1. Identify the type of evaluation, the perspective, the comparators and the time horizon.
2. Check the cost and outcome sources, discounting, and QALY or DALY calculations.
3. Explain the ICER and whether it is below the stated threshold.
4. Assess the sensitivity analyses and the uncertainty.
5. Judge transferability to Indian costs and willingness-to-pay thresholds.
Rules
Report the paper's own numbers and thresholds, and mark any Indian threshold as [VERIFY], because thresholds vary and are debated.
Output
Headed sections, then a transferability judgement.
Pro tipAn intervention can be cost-effective in one country and unaffordable in another. Emphasise that.
Try it withCost-effectiveness of a new diagnostic test for TB in a high-burden setting.

495Appraise a prognostic or prediction-model study
Standard
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen your paper develops or validates a risk score or prediction model.
Persona
You are a clinical prediction-model methodologist familiar with TRIPOD and PROBAST.
My context
The paper: [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Intended use of the model: [brief]
Task
1. Assess the participants, predictors, outcome definition and timing.
2. Assess the sample size and events per variable, the handling of missing data and continuous predictors, and the variable-selection method.
3. Assess performance: discrimination (C-statistic), calibration and clinical utility.
4. Check for internal and external validation.
5. Judge readiness for clinical use.
Rules
Distinguish development from validation clearly, because a model tested only on its own development data will look better than it is.
Output
A PROBAST-style table by domain, then the readiness judgement.
Pro tipCalibration matters as much as the C-statistic, and it is often not reported. Look for it.
Try it withA new score predicting in-hospital mortality in dengue.

496Appraise a clinical guideline (AGREE II)
Standard
2.2 Journal club · Faculty / Senior Resident
Use itWhen the journal-club document is a clinical practice guideline.
Persona
You are a guideline appraiser trained in AGREE II.
My context
The guideline (upload or paste the methods and recommendations): [UPLOAD]
Task
1. Appraise the AGREE II domains: scope and purpose, stakeholder involvement, rigour of development, clarity of presentation, applicability and editorial independence.
2. Give a domain score or judgement with evidence from the document.
3. Highlight the recommendations with weak evidence but strong wording.
4. Give an overall recommendation for use.
Rules
Base scores on what the document reports, and mark missing methodological details as [NOT REPORTED], because good guidelines document their methods transparently.
Output
An AGREE II domain table, the flagged recommendations, then the overall judgement.
Pro tipLook for how conflicts of interest among panel members were managed. It's often revealing.

497Check the trial registry for outcome switching
Standard
2.2 Journal club · PG Resident
Use itFor any RCT, before you present it.
Persona
You are a research-transparency analyst.
My context
Registration number and the registered primary and secondary outcomes, sample size and dates: [PASTE FROM THE REGISTRY]
What the paper reports: [PASTE]
Task
1. Compare the registered and reported primary outcomes: definition, measure and time point.
2. Compare the secondary outcomes, and note any added or dropped.
3. Compare the planned and actual sample sizes and dates (was it registered prospectively?).
4. Check whether the paper explains any changes.
5. Judge the impact on credibility.
Rules
Report only differences that are verifiable from the two sources, because an outcome switch is a serious accusation.
Output
A comparison table (item, registered, reported, explained yes or no), then the judgement.
Pro tipMany trials change outcomes legitimately with an explanation. Note whether one is given.

My purpose: [journal club / clinical question / thesis]
Task

2. Give the 3 questions to answer at each stage.

Standard

Section 2.3
2.3

Slide design & structure

Slides support the speaker; they are not the speech. One message per slide, visuals over paragraphs, and text readable from the back row.

40prompts
4Master
23Standard
13Quick
How to use this section

Use it once your content is ready, to turn it into clear slides that are readable from the back row.

Start with the Master prompts (#521–524) for the full workflow; use the Standard prompts (#525–547) for one task at a time; reach for the Quick prompts (#548–560) when you have two minutes. Tap any title below to jump to it, and follow → NEXT to move to the next step.
