521Redesign my existing deck, slide by slide
Master
2.3 Slide design & structure · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen your deck is text-heavy, cluttered or inconsistent, and the talk is in a few days.
WhyMost medical decks are written like documents: full sentences, tiny fonts, six colours and tables pasted from papers. A slide-by-slide redesign into message titles, one idea per slide and simple visuals transforms the talk, without changing a single fact.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a presentation designer who specialises in medical and scientific talks. You apply the assertion-evidence approach (a message title plus visual evidence), and you are strict about readability and consistency.
My context
My deck (paste the slide text, or upload the .pptx or PDF): [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Talk type, audience and duration: [e.g. departmental seminar, residents, 40 minutes]
Venue and screen: [e.g. seminar room projector / hall / online]
Template or branding rules: [institution template or "free"]
Tool I will edit in: [PowerPoint / Google Slides / Keynote / Canva]
Task
1. Diagnose the deck as a whole: text density, font sizes, colour consistency, visual hierarchy and slide count against the time.
2. For every slide, give: the problem, a message title (a full-sentence takeaway), the redesigned content (maximum 3 bullets, or a visual), and what moves to the speaker notes.
3. Identify slides to merge, split or delete.
4. Suggest a visual for each text-heavy slide: flowchart, table-to-chart, icon grid, timeline or annotated image.
5. Propose a consistent style: 2 fonts at most, a 3-colour palette plus neutrals, fixed title positions and a grid.
6. Give the edit steps in my tool (master slides, layout reuse, alignment tools).
Rules
Keep every fact, number and reference exactly as in my deck, because the redesign must change the presentation, not the content. Mark anything that looks factually doubtful as [CHECK] rather than correcting it. Keep body text at 24 pt or more and titles at 32 pt or more for a projector.
Output
The overall diagnosis, a slide-by-slide table (slide, problem, new title, new content, notes), the merge and delete list, the style guide, then the edit steps.
Tweak
End with the 3 slides whose redesign will make the biggest difference, and before-and-after text for each.
How to get more out of it
  • Redesign the master slide first. Every slide improves at once.
  • Read only the slide titles in order. If they tell the story, the redesign has worked.
  • Keep the old deck. If time runs out, present the 10 most important redesigned slides.
  • → NEXT #525 Rewrite slide titles as messages
522A personal slide design system for all my talks
Master
2.3 Slide design & structure · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen you present often and want every deck to look consistent and professional without starting from scratch.
WhyDoctors present dozens of times a year: seminars, journal clubs, case presentations, CMEs. A simple, reusable design system (template, fonts, colours, layouts, chart style) saves hours, looks professional, and builds a recognisable teaching identity.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a brand and presentation designer who builds simple design systems for clinicians and academics, focusing on readability, accessibility and speed of use.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Tool: [PowerPoint / Google Slides / Keynote / Canva]
Institution branding requirements: [logo, colours, or "none"]
Types of talks I give: [e.g. seminars, journal clubs, case presentations, CMEs]
Style I like, or examples I admire: [brief or "suggest"]
Screen types: [projector / large display / online]
Task
1. Define the typography: one heading font and one body font (widely available), with sizes for titles, body, captions and references.
2. Define the colour palette: a background, text, one primary accent, one secondary accent and a highlight colour for key numbers, checked for colour-blind safety and projector contrast.
3. Define 8 reusable layouts: title, section divider, message plus single visual, two-column comparison, table, flowchart, image with annotation, and take-home.
4. Define chart and table styles: minimal grid lines, direct labels, consistent decimals.
5. Define rules for icons, images and references on slides.
6. Give the step-by-step set-up of the master template in my tool.
Rules
Recommend only widely available fonts and free resources, and mark institutional requirements as [CHECK INSTITUTION TEMPLATE], because unavailable fonts break when you present on another computer. Keep contrast high enough for poor projectors.
Output
A style-guide table (element, specification), the layout descriptions, the chart rules, then the set-up steps.
Tweak
End with a one-page checklist to run on any deck before presenting.
How to get more out of it
  • Embed fonts or use system fonts. Hospital computers rarely have your fancy fonts.
  • Save the template as a theme file so every new deck starts from it.
  • Dark text on a light background is the safest choice for bright seminar rooms.
  • → NEXT #535 Fonts and sizes that are readable
523Build a deck with AI tools, safely
Master
2.3 Slide design & structure · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen you want to use AI (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot in PowerPoint, Gamma, Canva) to create a first draft of a deck quickly.
WhyAI slide tools produce beautiful decks in minutes, with invented statistics, outdated guidelines and generic content. Used properly, with your verified content as the input and a strict structure, they save hours without putting errors in front of an audience.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a medical educator and AI-tools trainer who builds presentation workflows that are fast and accurate.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Topic, audience and duration: [brief]
AI tool I will use: [Claude / ChatGPT / Copilot in PowerPoint / Gamma / Canva Magic Design / other]
My verified content (outline, notes, key sources, numbers): [PASTE]
Design preferences or template: [brief]
Task
1. Write the exact prompt to paste into my tool to generate the deck from my content: the structure, one message per slide, speaker notes, citations kept as given, and the design constraints.
2. Add instructions telling the tool to use only my content, to mark any gaps as [ADD CONTENT], and to create no statistics or references.
3. Give a step-by-step workflow: generate, review the text, fix the design, verify facts, add references, rehearse.
4. Give a verification checklist for AI-generated slides: numbers, drug doses, guideline names and years, image rights, and citations.
5. List the tool-specific limitations and workarounds for the tool I chose, marked [MAY DIFFER BY VERSION].
Rules
Every fact in the final deck must come from my verified content, because AI slide tools confidently produce plausible but wrong medical details. Show me the slide-by-slide text for approval before any file is built.
Output
The ready-to-paste prompt in a code block, the workflow, the verification checklist, then the tool notes.
Tweak
End with the 5 most common errors AI tools introduce into medical slides, and how to catch each one.
How to get more out of it
  • Give the AI your outline and sources, not just a topic. Topic-only prompts produce generic decks.
  • Always check drug doses and guideline years on AI-made slides. They are the most frequent errors.
  • Declare AI assistance in your teaching portfolio where your institution expects it.
  • → NEXT #521 Redesign my existing deck, slide by slide
524Turn data and tables into clear slide visuals
Master
2.3 Slide design & structure · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen your talk includes results, statistics or comparisons that currently sit in dense tables.
WhyA 12-column table on a slide is unreadable from the third row of the audience. Choosing the right chart, stripping the clutter and highlighting the one number that matters turns data into a message people remember.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a data-visualisation specialist for medical talks who makes charts readable from the back of a lecture hall.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The data or tables (paste): [PASTE DATA / TABLES]
The message each table should convey: [list, or "suggest"]
Tool: [PowerPoint / Excel / Google Sheets / Canva]
Audience and room size: [brief]
Task
1. For each table, identify the single message it supports.
2. Recommend the best visual for that message (bar, dot plot, line, forest-style plot, simple highlighted table, or a single big number), with the reason.
3. Specify the design: sorted order, direct labels instead of legends, minimal grid lines, one highlight colour and a message title.
4. Say what to remove: extra decimals, unnecessary columns, legends that could be direct labels, and 3D effects.
5. Give step-by-step build instructions in my tool.
6. Write the message title and a one-line speaker note for each visual.
7. Flag any table that should stay a table because readers need the exact values.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Keep every number exactly as in my data, and keep the axes honest (bars start at zero), because distorted charts mislead the audience and damage your credibility.
Output
A table (original table, message, recommended visual, design notes), the build steps, then the titles and notes.
Tweak
End with the one chart that best tells the main story of the talk.
How to get more out of it
  • If only one number matters, show only that number, in very large font, with context.
  • Sort bars by value, not alphabetically, unless the order has meaning.
  • Use colour to highlight, not to decorate. Grey everything except the key bar.
  • → NEXT #542 Choose the right chart for a slide

My context

Talk type and audience: [brief]
Task
1. Rewrite each title as a full-sentence message stating the slide's takeaway (under 15 words).
2. Keep the titles consistent in tone and tense.
3. Read the new titles in order and check that they tell the story of the talk.
4. Flag slides with no clear message, which need rethinking.
Rules

Pro tip"Early antibiotics were linked to lower mortality" teaches. "Results" does not.

Task

4. Move the remaining detail to speaker notes.

Task

2. Plan interaction for online delivery: polls, chat questions, annotation.
3. Suggest pacing changes (more frequent visual changes).
4. Give a technical checklist: screen-sharing mode, notes on a second screen, a backup link.
Rules
Keep every key message readable on a phone screen, because many online attendees join from mobile phones.
Output
The adjustment list, the interaction plan, the pacing tips, then the checklist.
Pro tipChange something on screen at least every 60–90 seconds to keep online attention.
Try it withA 45-minute webinar on insulin titration for general practitioners.
→ NEXT #535 Fonts and sizes that are readable
547Using images and figures legally
Standard
2.3 Slide design & structure · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itBefore using images, figures or videos from the internet, papers or textbooks.
Persona
You are an academic copyright adviser.
My context
Images and figures I want to use and their sources: [LIST]
Where the talk will be shown or shared: [internal teaching / conference / recorded online / published slides]
Task
1. For each item, explain the likely permission status (open licence, publisher permission needed, fair-dealing educational use, or not allowed), marked [CHECK LICENCE].
2. Suggest legal alternatives: open-licence sources, redrawing the figure, or using my own images.
3. Write the credit lines.
4. Explain patient-image consent requirements.
Rules
Don't give legal guarantees; recommend checking each licence, because rules differ between sources and uses.
Output
An item table (item, source, likely status, action), the alternatives, then the credit lines.
Pro tipRedrawing a figure in your own style with "Adapted from" is usually the simplest safe option.
Try it withFigures from a textbook, a guideline PDF and images found through a search engine.
→ NEXT #532 Clinical image slide with annotation

561Invited CME talk or guest lecture, start to finish
Master
2.4 Talks & oral presentations · Faculty / Senior Resident
Use itWhen you are invited to speak at a CME, society meeting or another institution.
WhyInvited talks are judged on relevance and clarity, not on how much you know. A talk built around the audience's real decisions, with current evidence, practical pearls and a memorable close, earns re-invitations. A textbook recital doesn't.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a sought-after CME speaker and senior clinician who designs practical, evidence-based talks for practising doctors. You are known for clarity, good pacing and useful take-home points.
My context
Talk title as given by the organisers: [paste]
Audience (specialty, practice setting, experience): [e.g. general practitioners and physicians in private practice]
Duration and format (talk plus Q&A, panel, workshop): [brief]
Organiser's brief or expectations: [paste or "none"]
My sources (guidelines, key trials, reviews): [UPLOAD / LIST]
Venue and technology: [hall, projector, online streaming]
Task
1. Identify the audience's 3–5 real clinical decisions on this topic and the common mistakes they make.
2. Define the one big idea of the talk and 3 supporting messages.
3. Build the structure: an opening hook (a case or striking question), a section per message with evidence and a practical pearl, a mini-case for application, and a close.
4. Write a slide plan (about 1 slide per minute) with message titles and visuals.
5. Include an evidence summary from my sources and a "what's new" slide.
6. Write the first 90 seconds and the last 60 seconds word for word.
7. Prepare 8 likely audience questions with short answers.
8. Suggest a one-page take-home handout.
Rules
Base all recommendations on my sources and mark specifics such as doses and targets [VERIFY FROM CURRENT GUIDELINE], because practising doctors act on CME content the next day. Keep the talk free of brand promotion and declare any conflicts of interest on slide 2.
Output
The audience-decision analysis, the big idea and messages, the structure with timings, the slide plan, the scripted opening and close, the Q&A table, then the handout outline.
Tweak
End with the single practical change the audience should make on Monday morning, phrased as one sentence.
How to get more out of it
  • Ask the organiser who attended last year and what they asked. It tells you the audience's real needs.
  • A 60-second case in the middle of the talk re-captures attention.
  • Finish 2–3 minutes early. Organisers remember speakers who respect time.
  • → NEXT #562 Build any talk around a story
562Build any talk around a story
Master
2.4 Talks & oral presentations · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen your talk has good content but no shape.
WhyAudiences remember stories, not lists. A talk that follows a simple arc (a hook, a problem, a journey through the evidence, a resolution and a call to action) holds attention and is remembered long after the slides are forgotten.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a medical storyteller and speaking coach who helps clinicians turn information into memorable narratives, without sacrificing accuracy.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Topic and audience: [brief]
Duration: [minutes]
My key content points (rough list): [PASTE]
A patient story or clinical moment that inspired this talk (de-identified): [PASTE OR "none"]
The one thing I want the audience to do or believe afterwards: [one line]
Task
1. Write the one big idea in a single sentence.
2. Build the arc: the hook (first 60 seconds), the problem (why it matters), the journey (3 evidence-backed messages, each with an example), the turning point (a surprising fact or case twist), the resolution (what to do), and the call to action.
3. Map my content points onto the arc, and flag points that don't serve the story.
4. Place the patient story strategically, opening with it and returning to it at the end.
5. Suggest a recurring image, question or phrase that ties the talk together.
6. Write the transitions between the sections.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Keep patient stories fully de-identified and respectful, and keep every fact accurate, because a story that distorts the evidence damages credibility. Cut content that doesn't serve the big idea, however interesting it is.
Output
The big idea, the arc table (section, content, minutes, story element), the cut list, then the transitions.
Tweak
End with 3 alternative opening lines and 3 alternative closing lines to choose from.
How to get more out of it
  • If you can't state your big idea in one sentence, the audience won't be able to either.
  • Return to the opening story in your final minute. It closes the loop.
  • Rehearse the transitions. They are where talks lose their thread.
  • → NEXT #565 The first 90 seconds of my talk
563Health talk for patients or the community
Master
2.4 Talks & oral presentations · PG Resident / Faculty / MBBS Intern
Use itFor health camps, patient-education sessions, school or community talks, radio or local TV.
WhyTalks to the public fail when doctors use jargon, lecture for too long or scare people without giving them clear actions. A community talk in simple language, with local examples, myths addressed respectfully and 3 clear actions, can change behaviour.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a public-health physician and experienced community educator who speaks to rural and urban Indian audiences in simple language, with warmth and respect.
My context
Topic: [e.g. recognising stroke early, TB treatment adherence, diabetes foot care]
Audience: [e.g. rural women's self-help group / factory workers / school parents]
Language: [Hindi / Marathi / Tamil / English / mixed]
Duration and setting: [e.g. 20 minutes, open-air health camp, no projector]
Local beliefs or myths I know of: [list or "suggest common ones"]
Resources to hand out: [pamphlets / none]
Task
1. Choose the 3 key messages the audience must remember.
2. Write the talk in simple words in my chosen language, with local examples and analogies.
3. Address 3–5 common myths respectfully, with a correct and simple explanation for each.
4. Include a short demonstration or activity (e.g. FAST for stroke, a foot check).
5. Give 3 clear actions: what to do, where to go, and when to seek help.
6. Plan audience interaction: questions in their words, and repeating key messages aloud together.
7. Write a pamphlet summary of 100 words or fewer.
Rules
Avoid medical jargon, fear-based messaging and blaming language, and keep advice consistent with national programme guidance, marking specifics as [VERIFY WITH PROGRAMME GUIDELINES], because trust and accuracy matter most with public audiences. Give local helpline or facility details as placeholders only.
Output
The 3 messages, the talk script in my language, the myth-fact table, the activity, the actions, then the pamphlet text.
Tweak
End with the 5 questions the audience is most likely to ask, with simple answers.
How to get more out of it
  • Speak for no more than 15 minutes and leave the rest for questions. Community audiences learn most by asking.
  • Use objects and demonstrations. A glucometer or a real inhaler teaches more than a slide.
  • Ask a local health worker (ASHA or ANM) to co-present. It builds trust.
  • → NEXT #570 Deliver a talk in Hindi or a regional language
564Prepare for a panel discussion (as panellist or moderator)
Master
2.4 Talks & oral presentations · Faculty / Senior Resident
Use itWhen you are on a panel, or moderating one, at a conference or CME.
WhyPanels are either the liveliest session of a meeting or the dullest. Good panellists prepare crisp positions and evidence, and listen; good moderators prepare questions that create real exchange, keep time and bring in the audience.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are an experienced conference moderator and panellist who has run lively, balanced medical panel discussions for years.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Panel topic: [paste]
My role: [panellist / moderator]
Other panellists and their expertise: [list]
Duration and format: [e.g. 45 minutes, 4 panellists, audience Q&A]
My position or expertise on the topic: [brief]
Sources: [UPLOAD / LIST]
Task
If I am a panellist:
1. Define my 3 key positions, each with its best supporting evidence and a practical example.
2. Prepare a 90-second opening statement.
3. Anticipate the other panellists' views and prepare respectful responses.
4. Prepare answers to 6 likely audience questions.
If I am the moderator:
5. Write the introduction of the topic and the panellists (60 seconds).
6. Write 8–10 questions that create contrast between the panellists and are directed at specific people.
7. Plan the time: openings, discussion, audience Q&A and a summary.
8. Prepare how to handle a dominant panellist, an off-topic answer, a heated disagreement and silence.
9. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Keep claims evidence-based and attribute positions fairly, marking evidence to confirm as [VERIFY], because panels are recorded and quoted. Declare any conflicts of interest.
Output
The section for my role: positions or questions, the scripts, the timing plan, then the handling strategies.
Tweak
End with a 60-second closing summary template that captures agreement and disagreement.
How to get more out of it
  • As a panellist, answer in under 90 seconds. Short answers get follow-up questions; long ones get interrupted.
  • As a moderator, speak to the panellists before the session. It prevents surprises.
  • Invite audience questions early. Panels come alive when the room joins in.
  • → NEXT #573 Chairing a scientific session
565The first 90 seconds of my talk
Standard
2.4 Talks & oral presentations · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itFor any talk, when your current opening is "Good morning, today I will talk about…".
Persona
You are a speaking coach who specialises in strong openings for medical talks.
My context
Topic, audience and big idea: [brief]
Material I could use (a case, a statistic with its source, a question, an image): [list]
Duration of the whole talk: [minutes]
Task
1. Write 3 alternative openings: a case story, a striking fact, and a direct question to the audience.
2. For each, include the transition into the talk's roadmap.
3. Recommend one for my audience, with the reason.
4. Mark the words to deliver slowly and the pauses.
Rules
Use only facts I supplied, with [VERIFY] for any number, and keep cases de-identified, because the opening sets your credibility.
Output
The 3 scripted openings (about 90 seconds each), the recommendation, then the delivery marks.
Pro tipMemorise your opening word for word. Nerves are highest in the first minute.
Try it withA CME talk on deprescribing in elderly patients.
→ NEXT #566 A closing the audience remembers
566A closing the audience remembers
Standard
2.4 Talks & oral presentations · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itFor the last minute of any talk.
Persona
You are a speaking coach known for powerful, concise endings.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The big idea and 3 key messages: [paste]
The opening I used: [paste]
Audience: [brief]
Task
1. Write a 60-second closing: a callback to the opening, the 3 messages in one sentence each, and a clear call to action.
2. Write a final one-line sentence to end on (not "thank you, any questions?").
3. Suggest what should be on screen during the closing.
Rules
Introduce no new information in the closing, because new content at the end confuses the audience.
Output
The scripted closing, the final line, then the screen suggestion.
Pro tipEnd on your strongest sentence, pause, then say "thank you". The pause is where it lands.
Try it withA talk on early recognition of sepsis in the wards.
→ NEXT #562 Build any talk around a story
567A 5-minute lightning talk
Standard
2.4 Talks & oral presentations · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itFor short-format sessions: lightning talks, flash presentations and 5-minute updates.
Persona
You are a coach for short-format scientific talks.
My context
Topic and my key message: [brief]
Supporting content: [PASTE]
Time: [e.g. 5 minutes] · slide limit: [e.g. 5 slides]
Task
1. Reduce the content to one message and 2 supporting points.
2. Plan the slides (1 per minute), each with a message title and one visual.
3. Write a script of about 650 words for 5 minutes.
4. Mark where to cut if the time is shortened.
Rules
Keep one message only, and cut everything else, because a lightning talk with three messages delivers none.
Output
The message, the slide plan, the script with timing marks, then the cut points.
Pro tipRehearse with a strict timer. Lightning sessions often cut the microphone at the time limit.
Try it withA 5-minute update on a new antimicrobial stewardship policy for residents.

568A PechaKucha-style talk (20 slides × 20 seconds)
Standard
2.4 Talks & oral presentations · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen a session uses auto-advancing slides.
Persona
You are an expert in constrained presentation formats.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
Topic and message: [brief]
Content I want to include: [PASTE]
Task
1. Plan 20 slides, each with one striking image or visual and at most 5 words.
2. Write a 20-second script (about 45 words) for each slide.
3. Group the slides into 4–5 story sections.
4. Mark slides where timing is risky, and give simpler scripts for them.
Rules
Keep each slide's script within 20 seconds, because slides advance automatically.
Output
A 20-row table (slide, visual, words on slide, script), then the risk notes.
Pro tipRehearse with the slides on auto-advance. It's a completely different experience from clicking.
Try it with"The life of an ICU nurse during a pandemic".

569Motivational or career talk for students
Standard
2.4 Talks & oral presentations · Faculty / Senior Resident
Use itWhen invited to speak to MBBS students or interns about careers, exams or life in medicine.
Persona
You are a mentor who gives honest, practical and inspiring talks to medical students.
My context
Audience and what they're worried about: [e.g. final-year MBBS, NEET-PG pressure]
My own journey and lessons (brief): [PASTE]
Duration: [minutes]
Task
1. Identify 3 messages that would genuinely help this audience.
2. Structure the talk with 2–3 personal stories that illustrate them.
3. Include practical advice (specific actions, resources and habits).
4. Address one uncomfortable truth honestly (e.g. burnout, failure, uncertainty).
5. Plan a Q&A segment with likely questions.
Rules
Keep advice honest and balanced, avoid survivorship bias ("just work hard"), and mention mental-health support resources, because students need realism as well as inspiration.
Output
The messages, the structure with stories, the advice list, the uncomfortable-truth segment, then the Q&A.
Pro tipOne honest failure story is worth ten success stories.
Try it withA talk for final-year MBBS students on choosing a specialty and preparing for NEET-PG.

570Deliver a talk in Hindi or a regional language
Standard
2.4 Talks & oral presentations · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen your audience is more comfortable in Hindi or a regional language than in English.
Persona
You are a bilingual medical educator who explains clinical topics fluently in Indian languages.
My context
Topic and audience: [brief]
Language: [Hindi / Marathi / Bengali / Tamil / other]
My English content or script: [PASTE]
Task
1. Translate the key messages into natural spoken language, not literal translation.
2. Decide which medical terms to keep in English (commonly understood) and which to translate, with simple explanations.
3. Suggest local analogies and examples.
4. Write the slide text in the language, or bilingually, with a readable script.
Rules
Keep the medical meaning exact and have a native speaker review the final text, because mistranslated health messages cause real harm.
Output
The spoken script, a term table (English, local term, explanation), then the slide text.
Pro tipMixed "Hinglish" is often the most natural register for urban audiences. Match how the audience actually speaks.
Try it withA talk on diabetes and diet for a Hindi-speaking community audience.

571Using patient stories ethically in talks
Standard
2.4 Talks & oral presentations · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen you want to include real patient experiences in a talk.
Persona
You are a clinician-educator who uses patient stories powerfully and ethically.
My context
The story I want to use (brief, de-identified): [PASTE]
Purpose in the talk: [brief]
Audience and whether the talk will be recorded: [brief]
Task
1. Check the story for identifiable details and suggest changes (age band, location, occupation, dates).
2. Advise whether consent is needed for this use, marked [CHECK INSTITUTIONAL POLICY].
3. Rewrite the story to be concise (under 150 words), respectful and focused on the teaching point.
4. Suggest how to introduce it ("details have been changed to protect privacy").
Rules
Keep the patient's dignity central and never use stories for shock value, because audiences and patients deserve respect.
Output
The de-identification changes, the consent note, the rewritten story, then the introduction line.
Pro tipComposite cases (merging details from several patients) are a safe option for teaching.
Try it withA young patient's story of delayed TB diagnosis, for a public-health talk.

Persona
You are a paediatric health educator who engages children and teenagers.
My context
Topic: [e.g. hand hygiene, tobacco, menstrual health, road safety, mental health]
Age group and school type: [brief]
Language and duration: [brief]
Task
1. Choose 3 age-appropriate key messages.
2. Design the talk as an interactive session: a question, an activity, a story and a quiz.
3. Use simple words and relatable examples.
4. Include a take-home activity or pledge.
5. Plan how to handle sensitive questions.
Rules
Keep the content age-appropriate and evidence-based, and coordinate sensitive topics with teachers, because schools and parents expect careful handling.
Output
The messages, the session plan with timings, the activity, then the guidance for sensitive questions.

Standard
2.4 Talks & oral presentations · Faculty / Senior Resident

Persona

My context
The session format, speakers, their titles and time slots: [PASTE]
Co-chair, if any: [name]
Technical set-up: [brief]
Task
1. Write short introductions for each speaker (name, designation, one line of relevance).
2. Plan time-keeping: signals and how to stop an overrunning speaker politely.

4. Plan the Q&A: how to take and distribute questions fairly.

Standard
2.4 Talks & oral presentations · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen you have to introduce a speaker at a CME, conference or departmental event.
Persona
You are an event host who writes warm, concise speaker introductions.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The speaker's CV or bio (paste): [PASTE]
Their talk title: [paste]
Event and audience: [brief]
Task

2. End with the talk title and an invitation to the speaker.
3. Mark names and terms to check pronunciation.

My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]

My context

Topic, speakers and audience size: [brief]
Duration: [minutes]

4. Plan engagement: polls and chat prompts.

579Manage stage fright before a talk
Standard
2.4 Talks & oral presentations · PG Resident / MBBS Student

My context
What happens to me when I speak (shaking, blanking, rushing): [brief]
The upcoming talk: [brief]
Task
1. Explain briefly why anxiety happens and why some of it helps.
2. Give preparation strategies: over-preparing the opening, rehearsal and visualisation.
3. Give strategies for the day: breathing techniques, arriving early, and speaking to audience members beforehand.
4. Give in-the-moment recovery techniques for blanking or rushing.
5. Give a debrief routine after the talk.

596Clinical protocol poster for a ward or ICU
Master
2.5 Posters & visual teaching aids · PG Resident / Faculty / Nursing educator
Use itWhen your unit adopts a protocol (sepsis bundle, hypoglycaemia, anaphylaxis, blood transfusion) and staff need it at a glance.
WhyProtocols in files are not followed; protocols on the wall, clear enough to use at 3 a.m., are. A well-designed poster turns a guideline into action, provided every dose and threshold is verified and it matches your hospital's approved protocol.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a clinical quality-improvement lead and medical illustrator who designs bedside protocol posters that nurses and doctors actually use in emergencies.
My context
Protocol topic: [e.g. management of hypoglycaemia in adult inpatients]
Source: our hospital's approved protocol or guideline: [UPLOAD / PASTE]
Users: [nurses / residents / all staff]
Where it will hang, and the size: [e.g. nursing station, A3]
Language(s): [English / Hindi / bilingual]
Drugs and equipment available locally: [list]
Task
1. Extract the steps that must be on the poster: recognition criteria, immediate actions, drug doses and routes, monitoring, escalation triggers and who to call.
2. Design a top-to-bottom flow: a trigger box, action steps, decision points (yes/no), and escalation.
3. Write the text for each box in under 12 words, using action verbs.
4. Specify the design: large fonts, a colour code (red for emergency actions), icons and plenty of white space.
5. Add a footer with the source protocol, version and date, the approving authority, and the review date.
6. Write a 5-minute staff briefing to launch the poster.
Rules
Take every dose, threshold and step only from the approved protocol I provided, and mark each [VERIFY AGAINST APPROVED PROTOCOL] until it is checked, because a wrong dose on a wall poster can harm patients. Match the local drug formulation and route. Get sign-off from the unit in-charge before printing.
Output
The content extraction, the flow description (box by box), the design specification, the footer, then the briefing script.
Tweak
End with a checklist for testing the poster: can a new nurse follow it correctly in 60 seconds?
How to get more out of it
  • Test the poster with 3 staff members before printing. Watch where they hesitate.
  • Laminate it and put a review date on it. Outdated protocol posters are dangerous.
  • Put the poster where the action happens, not where there's space.
  • → NEXT #602 Pocket quick-reference card
597Comic-style teaching infographic (AI image tools)
Master
2.5 Posters & visual teaching aids · PG Resident / Faculty / Medical educator
Use itWhen you want a shareable, memorable 5-panel comic on a clinical topic, using ChatGPT image generation, Gemini or similar tools.
WhyA comic with two recurring characters, one asking and one answering, turns five high-yield facts into a story students remember and share. The prompt fixes the layout, characters and style so the tool produces a consistent, legible single image, and you verify every fact first.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a medical educator and visual designer who writes precise image-generation prompts for educational comics, and who checks every clinical fact before it goes into an image.
My context
Topic: [e.g. hypokalaemia: 5 things you must know]
The 5 questions and answers, written and verified by me: [PASTE 5 Q&A PAIRS]
Character A (the asker): [e.g. a curious junior doctor in a white coat with a stethoscope, holding a clipboard]
Character B (the answerer): [e.g. a calm, confident senior physician in scrubs]
Brand colours and handle: [e.g. black and orange, @yourhandle]
Image tool: [ChatGPT image / Gemini / other]
Task
1. Check each of my 5 Q&A pairs for accuracy and brevity (answers under 12 words), and flag anything to verify.
2. Assign a tone to character A (curious, puzzled, worried, sceptical, alarmed, thinking) and an emotion to character B (reassuring, serious, knowing smile, warning finger) for each panel.
3. Write the complete image prompt: a single vertical comic-style infographic (portrait, 4:5), the title bar "[TOPIC]: 5 Things You Must Know", a clean modern medical-comic style with bold outlines, flat cell-shaded colouring and a soft palette, the brand colours on the title bar and panel borders, and 5 stacked numbered panels, each with both characters, a question bubble and an answer bubble.
4. Specify that both characters look identical in every panel, the text is short and legible, nothing is cropped, and a footer bar shows my handle.
5. Write 2 fix-up prompts for common problems: garbled text in one panel, and characters that drift between panels.
Rules
Put only facts I have verified into the image, and flag doubtful ones as [VERIFY] before generating, because errors in viral images can't be corrected once shared. Keep each bubble's text short, because image tools garble long text.
Output
The accuracy check, the tone table, the full image prompt in a code block, then the fix-up prompts.
Tweak
End with a caption of under 60 words for posting the comic, with 2 references to cite.
How to get more out of it
  • Fix one panel at a time: "Fix the spelling in panel 3 only, keep everything else."
  • Keep answers under 12 words. Longer text is where image tools make spelling errors.
  • Read the generated image letter by letter before posting. Image tools still misspell medical terms.
  • → NEXT #600 A medical infographic for teaching or social media
598Handwritten-style revision notes image
Master
2.5 Posters & visual teaching aids · MBBS Student / PG Resident / Medical educator
Use itWhen you want an attractive A4 handwritten-style revision sheet on a topic, generated with an AI image tool.
WhyStudents love revising from colour-coded handwritten notes, and a consistent design system (paper, handwriting, colour-coded boxes, highlights and sketches) makes every topic look like a page from the same notebook. The content must be verified first, because image tools reproduce errors beautifully.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a medical educator and designer who creates handwritten-style study sheets with AI image tools, and who checks every fact before generating.
My context
Topic: [TOPIC NAME]
The verified content outline (definition, anatomy or pathophysiology, key features, clinical presentation, tests, differentials, treatment, complications, key points): [PASTE]
Diagrams I want (2–4), described: [list]
Footer text: [e.g. "1 / 1 | @yourhandle"]
Image tool: [ChatGPT image / Gemini / other]
Task
1. Check my outline for accuracy and trim it so it fits one A4 page.
2. Write the full image prompt with this design system: warm cream background (#FEFDF6) with faint blue ruled lines; neat, slightly imperfect dark-navy gel-pen handwriting; rounded section boxes with solid header bars rotating between blue #3B5FAC, green #1E7A3D, red #C0392B and purple #6C3483, with white bold uppercase headings; highlighting in yellow #FFF176 for mnemonics, blue #BBDEFB for definitions, green #C8E6C9 for treatment, pink #F8BBD9 for clinical features and orange #FFCC80 for warnings; bullets, red stars before key points, and underlined key words.
3. Specify 2–4 small pen-and-ink labelled sketches with captions.
4. Specify the section order from my outline, a full-width yellow "key distinction" warning banner, and a "key points" box at the bottom.
5. Add the footer, and the instruction that it must look hand-done, not typed or printed.
6. Write 2 fix-up prompts: overcrowded text, and a misspelled term.
Rules
Include only content I have verified, marking anything doubtful [VERIFY] before generating, and don't reproduce copyrighted atlas plates, only original sketches "in the style of" clean anatomical line drawings, because both errors and copyright problems multiply once images are shared.
Output
The accuracy check, the trimmed outline, the full image prompt in a code block, then the fix-up prompts.
Tweak
End with a list of the 5 terms most likely to be misspelled in the image, to proofread first.
How to get more out of it
  • One topic per page. If the outline is long, split it into two sheets.
  • Proofread every word of the generated image. Handwriting styles hide spelling errors.
  • Keep the design system identical across topics. It makes a recognisable series.
  • → NEXT #600 A medical infographic for teaching or social media
599Awareness poster series for a health day
Master
2.5 Posters & visual teaching aids · PG Resident / Faculty / Community Medicine
Use itFor World TB Day, World Diabetes Day, Breastfeeding Week and similar campaigns in the hospital, community or social media.
WhyAwareness posters often say too much, scare people, or repeat the same slogan everywhere. A small, coordinated series with one message per poster, local language, a clear action and consistent design reaches more people and changes behaviour.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a public-health communication specialist who designs health-awareness campaigns for Indian audiences in hospitals, communities and online.
My context
Health day or theme: [e.g. World TB Day]
Official theme for the year, if any: [paste or "check"]
Audiences: [patients in OPD / community / students / social media followers]
Languages: [list]
Where the posters will be used: [OPD walls / health camp / Instagram / WhatsApp]
Key programme information (free services, helplines, facilities) from official sources: [PASTE]
Task
1. Define 4–5 key messages, one per poster, each with a single action (e.g. "Cough for more than 2 weeks? Get tested free at [facility].").
2. For each poster, write the headline (under 8 words), 2 supporting lines, the call to action and a visual idea.
3. Define a consistent design: colours, fonts, logo placement, and the space for local information.
4. Adapt the messages to each language, simply, not literally.
5. Adapt the formats: A3 print, a 1:1 social post and a WhatsApp status.
6. Suggest how to launch and distribute the series, and how to measure reach.
Rules
Take programme details only from the official sources I provided, marking anything else [VERIFY WITH PROGRAMME], and avoid stigmatising images and words, because stigma keeps people from seeking care. Follow the official campaign's branding rules if it has any.
Output
A message table, the poster-by-poster text and visuals, the design system, the language versions, the format list, then the distribution plan.
Tweak
End with the one poster that would work best alone if only one could be printed.
How to get more out of it
  • Show people like your audience in the visuals. People respond to posters that look like them.
  • Always include where to go and that services are free, if they are. That's the action people need.
  • Test the headline with 3 people from the audience. If they can't repeat it back, simplify it.
  • → NEXT #601 A patient-education leaflet

Persona

601A patient-education leaflet
Standard
2.5 Posters & visual teaching aids · PG Resident / Faculty / Nurse educator
Use itFor patients to take home after a diagnosis, procedure or discharge.
Persona
You are a patient-education specialist who writes clear leaflets at a low reading level.
My context
Topic: [e.g. living with heart failure / preparing for colonoscopy]
Patient group and language: [brief]
Our hospital's advice and contact details (placeholders are fine): [PASTE]
Task
1. Structure the leaflet: what it is, why it matters, what you should do, warning signs to come back for, and who to contact.
2. Write it at about a sixth-to-eighth-grade reading level, in short sentences.
3. Suggest simple pictures or icons.
4. Make a version in [LANGUAGE] if requested.
5. Keep it to one or two sides of A4.
Rules
Keep all advice consistent with our hospital's protocols, marking specifics [VERIFY WITH TREATING TEAM], because patients follow leaflets literally.
Output
The leaflet text with headings, the picture suggestions, then the translated version if requested.
Pro tipTest the leaflet on a patient's relative. If they can't tell you the warning signs afterwards, rewrite them.
Try it withA discharge leaflet on inhaler use and COPD warning signs, in Hindi and English.

Standard
2.5 Posters & visual teaching aids · PG Resident / MBBS Intern

Persona
You are a clinical educator who designs dense but readable quick-reference cards.
My context
Topic: [e.g. ABG interpretation steps / common emergency drug doses / GCS]
Verified content from source: [PASTE WITH SOURCE]
Size: [ID card / half A5 / phone screen]
Task
1. Select the essential information that fits.
2. Organise it into a clear layout (sections, tables, a mnemonic).
3. Suggest a front and back design.
4. Add the source and version date in small print.
Rules
Mark every dose and threshold [VERIFY FROM SOURCE] until checked, and include "check the local protocol" wording, because pocket cards get used for years after guidelines change.
Output
The card content by side, the layout, then the source line.
Pro tipPut the date on the card, and replace it when the guideline updates.

603A concept map for a complex topic
Standard
2.5 Posters & visual teaching aids · MBBS Student / PG Resident / Faculty
Use itFor teaching or revising topics with many connected ideas.
Persona
You are a medical educator who uses concept maps to show how knowledge connects.
My context
Topic: [TOPIC]
Level: [brief]
Key concepts I want included: [list or "suggest"]
Task
1. Identify the central concept and 12–20 linked concepts.
2. Define the links with labelled arrows ("causes", "leads to", "treated by", "detected by").
3. Organise them into clusters (e.g. mechanisms, features, tests, treatment).
4. Describe the layout for drawing by hand or in a tool (e.g. draw.io, Miro).
5. Suggest 3 questions to test understanding using the map.
Rules
Keep every link clinically accurate and mark any uncertain relationship [VERIFY], because a wrong arrow teaches a wrong mechanism.
Output
A concept list, a link table (from, label, to), the layout description, then the questions.
Pro tipAsk students to build the map themselves first, then compare it with yours. That's where the learning happens.
Try it withTopic: heart failure (causes, mechanisms, features, investigations and drug classes).

604Plan a chalk-and-talk or whiteboard session
Standard

Persona
You are a master chalk-and-talk teacher.
My context
Topic and duration: [brief]
Audience and group size: [brief]
Board size: [small whiteboard / large blackboard]
Task
1. Plan the board layout in zones: title, a central diagram, key points, and a "parking lot" for questions.
2. Plan the build order: what to draw first, and when to add each element as you talk.
3. Specify the diagrams to draw, with simple step-by-step drawing instructions.
4. Suggest colour use (if markers are available).
5. Plan a final summary that the finished board shows.
Rules
Keep drawings simple enough to draw in under 2 minutes each, because long drawing loses the audience.
Output
The board-zone layout, the build sequence with timings, the drawing instructions, then the summary.
Pro tipPractise the diagram twice beforehand. Confident drawing looks expert; hesitant drawing looks unprepared.

Reference sources (textbook, atlas, published figure): [LIST]

What I need (concept, diagram or scene): [brief]
Where it will be used: [slide / poster / social post]
Tool: [name]
Task
1. Write a detailed image prompt: subject, style (flat vector, line drawing, 3D render), composition, colours, text to include (minimal) and aspect ratio.
2. Add instructions to avoid anatomical inaccuracies and to keep text minimal.

Don't rely on AI images for precise anatomy or data, and label them "illustrative", because AI images frequently contain anatomical and text errors.

The image prompt in a code block, the approach, then the review checklist.

Section 2.6
2.6

Case presentations & grand rounds

A good case presentation tells a clinical story in the order the evidence arrived, reasons aloud, and ends with what everyone in the room should learn.

40prompts
5Master
23Standard
12Quick
How to use this section

Use it before case presentations, grand rounds and mortality meetings.

Start with the Master prompts (#631–635) for the full workflow; use the Standard prompts (#636–658) for one task at a time; reach for the Quick prompts (#659–670) when you have two minutes. Tap any title below to jump to it, and follow → NEXT to move to the next step.

631Departmental case presentation, start to finish
Master
2.6 Case presentations & grand rounds · PG Resident / MBBS Intern
Use itWhen you present a case at a departmental case discussion or clinical meeting.
WhyCase presentations are where residents show clinical reasoning. A structured presentation (a crisp history, focused examination, a summary, a justified differential, a rational work-up and a clear plan) shows your thinking and invites useful discussion. A disorganised one invites interruption.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a senior physician and clinical teacher who has trained generations of residents in case presentation. You value clinical reasoning over exhaustive lists, and you expect every statement to be justified.
My context
Specialty and my level: [e.g. MD Medicine, year 1]
De-identified case notes (history, examination, investigations with results and dates as Day 0, Day 2…, treatment and course): [PASTE NOTES]
Time allowed: [e.g. 15 minutes + 15 minutes discussion]
Format: [bedside / slides / verbal]
The discussion point my unit wants: [diagnostic dilemma / management decision / teaching]
Task
1. Write the opening one-liner (age band, sex, key background, presenting problem and duration).
2. Structure the history: presenting complaint, history of present illness in chronological order with pertinent positives and negatives, and relevant past, drug, family, social and personal history.
3. Present the examination findings: general, vitals and systemic, relevant findings first, with pertinent negatives.
4. Write a 3–4 line summary that frames the problem.
5. Give a provisional diagnosis and a ranked differential, each with supporting and opposing features.
6. Present investigations in a logical order, with results interpreted and trends shown.
7. Present the management and course, with the reasoning behind key decisions.
8. End with the discussion points or questions for the audience, and 3 learning points.
Rules
Use only facts from my notes, keep everything de-identified, and write [NOT DOCUMENTED] where a key detail is missing rather than inventing it, because the audience will ask about it. Reason step by step when justifying the differential. This is for learning, not a substitute for the treating team's judgement.
Output
The full presentation in sections, suitable to speak or to put on 10–12 slides, then the discussion points and learning points.
Tweak
End with the 5 questions the chairperson is most likely to ask, and short, evidence-aware answers marked [VERIFY] where guideline-dependent.
How to get more out of it
  • Present in the order the information became available. It lets the audience reason along with you.
  • Pertinent negatives are as important as positives. They show you considered the differential.
  • Rehearse the summary until you can say it without notes. It's the part everyone remembers.
  • → NEXT #636 A three-line case summary
632Grand rounds presentation
Master
2.6 Case presentations & grand rounds · Senior Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen you present at hospital or departmental grand rounds.
WhyGrand rounds combine a case with a broader teaching review for a mixed, often senior audience. The best ones use the case as a doorway into current evidence, practical controversies and system lessons, and they keep time.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are an academic physician who has presented and chaired grand rounds for many years. You design sessions that are clinically grounded, evidence-rich and relevant to the whole hospital.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The case (de-identified summary): [PASTE]
The broader topic the case illustrates: [e.g. drug-induced liver injury]
Audience (departments, seniority): [brief]
Duration: [e.g. 45 minutes]
Sources for the review part (guidelines, key papers): [UPLOAD / LIST]
Guest discussants, if any: [brief]
Task
1. Plan the structure: case presentation (10 minutes), case discussion or discussant (10 minutes), topic review (15 minutes), take-home points and system lessons (5 minutes), and Q&A.
2. Condense the case into a presentation with a clear clinical question.
3. Build the topic review from my sources: epidemiology, mechanisms relevant to the case, diagnosis, management and current evidence, with slide titles.
4. Identify system or quality lessons for the hospital, if any.
5. Write briefing questions for the discussant.
6. Write the take-home points.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Base the review on my sources and mark guideline or trial specifics [VERIFY], because grand-rounds audiences include experts in the topic. Keep the case de-identified and blame-free.
Output
The session plan with timings, the case slides, the review slide outline, the system lessons, the discussant questions, then the take-home points.
Tweak
End with the question the most senior person in the room is most likely to ask, and how to handle it.
How to get more out of it
  • Invite a discussant from another department. It broadens the discussion and the audience.
  • Keep the review focused on what the case raised. Grand rounds aren't a textbook chapter.
  • Circulate the take-home points afterwards. They extend the reach beyond the room.
  • → NEXT #649 A 10–12 slide case-presentation deck
633Morbidity and mortality (M&M) presentation
Master
2.6 Case presentations & grand rounds · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen presenting an adverse outcome, complication or death at an M&M or death-audit meeting.
WhyM&M meetings exist to learn and prevent recurrence, not to blame. A structured presentation (the facts, a timeline, the analysis of contributing factors using a systems lens, the evidence, and concrete actions) makes the meeting productive and psychologically safe.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a patient-safety physician who runs M&M meetings using a systems approach and a just culture. You are factual, balanced and focused on learning.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The case, de-identified, with a timeline of events: [PASTE]
The outcome (complication or death): [brief]
Local protocols relevant to the case: [list]
Institutional M&M format, if any: [paste]
Task
1. Present the case factually as a timeline, without judgemental language.
2. Identify the key decision points and what information was available at each one.
3. Analyse the contributing factors with a structured framework: patient factors, task and technology, individual, team, environment and organisation.
4. Classify the event (e.g. known complication, possible error, system failure, unavoidable) as a discussion point, not a verdict.
5. Summarise the relevant evidence or guideline standards, marked [VERIFY].
6. Propose 3–5 specific, actionable system improvements with owners and timelines (as suggestions).
7. Write discussion questions for the meeting, including one on how a similar event could be detected earlier.
8. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Use neutral, non-blaming language and no names or identifiers, because psychological safety is what makes M&M work. Use only facts from my timeline, and mark unknowns [NOT KNOWN].
Output
The timeline, the decision-point table, the contributing-factor analysis, the classification, the evidence summary, the improvement proposals, then the discussion questions.
Tweak
End with one-line "learning messages" suitable for circulating to the department.
How to get more out of it
  • Ask "what made sense to the team at that time?" rather than "who made the mistake?".
  • Track your action items. An M&M without follow-up changes nothing.
  • Keep the presentation confidential according to your institution's rules for quality-improvement meetings.
  • → NEXT #655 Root-cause analysis for an M&M case
634Short "interesting case" presentation with teaching
Master
2.6 Case presentations & grand rounds · PG Resident
Use itFor 10-minute "interesting case" or "case of the week" slots.
WhyShort case slots succeed when they are tightly structured: the hook, the key findings, the reasoning to diagnosis, and one or two strong teaching points. Presenters who try to include everything run over and teach nothing.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a clinical teacher who coaches residents to present interesting cases in 10 minutes with maximum teaching value.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The case (de-identified notes): [PASTE]
What makes it interesting: [rare diagnosis / atypical presentation / diagnostic twist / management lesson]
Time: [e.g. 10 minutes]
Audience: [brief]
The key image or result that cracked the case: [describe]
What the treating team would do differently next time: [brief]
Task
1. Write a hook for the first 30 seconds.
2. Select only the history, examination and investigation findings that drive the reasoning.
3. Present the case as an unfolding puzzle: reveal the information in stages and pause for audience guesses.
4. Reveal the diagnosis and exactly how it was confirmed (the test, finding or response to treatment).
5. Deliver 2 teaching points with brief evidence, marked [VERIFY].
6. Add a 30-second "what we would do differently" reflection.
7. Write 3 audience questions to use at the pauses, with the expected answers.
8. Plan 6–8 slides with timings that fit the slot exactly.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Keep it fully de-identified and include only facts from my notes, because interesting cases are often recognisable to colleagues.
Output
The hook, the selected findings, the staged reveal plan, the diagnosis reveal, the teaching points, then the slide plan.
Tweak
End with one "take-home pearl" for the audience to remember.
How to get more out of it
  • The pause before revealing the diagnosis is where the audience learns. Don't rush it.
  • Show one key image or result, large, at the turning point.
  • Finish with what you would do differently next time. It's the most useful sentence in the talk.
  • → NEXT #647 Teaching points from a case
635Presenting at a multidisciplinary team meeting or tumour board
Master
2.6 Case presentations & grand rounds · PG Resident / Senior Resident
Use itWhen presenting a patient at an MDT, tumour board, or joint medical-surgical meeting.
WhyMDTs make major decisions in minutes. A crisp, standardised presentation with the right information for each specialty (radiology, pathology, oncology, surgery) leads to better decisions and saves everyone's time.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are an MDT coordinator and senior clinician who has run tumour boards and multidisciplinary meetings for years.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Meeting type: [tumour board / ILD MDT / complex-case MDT]
Patient summary (de-identified): age band, sex, performance status, comorbidities: [PASTE]
Relevant history, imaging, pathology and prior treatment: [PASTE]
The specific question for the MDT: [e.g. surgery versus chemoradiotherapy?]
Patient's preferences, if known: [brief]
Task
1. Write a 60-second standardised presentation: the one-liner, the key history, performance status, and the question.
2. Organise the data by specialty: imaging findings for radiology, pathology findings and markers, and staging if applicable.
3. List the options to be discussed, with the relevant considerations for each.
4. Prepare a template for documenting the MDT outcome.
5. Flag missing information needed for a decision, and who should obtain it before the meeting.
6. Note any patient-specific factors (frailty, social support, finances) the MDT should weigh.
6. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
State staging and markers exactly as in the reports, marking any staging version as [VERIFY EDITION], and include the patient's preferences where known, because MDT decisions must be accurate and patient-centred.
Output
The spoken presentation, the specialty data sections, the options table, the missing-information list, then the documentation template.
Tweak
End with the 3 questions the MDT is most likely to ask the presenter.
How to get more out of it
  • State the question for the MDT first, not last. It focuses everyone's attention.
  • Have the images and pathology slides ready to display. MDTs stall while people search for them.
  • Document the decision and the rationale before leaving the room.

Persona

My context
Audience or purpose: [brief]
Case details (de-identified): [PASTE]
Specialty: [brief]
Task

My context
Case summary with key findings: [PASTE]
My provisional diagnosis and differentials: [list]
Task

2. Identify the can't-miss diagnoses and whether they have been excluded.

653Learning from a delayed or missed diagnosis
Standard
2.6 Case presentations & grand rounds · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itFor teaching sessions on diagnostic error, using a de-identified case.
Persona
You are a diagnostic-reasoning expert who teaches cognitive bias without blame.
My context
The case timeline and the eventual diagnosis: [PASTE]
The points where the diagnosis could have been made: [brief]
Task
1. Map the diagnostic journey on a timeline.
2. Identify the cognitive biases likely at play (anchoring, premature closure, availability, framing) at each point.
3. Identify the system factors (workload, handover, test delays).
4. Suggest de-biasing strategies and system fixes.
5. Write the teaching points.
Rules
Frame the analysis around thinking processes and systems, not individuals, and keep it de-identified, because blame shuts down learning.
Output
The timeline, the bias table, the system factors, the strategies, then the teaching points.
Pro tipA "diagnostic time-out" (asking "what else could this be?") is a simple, teachable de-biasing tool.
Try it withA pulmonary embolism initially treated as pneumonia for 3 days.
→ NEXT #633 Morbidity and mortality (M&M) presentation
654The questions the head of department will ask
Standard
2.6 Case presentations & grand rounds · PG Resident
Use itThe day before presenting a case to your unit head or at a departmental meeting.
Persona
You are a senior professor known for incisive case-discussion questions.
My context
My case presentation: [PASTE]
My specialty and year: [brief]
Task
1. List 12 likely questions: on the history, examination technique, differential, investigations, management choices, recent evidence, and "what would you do if…".
2. Give a model answer for each, grounded in the case, with [VERIFY] for guideline facts.
3. Mark the 3 hardest questions and suggest how to prepare for them.
Rules
Base questions on the actual case and my level, and admit uncertainty in the model answers where appropriate, because bluffing is easily detected.
Output
A question-and-answer table, then the preparation plan for the hardest three.
Pro tip"I don't know, but I would find out by…" is a respectable answer. Guessing isn't.
Try it withA presentation of a young patient with a first episode of status epilepticus.
→ NEXT #631 Departmental case presentation, start to finish
655Root-cause analysis for an M&M case
Standard
2.6 Case presentations & grand rounds · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen preparing the analysis part of an M&M or quality-improvement meeting.
Persona
You are a patient-safety specialist trained in root-cause analysis.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The event timeline (de-identified): [PASTE]
Initial thoughts on contributing factors: [brief]
Task
1. Build a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram description with categories: people, processes, equipment, environment, communication and policies.
2. Apply "5 whys" to the 2 most important contributing factors.
3. Distinguish root causes from contributing factors.
4. Propose SMART corrective actions.
Rules
Focus on systems and processes, not individual blame, and base the analysis on the facts in the timeline, because RCA aims at prevention, not punishment.
Output
The fishbone description, the 5-whys chains, the root-cause list, then the actions table.
Pro tipIf your "root cause" is "human error", ask "why" at least twice more.
Try it withA delayed administration of antibiotics to a septic patient in the emergency department.
→ NEXT #633 Morbidity and mortality (M&M) presentation
656Present a follow-up update on a previous case
Standard
2.6 Case presentations & grand rounds · PG Resident
Use itWhen the department wants to hear how a previously presented patient did.
Persona
You are a clinical teacher who closes the loop on cases.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The original presentation summary: [PASTE]
The follow-up course and outcome: [PASTE]
Task
1. Remind the audience of the case in 2 lines.
2. Summarise the course since then: treatment response, complications and the current status.
3. Say whether the outcome confirms or changes the original diagnosis or plan.
4. Draw updated lessons.
Rules
Keep it de-identified and factual, and acknowledge it plainly if the original reasoning was wrong, because honest follow-up is powerful teaching.
Output
The reminder, the course summary, the diagnostic check, then the updated lessons.
Pro tipFollow-up presentations teach humility and the natural history of disease. Do more of them.
Try it withA 6-month follow-up of a patient with autoimmune encephalitis.
→ NEXT #647 Teaching points from a case
657Turn a case into a teaching session for MBBS students
Standard
2.6 Case presentations & grand rounds · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen teaching undergraduates using a real ward case.
Persona
You are a clinical tutor for MBBS students.
My context
The case (de-identified): [PASTE]
Students' year and what they have learned so far: [brief]
Time: [minutes]
Task
1. Choose 3 learning objectives appropriate for the students' level.
2. Plan a Socratic session: questions at each stage of the case.
3. Include one clinical skill to practise (e.g. eliciting a sign) if possible.
4. Link the case to their exam topics (e.g. NEET-PG and university exams).
5. Write 5 check questions.
Rules
Keep the questions at the students' level and correct misconceptions gently, and obtain the patient's consent for bedside teaching, because respect for patients is itself a lesson.
Output
The objectives, the Socratic question plan, the skill station, the exam links, then the check questions.
Pro tipAsk students to commit to an answer before you reveal it. Commitment drives learning.
Try it withA patient with mitral stenosis for third-year MBBS students.
→ NEXT #647 Teaching points from a case
658Link a case to a recent paper
Standard
2.6 Case presentations & grand rounds · PG Resident / Faculty
Use itWhen a case presentation would be stronger with one recent, relevant study.
Persona
You are an academic clinician who connects bedside cases to current evidence.
My context
The case summary and its key clinical question: [PASTE]
The recent paper I found (upload or paste the abstract): [UPLOAD / PASTE]
Audience: [brief]
Task
1. Summarise the paper in 3 lines (design, population, key result).
2. Explain how it applies, or doesn't apply, to this patient.
3. Note the paper's main limitation for this context.
4. Write one slide connecting the case and the paper.
Rules
Use only the paper I provided, and don't overstate how directly it applies to one patient, because case-to-trial reasoning is easy to overstretch.
Output
The summary, the applicability note, the limitation, then the slide text.
Pro tipOne well-chosen recent paper makes a case discussion feel current and evidence-based.
Try it withA patient with severe community-acquired pneumonia and a recent trial of corticosteroids.
→ NEXT #648 A brief literature review for my case

Section 2.7
2.7

Delivery, Q&A & teaching

Content earns attention; delivery keeps it. Handle questions with honesty, teach with methods that work, and give feedback that helps people grow.

How to use this section

Use it in the last days before any talk, and whenever you teach or give feedback.

Start with the Master prompts (#671–674) for the full workflow; use the Standard prompts (#675–691) for one task at a time; reach for the Quick prompts (#692–700) when you have two minutes. Tap any title below to jump to it, and follow → NEXT to move to the next step.
