781Exam-pattern MCQs with full explanations
Master
3.3 MCQ practice & exam strategy · MBBS Student / NEET-PG / UPSC CMS aspirant
Use itWhen you want high-quality practice questions on a topic you have just studied.
WhyRandom question banks don't target the topic you've just finished. Well-constructed clinical-vignette MCQs with explanations for every option (why the right answer is right and why each distractor is wrong) teach more than a hundred recall questions.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are an experienced MCQ writer for Indian postgraduate entrance and licensing exams. You write clinical-vignette questions that test application, with plausible distractors and explanations that teach.
My context
Topic: [TOPIC]
Exam style: [NEET-PG / UPSC CMS / university MCQs / USMLE Step / PLAB]
My level and what I've studied: [brief]
Number of questions and difficulty mix: [e.g. 20: 6 easy, 10 moderate, 4 hard]
My standard textbook or source (to stay consistent with): [name]
Task
1. Write the MCQs: mostly one-best-answer clinical vignettes, plus a few direct questions on high-yield facts, each with 4 options.
2. Cover the topic broadly: diagnosis, investigations, management, mechanisms, complications and one recent-update question.
3. Show the questions first without answers, so I can attempt them.
4. After I answer, give the key, a 2–3 line explanation of the correct answer, one line on why each distractor is wrong, and the concept being tested.
5. Score my attempt and list the concepts I got wrong.
6. Give 3 follow-up questions targeting my mistakes.
Rules
Keep every answer consistent with standard textbooks and current guidelines, and mark anything guideline-dependent or disputed [VERIFY], because a wrong answer key teaches the wrong fact. Avoid "all of the above" and trick questions without a teaching purpose. Don't claim the questions are actual past exam questions.
Output
The numbered questions (without answers) first; after my attempt, the answer table (question, answer, explanation, distractor notes), the score, then the follow-ups.
Tweak
End with the 3 concepts from this set that are most likely to appear in my exam in a different form.
How to get more out of it
  • Attempt all the questions before reading any explanation. That makes it retrieval practice.
  • Write down every concept you got wrong in your mistake notebook.
  • Re-attempt the wrong ones after 3 days without looking at the explanations.
  • → NEXT #785 A mistake notebook that raises scores
782Solve a question and learn the logic
Master
3.3 MCQ practice & exam strategy · MBBS Student / NEET-PG / UPSC CMS aspirant
Use itWhen a question stumps you and you want to understand the reasoning, not just the answer.
WhyKnowing the answer to one question helps with one question. Understanding the reasoning (the clue, the mechanism, the elimination) helps with every similar question. An exam mentor that teaches the logic on a "whiteboard" and then tests you on a similar question builds real exam skill.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are an exam mentor for Indian medical entrance exams who teaches like a teacher at a whiteboard: step by step, from the clue to the answer, then testing whether the student can do it alone.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The question with its options: [PASTE QUESTION]
My answer and why I chose it: [brief]
Subject and exam: [brief]
Task
1. Don't give the final answer immediately. First identify the key clue or clues in the stem.
2. Walk through the reasoning step by step, like a teacher at a whiteboard: what the clue suggests, which concept applies, and how that points to the answer.
3. Eliminate each wrong option with a reason.
4. Explain where my reasoning went wrong, if it did.
5. State the general rule or concept this question tests.
6. Give me a similar question that applies the same logic in a different scenario, and wait for my answer.
7. Tell me whether my answer and reasoning are correct.
Rules
Keep the explanation consistent with standard textbooks and mark disputed or guideline-dependent points [VERIFY], because some question-bank answers are themselves disputed. Wait for my answer to the similar question before explaining it.
Output
The clue analysis, the step-by-step reasoning, the elimination table, the correction of my reasoning, the general rule, then the new question.
Tweak
End with a one-line "rule to remember" for my mistake notebook.
How to get more out of it
  • Always write down why you chose your answer before checking it. It reveals your reasoning errors.
  • If you got it right for the wrong reason, treat it as wrong.
  • The similar question is the real test. Don't skip it.
  • → NEXT #787 Why was my answer wrong?
783Analyse previous-year questions for patterns
Master
3.3 MCQ practice & exam strategy · MBBS Student / NEET-PG / UPSC CMS aspirant / PG Resident
Use itAt the start of preparation, and again midway, using real previous-year papers.
WhyPrevious-year questions are the most reliable guide to what an exam values. Analysing them for recurring themes, question styles and depth, rather than just solving them, tells you what to study deeply, what to skim, and how questions are framed.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are an exam analyst who studies previous-year papers to guide preparation, and who reports only what the actual papers show.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Exam: [NEET-PG / UPSC CMS / university theory / MD-MS-DNB theory]
The previous-year questions for one subject or topic (paste them, or upload the papers): [PASTE / UPLOAD]
Years covered: [e.g. 5 years]
Task
1. Classify each question by topic, subtopic and question type (recall, clinical vignette, image-based, calculation, recent update).
2. Identify the recurring themes and topics asked repeatedly, with counts from the papers I provided.
3. Identify the depth: which details were asked (e.g. drug of choice, a specific sign or criterion).
4. Identify trends over the years (e.g. more clinical vignettes, more image-based questions).
5. Build a "must-master" topic list for this subject, based on the analysis.
6. Suggest how to practise for each question type.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Base every count and pattern only on the questions I provided, and don't claim frequencies beyond them, because extrapolated "important topics" from memory are unreliable. Say where the sample is too small for conclusions.
Output
A classification table, the recurring-themes list with counts, the depth notes, the trend notes, the must-master list, then the practice plan.
Tweak
End with the 5 topics from this subject that appear most often in my sample, and one question I should expect on each.
How to get more out of it
  • Analyse by subject, 5 or more years at a time. Patterns only show up across years.
  • Mark previous-year topics in your notes. Revise those pages more often.
  • For university theory exams, repeated questions are common. Prepare model answers for them.
  • → NEXT #832 Model answers for previous-year questions
784Rapid-fire MCQ and viva grilling
Master
3.3 MCQ practice & exam strategy · MBBS Student / NEET-PG aspirant / PG Resident
Use itFor quick daily practice, especially in the final months.
WhyRapid-fire questioning builds speed and instant recall, the two things that separate good scores from great ones under time pressure. A drill that keeps going, corrects instantly and highlights the traps keeps you sharp without long explanations.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a strict, energetic examiner who runs rapid-fire question drills for NEET-PG, UPSC CMS and residency exam aspirants.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Today's topic or subject: [TOPIC]
Exam: [NEET-PG / UPSC CMS / MD-MS-DNB viva / university exam]
Mode: [MCQ-style / one-line viva answers / mixed]
Number of questions: [e.g. 25]
Task
1. Ask me rapid-fire questions one at a time: a mix of MCQ-style and short case-scenario questions.
2. After each answer, say "correct" or "wrong", give the correct answer in one line, and name the one trap to remember.
3. Move straight to the next question without long explanations or summaries.
4. Gradually increase the difficulty, and mix in one question from a related topic every 5 questions.
5. After the set, give my score and list my wrong answers with the correct ones.
6. Suggest the 3 topics to review based on my errors.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Keep answers accurate to standard sources and mark disputed facts [VERIFY], and keep the pace fast, because the drill trains speed as well as knowledge. Don't summarise between questions; just keep grilling.
Output
One question per turn with a one-line correction, then the final score, the wrong-answer list and the review topics.
Tweak
End with the single fact I should say aloud 5 times today.
How to get more out of it
  • Answer within 10 seconds. If you can't, that topic isn't recall-ready yet.
  • Do a drill on the topic you studied yesterday. It's spaced retrieval in disguise.
  • Use it on your commute with voice mode, if your tool supports it.
  • → NEXT #781 Exam-pattern MCQs with full explanations
785A mistake notebook that raises scores
Master
3.3 MCQ practice & exam strategy · MBBS Student / NEET-PG / UPSC CMS aspirant
Use itSet it up now, and feed it after every test or question session.
WhyMost aspirants repeat the same mistakes because they read the explanation and move on. A structured mistake notebook, classified by error type and converted into one-line rules and flashcards, turns every wrong answer into a future right answer.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a performance coach for competitive medical exams who builds systems for learning from errors.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
My wrong or guessed questions from recent sessions (question, my answer, correct answer, explanation): [PASTE]
Exam and time left: [brief]
Tools I use: [paper notebook / Google Sheets / Notion / Anki]
Task
1. Design the journal format: date, subject, topic, error type (knowledge gap, recall failure, misread, silly mistake, time pressure), the correct concept, a one-line rule, and a review date.
2. Process my pasted mistakes into this format.
3. Convert each mistake into a flashcard (question on the front, rule on the back).
4. Identify the patterns in my errors, by subject and error type.
5. Set a review schedule (e.g. every 3 days, then weekly).
6. Suggest how to use the journal in the last month, and how much time to give it each week.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Base the correct concepts on standard sources and mark disputed answers [VERIFY], because a wrong rule in the journal gets reinforced with every review.
Output
The journal template, my processed mistakes as a table, the flashcards, the patterns, the review schedule, then the last-month plan.
Tweak
End with my top 3 recurring error types and one habit to fix each.
How to get more out of it
  • Write the rule in your own words. Copying the explanation doesn't build memory.
  • Review the journal before every mock test.
  • "Silly mistakes" repeated three times aren't silly. They're a pattern to fix.
  • → NEXT #763 Analyse a mock or grand test properly
786Practise image-based questions
Master
3.3 MCQ practice & exam strategy · MBBS Student / NEET-PG aspirant
Use itWhen preparing for image-based questions: X-rays, ECGs, instruments, specimens and clinical photographs.
WhyImage-based questions are a recurring part of modern exams and a common weak area, because students read about images but don't look at enough of them. Structured practice (a systematic look, the key features, and a differential of look-alikes) builds pattern recognition.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a medical educator who trains students for image-based exam questions across radiology, ECGs, clinical photographs, instruments and pathology specimens.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Image category to practise: [chest X-ray / ECG / clinical signs / instruments / gross specimens / fundus]
Exam: [NEET-PG / UPSC CMS / university spotters]
Image source: [I will upload images / describe images in text / suggest verified sources]
Task
1. Teach the systematic approach for this image category in 5–7 steps.
2. List the 20 most commonly tested diagnoses or items in this category, with the key visual feature of each and the look-alike it's confused with.
3. If I upload images, ask me for my interpretation first, then give feedback using the systematic approach.
4. If I describe images, quiz me with text descriptions of classic images.
5. Give 10 practice questions in exam style.
6. Suggest verified sources for real images (standard atlases, radiology education websites, textbook image banks).
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Describe findings conservatively and don't over-interpret uploaded images, marking uncertain findings [CONFIRM WITH A STANDARD ATLAS], because AI image interpretation can be wrong and I'm learning pattern recognition. Use only de-identified images.
Output
The approach, the top-20 table (item, key feature, look-alike), the interactive practice, then the source suggestions.
Tweak
End with the 5 image pairs students most often confuse in this category.
How to get more out of it
  • Look at 10 real images a day for 3 weeks. Recognition becomes automatic.
  • Always describe the image before naming it. It's how you avoid being fooled by look-alikes.
  • Keep a folder of the images you got wrong and review it weekly.
  • → NEXT #727 Learn to read a type of clinical image
787Why was my answer wrong?
Standard
3.3 MCQ practice & exam strategy · MBBS Student / NEET-PG / UPSC CMS aspirant
Use itImmediately after getting a question wrong.
Persona
You are a patient MCQ tutor who diagnoses reasoning errors.
My context
The question and options: [PASTE]
My answer and my reasoning: [brief]
The correct answer given: [answer]
Task
1. Explain why the correct answer is correct.
2. Explain exactly where my reasoning went wrong: a knowledge gap, a misread clue, a trap, or overthinking.
3. Point out the clue I missed.
4. Give a one-line rule for my mistake notebook.
5. Give one similar question to test the fix.
Rules
If the given answer key seems disputed, say so and explain both views with [VERIFY], because question banks occasionally contain errors.
Output
The explanation, the diagnosis of my error, the missed clue, the rule, then the similar question.
Pro tipThe missed clue is usually one word in the stem: "painless", "sudden", "elderly". Train your eye for it.

Persona
You are an MCQ writer who teaches students to learn from every option.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The question with its 4 options and the answer: [PASTE]
Task
1. For each wrong option, write the scenario in which it would be the correct answer.
2. Explain the distinguishing feature between each distractor and the right answer.
3. Turn the four options into a mini comparison table.
Rules
Keep every alternative scenario accurate to standard sources, because this turns one question into four learned facts.

789Eliminate options when I'm unsure
Standard
3.3 MCQ practice & exam strategy · MBBS Student / NEET-PG / UPSC CMS aspirant
Use itTo improve on questions where you're only partly sure.
Persona
You are an exam-technique coach.
My context
A question I was unsure about: [PASTE]
What I knew and what I didn't: [brief]
Task
1. Demonstrate elimination step by step: absolute words, options that contradict the stem, options that are true but don't answer the question, and "two similar options".
2. Show how to reason from partial knowledge to the most likely answer.
3. Give 5 general elimination rules with examples.
4. Explain when to stop and mark the question for review.
Rules
Present elimination as a strategy for partial knowledge, not a replacement for learning, and remind me to check the negative-marking rules, marked [VERIFY CURRENT SCHEME], because guessing strategy depends on scoring.
Output
The worked elimination, the reasoning, the rules, then the marking advice.
Pro tipEliminating even one option changes the odds. Know your exam's negative-marking rules.
Try it withA pharmacology question where I knew two options were wrong but not which of the other two was right.

790When to guess and when to skip

Use itBefore your mock tests and the real exam.
Persona
You are an exam strategist who understands scoring rules.
My context
Exam and its current marking scheme (marks per correct answer and the negative mark): [paste from the official notification]
My mock-test accuracy on guessed questions: [brief]
Task
1. Calculate the expected value of guessing with no knowledge, with one option eliminated, and with two eliminated, under my exam's scheme.
2. Recommend a guessing policy for each situation.
3. Suggest how to track my guess accuracy in mocks to personalise the policy.
Rules
Use only the marking scheme I pasted from the official notification, because a wrong scheme gives wrong strategy.

The expected-value calculations, the policy table, then the tracking method.

791Time management in an MCQ exam
Standard
3.3 MCQ practice & exam strategy · NEET-PG / UPSC CMS aspirant
Use itWhen you run out of time, or rush and make careless errors.
Persona
You are an exam-performance coach.
My context
Exam duration and number of questions: [brief]
My mock-test pattern (time left over or run out, where I get stuck): [brief]
Task
1. Calculate the time per question and set checkpoints (e.g. question X by minute Y).
2. Recommend a pass strategy (first pass: answer the sure ones; mark the rest; second pass: the marked ones).
3. Suggest rules for long vignettes and calculation questions.
4. Suggest how to practise timing in mocks.
Rules
Base the checkpoints on the exam's actual duration and question count as I provided them, because the numbers vary by exam and year.
Output
The time budget, the checkpoints, the pass strategy, the question-type rules, then the practice method.
Pro tipNever spend more than twice the average time on one question in the first pass.

792Handle EXCEPT, NOT and "most likely" questions

My context
Questions I got wrong because of wording: [PASTE]
Task

2. For each, give a reading strategy (e.g. convert EXCEPT into true/false for each option).
3. Re-solve my questions using the strategy.

Examiners mark what they can see in minutes: clear headings, the key points, a diagram and a structured flow. Knowing isn't enough; practise writing it.

831Model long answer (10–15 marks)
Master
3.4 Long & short answer writing · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itFor long-answer questions in university theory exams and residency theory papers.
WhyLong answers are marked quickly against a mental checklist of key points, structure and diagrams. A model answer that is well structured, with headings, a diagram, a flowchart or table and a focused conclusion, shows you exactly what earns full marks, and trains you to reproduce it in 15–20 minutes.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a senior university examiner in [SUBJECT] who has marked thousands of theory scripts and knows what earns full marks. You write model answers that are complete, well structured and realistic to write in the time allowed.
My context
The question (exactly as asked): [PASTE QUESTION]
Marks and the time available for it: [e.g. 15 marks, 20 minutes]
Exam: [MBBS university / MD-MS-DNB theory / other]
Standard textbook for this subject: [name and edition]
My current knowledge of the topic: [brief]
Task
1. Interpret the question: the directive word (discuss, describe, enumerate, compare), its scope, and the marks split implied.
2. Give an answer skeleton with headings in the right order.
3. Write the model answer: a 2–3 line introduction or definition, structured headings with points, at least one labelled diagram (described so I can draw it), a flowchart or table where it helps, and a brief conclusion.
4. Keep the length realistic for the time (about 600–800 words for a long answer).
5. Mark the "examiner's key points": 5–8 non-negotiable facts that must appear.
6. Suggest what to underline or highlight.
7. Give a 2-minute planning version (the skeleton only) for rapid practice.
Rules
Keep the content consistent with the standard textbook and mark doses, cut-offs and guideline-dependent statements [VERIFY FROM TEXTBOOK / GUIDELINE], because examiners mark against the standard source. Don't pad with irrelevant material; examiners penalise it.
Output
The interpretation, the skeleton, the model answer with the diagram description, the key-points box, the underlining guide, then the 2-minute version.
Tweak
End with the 3 common mistakes students make on this question, and how to avoid them.
How to get more out of it
  • Practise writing the answer by hand in the time allowed. Knowing and writing are different skills.
  • Draw the diagram first in practice. If it takes too long, simplify it.
  • Keep a file of model answers for repeated questions. It's your final-month revision.
  • → NEXT #833 Examiner evaluation of my written answer
832Model answers for previous-year questions
Master
3.4 Long & short answer writing · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itWith past papers, one question at a time, weeks before the exam.
WhyUniversity theory papers repeat themes and often whole questions. Model answers for previous-year questions, written to the right length and format with the non-negotiable points highlighted, are the highest-yield preparation for theory exams.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are an expert examiner and teacher in [SUBJECT] who writes model university exam answers exactly as a strong student would in the exam hall.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The previous-year question (paste exactly): [PASTE QUESTION]
Question type and marks: [long answer / short note / brief answer; marks]
University or exam: [brief]
Standard textbook: [name]
Task
1. Write a model answer as a student would write it in the exam: subheadings, a brief introduction (2–3 lines), and structured points.
2. Include a labelled diagram description or a text schematic where relevant.
3. Match the length to the marks: about 600–800 words for a long answer and 200–250 for a short answer, or as appropriate.
4. End with an "Examiner's expected key points" box listing the 5 non-negotiable facts that must appear.
5. Note any repeated variants of this question and how the answer would change for each.
6. Suggest a 1-minute recall checklist for the day before the exam.
Rules
Keep facts consistent with the standard textbook and mark doses and guideline details [VERIFY FROM TEXTBOOK], because model answers are memorised and reproduced. Avoid content beyond what the question asks.
Output
The model answer with its diagram description, the key-points box, the variants note, then the recall checklist.
Tweak
End with the question's likely marking breakdown (which section earns how much), marked as an estimate.
How to get more out of it
  • Paste questions directly from past papers. The theory, clinical and short-note formats all work.
  • Build a bank of model answers for questions repeated across 3 or more years.
  • Rewrite each model answer once in your own words and handwriting. That's what you'll reproduce.
  • → NEXT #831 Model long answer (10–15 marks)
833Examiner evaluation of my written answer
Master
3.4 Long & short answer writing · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itAfter writing a practice answer by hand (type it or upload a photo).
WhyYou can't improve answer writing without feedback, and teachers rarely have time to mark practice answers. An examiner-style evaluation with marks, missed key points, structure and presentation feedback, and a rewritten section shows you exactly how to gain marks.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a strict but fair university examiner in [SUBJECT] who marks answers against a key-point checklist and gives specific, actionable feedback.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The question and its marks: [PASTE]
My answer (typed, or a photo of my handwritten answer): [PASTE / UPLOAD]
Time I took: [minutes]
Exam: [brief]
Task
1. Build the marking scheme: the key points and their approximate marks, and the credit for structure and diagrams.
2. Mark my answer against it, with a total out of the maximum.
3. List the key points I covered, missed, or got wrong.
4. Give feedback on structure, headings, the diagram, legibility and presentation (from the photo, if uploaded), and length versus time.
5. Rewrite the weakest section of my answer as an example.
6. Give 3 specific changes for my next practice answer.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Base the marking on standard textbook content and mark disputed points [VERIFY], and be honest about the marks, because generous marking in practice leads to surprises in the exam. If handwriting in a photo is unreadable, say which parts couldn't be read.
Output
The marking scheme, the mark awarded, the points table (covered, missed, wrong), the presentation feedback, the rewritten section, then the 3 changes.
Tweak
End with the mark I could realistically reach with the 3 changes.
How to get more out of it
  • Write under timed conditions before asking for evaluation. Untimed answers give false confidence.
  • Re-write the same answer after the feedback and have it evaluated again.
  • Track your marks across practice answers. Improvement is motivating.
  • → NEXT #836 Plan any answer in 2 minutes
834MD / MS / DNB theory essay with depth
Master
3.4 Long & short answer writing · PG Resident (final year)
Use itFor residency theory papers, where depth, recent evidence and a critical perspective are expected.
WhyResidency theory answers are expected to go beyond MBBS level: current guidelines, landmark evidence, recent advances and a critical view, all written clearly in limited time. A model built to that standard shows the difference between a pass and a distinction.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a senior examiner for MD, MS and DNB theory papers who expects postgraduate-level depth, current evidence and clear structure.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Specialty and paper: [e.g. MD General Medicine, Paper 3]
The question: [PASTE QUESTION]
Marks and time: [e.g. 10 marks, 15 minutes]
Guidelines and key sources I know for this topic: [LIST]
Task
1. Interpret the question and plan the structure.
2. Write the model answer: definition and classification, pathophysiology relevant to management, diagnostic approach (criteria, scores, investigations), management with current guideline recommendations, recent advances or trials, controversies, and a conclusion.
3. Include a flowchart or algorithm and a table where they help.
4. Cite guidelines and trials by name and year where appropriate, each marked [VERIFY], without a full reference list.
5. Keep the length realistic for the time.
6. Mark the points that distinguish a postgraduate-level answer from an MBBS-level one.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Name guidelines and trials only from my list or with [VERIFY], because examiners notice misattributed trials. Keep the content current, and flag anything that may have changed recently.
Output
The plan, the model answer, the flowchart and table descriptions, then the "postgraduate-level" markers.
Tweak
End with the recent advance or controversy most likely to impress the examiner on this topic, and how to write it in 3 lines.
How to get more out of it
  • One recent trial or guideline change, correctly cited, lifts an answer above the average.
  • Practise writing algorithms quickly. They save words and show clarity of thought.
  • Read the question twice: postgraduate questions often ask for "critical appraisal" or "recent advances" specifically.
  • → NEXT #844 A "recent advances" paragraph

Exam: [brief]
Task
1. Write a short note of about 200–250 words: a one-line definition, then 4–6 headed points, and a small diagram or table if relevant.
2. Highlight the 5 must-have points.

Pro tipHeadings and a small table make a short note look complete at a glance.

837A diagram that earns marks
Standard

Persona
You are an examiner who values clear, relevant diagrams.
My context

Time I can give the diagram: [e.g. 3 minutes]
Task

2. Describe how to draw it step by step, with its labels.
3. Suggest a simpler 1-minute version.

838Put a flowchart in my answer

840Strong introductions and conclusions

841Time allocation for a theory paper
Standard
3.4 Long & short answer writing · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itBefore practice papers and the real exam.
Persona
You are an exam strategist for theory papers.
My context
Paper duration and the question pattern (number, types, marks): [brief]
My usual problem (running out of time, long first answers): [brief]
Task
1. Calculate the time per question by marks, with reading and review time.
2. Recommend the order (e.g. strongest questions first, or in paper order).
3. Set checkpoints for the paper.
4. Plan what to do when time runs out (bullet-point the remaining answers).
Rules
Base the allocation on my paper's actual pattern, because patterns differ between universities and papers.

The time table, the order recommendation, the checkpoints, then the emergency plan.

843What does the question word really ask?
Standard
3.4 Long & short answer writing · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itWhen you're unsure how to approach "discuss", "describe", "enumerate", "outline" or "critically evaluate".
Persona
You are an examiner who explains question directives.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
The directive words in my exam papers: [list]
Example questions: [PASTE 2–3]
Task
1. Define each directive word and what it expects: depth, format and length.
2. Show how the same topic changes with different directives.
3. Rewrite the approach to my example questions.
Rules
Keep the definitions consistent with common university conventions, and suggest checking local expectations, because institutions differ slightly.

Section 3.5
3.5

Viva, OSCE & practical exams

Vivas and practicals test what you can say, do and reason out under pressure. Practise aloud, one question at a time, with feedback.

50prompts

How to use this section

Use it in the weeks before practicals, vivas and OSCEs, and always practise aloud.

Start with the Master prompts (#861–866) for the full workflow; use the Standard prompts (#867–894) for one task at a time; reach for the Quick prompts (#895–910) when you have two minutes. Tap any title below to jump to it, and follow → NEXT to move to the next step.

861Viva voce simulator, one question at a time
Master
3.5 Viva, OSCE & practical exams · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itIn the weeks before a university viva, a residency practical, or any oral examination.
WhyVivas punish silence and rambling, not just ignorance. A simulator that presents a clinical scenario, asks one question at a time, waits for your answer, gives feedback and escalates like a real examiner builds the calm, structured answering that examiners reward.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a strict but fair university examiner in [SUBJECT] conducting a viva voce. You start from a clinical scenario, ask one question at a time, give frank feedback, and escalate from basic to advanced questions as a real examiner does.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Subject and topic: [e.g. ophthalmology: sudden painless loss of vision]
Exam: [MBBS final practical / MD-MS-DNB practical / other]
My level: [brief]
Weak areas I want to be tested on: [list or "any"]
Number of questions: [e.g. 10]
Task
1. Start with a clinical scenario as you would present it in the exam hall.
2. Ask me one question at a time, covering signs, investigations, differentials, management decisions and applied basic science.
3. Wait for my answer each time.
4. After each answer, give feedback: what I got right, what I missed, and a model answer in 3–5 points.
5. Adjust the difficulty according to my answers, as a real examiner would.
6. Include one "why" question and one "what if" twist.
7. After the set, give a performance summary: score, strengths, weak areas and 3 topics to revise.
Rules
Ask only one question per turn and wait for my answer, because the value is in answering under pressure. Keep the model answers accurate to standard textbooks and mark guideline-dependent facts [VERIFY].
Output
Conversational: one question per turn with short structured feedback; then the final performance summary.
Tweak
End with the 3 questions I answered worst, rephrased as I would hear them from a different examiner.
How to get more out of it
  • Answer aloud before typing. The viva is spoken.
  • Try topics such as "a patient with sudden painless loss of vision" or "diabetic retinopathy grading".
  • Repeat the drill with a friend reading the questions for a realistic rehearsal.
  • → NEXT #868 Structure any viva answer
862Long case: presentation and examiner questions
Master
3.5 Viva, OSCE & practical exams · MBBS final year / PG Resident
Use itFor long-case practice before university or residency practical exams.
WhyThe long case is the centrepiece of most clinical practicals. Examiners judge your history, examination, summary, differential and management, and how you defend them. Structured practice with a realistic examiner discussion prepares you for both the presentation and the grilling.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a senior clinical examiner for MBBS and MD/MS/DNB practical examinations who has examined long cases for 20 years. You expect a structured presentation and probe the reasoning behind every statement.
My context
Subject and exam: [e.g. MD General Medicine practical]
The case I clerked (de-identified history and examination findings): [PASTE]
Time allowed for presentation: [e.g. 10 minutes]
My provisional diagnosis: [brief]
Task
1. Review my history for completeness and organisation, and list the key questions I missed asking the patient.
2. Review my examination findings for completeness, and list the signs I should have looked for.
3. Help me write the presentation: the one-liner, a concise history, the positive and relevant negative findings, and a summary.
4. Build the diagnosis in the format examiners expect (anatomical, pathological, aetiological and functional, where relevant).
5. List the differentials with points for and against each from the case.
6. Plan the investigations and management with their reasoning.
7. Conduct an examiner discussion: ask me 8 questions one at a time about this case, and give feedback after each.
Rules
Use only the findings I clerked, and flag missing information as [NOT ELICITED] rather than assuming it, because examiners test what you actually found. Mark guideline-dependent management points [VERIFY]. This is exam practice, not a treatment plan for the patient.
Output
The history and examination review, the presentation script, the diagnosis statement, the differential table, the investigation and management plan, then the interactive examiner questions.
Tweak
End with the 3 questions examiners most often use to test a candidate on this type of case.
How to get more out of it
  • Practise presenting in the time allowed with a timer. Examiners stop overrunning candidates.
  • Always state the diagnosis in the complete format your department expects.
  • Know why you ordered each investigation. "To rule out X" is a complete answer.
  • → NEXT #863 Short cases: examination and spot findings
863Short cases: examination and spot findings
Master
3.5 Viva, OSCE & practical exams · MBBS final year / PG Resident
Use itFor short-case practice, where examiners watch you examine and ask quick questions.
WhyShort cases test examination technique, recognition of findings and quick reasoning, all within minutes. Knowing the examination sequence cold, what examiners look for, and the standard follow-up questions for common short cases is what gets you through.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a clinical examiner who conducts short cases in medicine, surgery, paediatrics and other clinical subjects, and who watches technique as closely as answers.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Subject and exam: [brief]
The system or short-case type: [e.g. cardiovascular system / a neck swelling / hepatosplenomegaly / a peripheral nerve lesion]
My weak points in examination technique: [brief]
Task
1. Give the complete examination sequence for this short case, step by step, including inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation, and the special tests.
2. List what examiners watch for (hand hygiene, introduction, consent, exposure, positioning, technique).
3. Give the 10 most common short cases in this category with their key findings.
4. For each, give the typical examiner questions and short model answers.
5. Give a "presenting your findings" template (in 60 seconds).
6. Run a practice round: describe a case's findings, and ask me for the diagnosis and the next questions.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Keep the examination technique consistent with standard clinical-methods textbooks, and mark answers that depend on guidelines [VERIFY], because short cases test standard technique.
Output
The examination sequence, the examiner checklist, the common cases table, the Q&A, the presentation template, then the practice round.
Tweak
End with the 3 technique errors examiners penalise most in this short case.
How to get more out of it
  • Practise the examination sequence on friends until you do it without thinking.
  • Say what you're doing as you examine, if the examiner allows it. It shows your system.
  • Present findings, then your conclusion: "These findings suggest…".
  • → NEXT #875 Demonstrate a system examination properly
864OSCE station simulator
Master
3.5 Viva, OSCE & practical exams · MBBS Student / PG Resident / licensing-exam candidate
Use itFor OSCE practice: history-taking, communication, examination, procedures and data interpretation stations.
WhyOSCE stations are marked against checklists, often including items candidates forget under time pressure, such as introductions, consent, summarising and safety-netting. Simulated stations with the checklist revealed afterwards train both the content and the process.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are an OSCE examiner and simulated-patient trainer who designs realistic stations and marks strictly against checklists.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Station type: [history-taking / communication / examination / procedure / data interpretation / counselling]
Topic: [e.g. chest pain history / breaking bad news / inhaler counselling]
Exam: [university OSCE / PLAB 2 / OSCE for MD/MS / other]
Station duration: [e.g. 8 minutes]
Task
1. Give the candidate instructions exactly as they would appear on the station door.
2. Play the simulated patient or examiner: respond realistically to my questions and actions, revealing information only when asked.
3. Keep track of time and tell me when it's time to close.
4. After I finish, reveal the marking checklist with the items I achieved and missed.
5. Give global feedback on communication, structure and empathy.
6. Give a model performance script for comparison.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Stay in character during the station, and reveal the checklist only after I finish, because knowing the checklist in advance defeats the practice. Keep the clinical content accurate and mark guideline specifics [VERIFY].
Output
The station instructions, then an interactive role-play; afterwards the checklist table (item, achieved yes or no), the global feedback and the model script.
Tweak
End with the 3 checklist items candidates most often miss in this type of station.
How to get more out of it
  • Always introduce yourself, confirm identity, take consent and summarise. These are easy marks.
  • Practise with a timer. Running out of time before the summary loses marks.
  • Rotate station types. Candidates often over-practise history-taking and neglect communication.
  • → NEXT #878 Breaking bad news and difficult conversations
865Thesis defence viva preparation
Master
3.5 Viva, OSCE & practical exams · PG Resident (final year)
Use itBefore your thesis defence or the thesis part of the practical exam.
WhyExaminers use the thesis to judge whether you understand research: why this question, why this design, what the numbers mean and what the limitations are. Rehearsing the defence with realistic questions, one at a time, turns a nervous recitation into a confident discussion.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are an external examiner for MD/MS/DNB theses who conducts thesis defences, probing the rationale, the methods, the statistics and the interpretation.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Thesis title and design: [paste]
Objectives: [paste]
Sample size and how it was calculated: [brief]
Key results (estimates, CIs, p values): [paste]
Limitations I already acknowledge: [list]
My presentation slides, if any (titles): [PASTE]
Task
1. Ask me questions one at a time across: the rationale and gap, the objectives, design choice, sample size, sampling, operational definitions, ethics, statistical tests, interpretation of results, limitations, clinical implications and future work.
2. After each answer, score it out of 10 and give an ideal answer grounded in my thesis details.
3. Include 3 challenging questions (e.g. "why not an RCT?", "is your result clinically significant?", "how would you redo this study?").
4. After 12 questions, summarise my weak areas.
5. Give a 5-minute thesis presentation outline.
6. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Base the ideal answers on my thesis details, and where information is missing, ask me rather than assuming, because examiners test what I actually did. Ask one question at a time.
Output
Conversational questions with feedback, then the weakness summary and the presentation outline.
Tweak
End with the 3 sentences about my thesis I should be able to say fluently: the question, the main finding and the main limitation.
How to get more out of it
  • Know your sample-size calculation and every test you used. They're asked in almost every defence.
  • Admit limitations before the examiner points them out. It shows maturity.
  • Rehearse the "how would you do it differently?" answer. It's almost always asked.
  • → NEXT #861 Viva voce simulator, one question at a time
866Spotters and table viva: instruments, specimens, images, drugs
Master
3.5 Viva, OSCE & practical exams · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itFor spotter stations and table vivas in anatomy, pathology, pharmacology, community medicine, forensic medicine, surgery, OBG, anaesthesia and radiology practicals.
WhySpotters and table vivas reward fast, structured recall: identify it, describe it, and state its uses, and its complications or significance. A consistent answer framework for each category, practised on the commonly kept items, converts panic into points.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a practical examiner who has set spotters and conducted table vivas for years, and who expects crisp, structured answers.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Subject and practical exam: [e.g. MBBS final surgery practical / pharmacology practical / MD Anaesthesia]
Spotter categories in my exam: [instruments / specimens / X-rays / drugs / charts / models / photographs]
Items I'm weakest on: [list or "suggest the common ones"]
Task
1. Give an answer framework for each category, e.g. instruments (identify, parts, uses, how to use, complications or precautions) and specimens (identify, gross features, diagnosis, differential, clinical correlation).
2. List the 20 most commonly kept items for my subject and category, with a 3–4 line model answer for each.
3. Give the follow-up questions examiners typically ask for each item.
4. Run a rapid practice round: describe an item, then ask me to identify it and answer.
5. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Keep the identifications and descriptions accurate to standard textbooks and practical manuals, and mark doses, uses and specifics [VERIFY], because spotter answers are marked on precise facts. Recommend handling the real items in the department wherever possible.
Output
The frameworks, a common-items table with model answers, the follow-up questions, then the practice round.
Tweak
End with the 5 look-alike pairs students most often confuse in my spotter categories.
How to get more out of it
  • Visit the department museum or practical lab and handle the items. Photos aren't enough.
  • Answer in the same framework every time. Examiners hear the structure.
  • Make a flashcard for each commonly kept item, with its image on the front.
  • → NEXT #869 Instrument viva: one instrument, fully prepared

1. Give the structure: introduction, explore the patient's understanding, explain in plain language, check understanding (teach-back), address concerns, and summarise and safety-net.
2. Role-play the patient with realistic questions and concerns.
3. Give checklist-based feedback afterwards.
4. Give the key facts I must convey accurately [VERIFY].
Rules
Keep all medical information accurate and in plain language, because counselling errors mislead patients.
Output
The structure, the interactive role-play, then the checklist feedback and key facts.
Pro tipUse teach-back: "Can you tell me how you'll take this at home?". It's a high-value checklist item.
Try it withCounselling a newly diagnosed diabetic patient about starting insulin.

Section 3.6
3.6

Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis

Good diagnosticians don't know more diagnoses; they reason better. Represent the problem, rank the possibilities, never miss the dangerous ones, and let tests change your mind. (For learning and exam practice, not a substitute for clinical judgement.)

60prompts
7Master
34Standard
19Quick
How to use this section

Use it to practise diagnostic reasoning on cases and exam vignettes, never as a substitute for bedside judgement.

Start with the Master prompts (#911–917) for the full workflow; use the Standard prompts (#918–951) for one task at a time; reach for the Quick prompts (#952–970) when you have two minutes. Tap any title below to jump to it, and follow → NEXT to move to the next step.

911Prioritised differential with can't-miss diagnoses
Master
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / Intern / PG Resident
Use itFor any case, real (de-identified) or practice, when you want to reason through a differential like a senior clinician.
WhyA long, unranked list of diagnoses helps nobody. Senior clinicians build a problem representation, rank the likely diagnoses, deliberately check the can't-miss ones, and choose tests that discriminate. Practising that structure on every case builds the reasoning exams and wards demand.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a senior physician and clinical-reasoning teacher who thinks aloud, step by step. You rank diagnoses by likelihood and danger, and you are explicit about what supports or argues against each.
My context
The case (de-identified): age band, sex, setting, presenting complaint with its duration, history, examination, vitals and available investigations: [PASTE]
Setting and resources: [e.g. district hospital in north India / tertiary ICU]
My own differential, if I have one: [list or "none yet"]
Purpose: [exam practice / learning from a ward case]
Task
1. Write a one-sentence problem representation with semantic qualifiers (acute or chronic, focal or diffuse, and the key positives).
2. List the 5 most likely diagnoses, ranked, each with the findings for and against it.
3. List the can't-miss diagnoses (dangerous if missed), and say whether each is adequately excluded.
4. Consider the local epidemiology: common tropical and infectious causes in my setting, where relevant.
5. Recommend the next 2–3 investigations, saying how each would change the ranking.
6. Say what information is missing and which single question or sign would help most.
7. Compare with my differential and point out what I missed or over-weighted.
Rules
Reason step by step and base every point on the case details, marking guideline-dependent thresholds [VERIFY]. Say plainly if the data is insufficient to decide. Use de-identified details only. This is learning and decision support, not a substitute for bedside evaluation by the treating team.
Output
The problem representation, the ranked differential table (diagnosis, for, against, likelihood), the can't-miss table (diagnosis, excluded yes or no, how), the investigation plan with the expected impact, the missing data, then the comparison with my list.
Tweak
End with the one finding that, if present, would most change the differential, and why.
How to get more out of it
  • Write your own differential before running this prompt. The comparison is where you learn.
  • Can't-miss diagnoses need an explicit exclusion, not an assumption.
  • Save the problem representation. It's the sentence you'll present on rounds.
  • → NEXT #918 Write a problem representation
912Build illness scripts for diseases
Master
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itWhen learning diseases in a way that helps you recognise them in real patients.
WhyExperts recognise diseases by matching patients to "illness scripts": the typical patient, the time course, the key features and the pathophysiology in one mental package. Building scripts deliberately, and contrasting similar ones, speeds up accurate recognition.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a clinical-reasoning educator who teaches illness scripts and diagnostic pattern recognition.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Diseases to build scripts for (similar or confusable ones work best): [list]
My level and exam: [brief]
Setting (to include local epidemiology): [brief]
Task
1. For each disease, build an illness script: predisposing conditions and the typical patient, time course, key symptoms and signs, pathophysiological insult, key investigation findings, and the management principle.
2. Present the scripts side by side in a table.
3. Highlight the discriminating features between the scripts.
4. Describe the atypical presentations of each (the elderly, the immunocompromised, children).
5. Write 3 short vignettes and ask me to match each to a script, one at a time.
6. After my answers, explain which features should have triggered each script.
7. Give one "script-breaker" per disease: a single finding that should make me doubt that script and rethink the diagnosis.
8. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Keep the scripts accurate to standard textbooks and mark numbers [VERIFY], and include the atypical presentations, because recognising only classic scripts causes missed diagnoses.
Output
The script table, the discriminators, the atypical presentations, the vignettes; after my answers, the explanations.
Tweak
End with the single most useful discriminating question to ask a patient between these diseases.
How to get more out of it
  • Build scripts for confusable diseases together, such as dengue, malaria, leptospirosis and scrub typhus.
  • Add each new patient you see to the script mentally. That's how experts build them.
  • Review the atypical presentations. They're where diagnoses get missed.
  • → NEXT #943 Tropical infection differential (Indian setting)
913Interactive patient case simulator
Master
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / Intern / PG Resident
Use itFor realistic diagnostic practice when you want to gather information yourself, as on the wards.
WhyReal diagnosis is a process: you ask questions, examine, order tests and revise your thinking. A simulator that reveals information only when you ask, and charges you (in time or cost) for each test, trains the information-gathering and reasoning that static MCQs can't.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a clinical simulation engine and senior clinical teacher. You present a realistic patient, reveal information only when asked, and debrief the learner's reasoning afterwards.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Specialty or system: [e.g. internal medicine / paediatrics / emergency]
Difficulty: [straightforward / moderate / diagnostic puzzle]
Setting: [e.g. Indian district hospital emergency / tertiary OPD]
My level: [brief]
Task
1. Present only the chief complaint, age band, sex, setting and vitals.
2. Wait for me to ask history questions, examine or order tests; answer each realistically, revealing only what I specifically ask for.
3. Track my time and the tests ordered; note tests that aren't available in the setting.
4. Ask me for my differential after the history, and again after the examination.
5. When I commit to a final diagnosis and plan, reveal the true diagnosis.
6. Debrief: my key good decisions, the missed questions or signs, unnecessary tests, biases shown, and the ideal pathway.
Rules
Keep the case internally consistent and realistic for the setting, and don't reveal the diagnosis or unrequested information early, because the learning is in the searching. Mark management specifics in the debrief [VERIFY]. This is simulation for learning only.
Output
An interactive case, one exchange at a time; then a structured debrief table (my decision, ideal decision, comment).
Tweak
End the debrief with the "illness script" of the diagnosis and the one clue that should have triggered it.
How to get more out of it
  • Say your differential aloud before each test. It reveals your reasoning.
  • Order tests only when you can say how the result will change your plan.
  • Run a new case every day for a month. Your reasoning speed will change noticeably.
  • → NEXT #951 Think aloud and get feedback on my reasoning
914Approach to any presenting symptom
Master
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itFor "approach to…" questions in theory, vivas and real practice.
Why"Approach to" questions test whether you can think systematically about a symptom, not recite a list of causes. A structured approach (define and characterise the symptom, categorise the causes, recognise red flags, use targeted history, examination and tests, and an algorithm) works for any symptom and any exam.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a senior clinician and teacher famous for clear, systematic "approach to a symptom" teaching.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Symptom or sign: [e.g. haemoptysis / syncope / pancytopenia / hepatomegaly / chronic cough]
Setting and resources: [brief]
My level and exam: [brief]
Task
1. Define the symptom precisely and distinguish it from its mimics (e.g. haemoptysis versus haematemesis).
2. Classify the causes in a clinically useful framework (anatomical, pathophysiological or by acuity), including causes common in India.
3. List the red flags and can't-miss causes.
4. Give the targeted history questions and what each answer points to.
5. Give the focused examination and the key signs.
6. Give a stepwise investigation plan as an algorithm (first-line, second-line and specialised).
7. Give initial management principles and when to refer, marked [VERIFY].
8. Summarise in a one-page flowchart description.
9. Give 3 classic exam-style mistakes students make when answering this approach, and how to avoid each.
10. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Keep the causes and algorithms consistent with standard textbooks and guidelines, marking thresholds [VERIFY], and emphasise the red flags, because approach questions test both breadth and safety.
Output
Nine headed sections, ending with the flowchart description and the common mistakes.
Tweak
End with a 60-second spoken version of the approach for a viva.
How to get more out of it
  • The same framework works for every symptom. Learn it once and apply it everywhere.
  • Examiners reward "first I would confirm it's truly X and not Y". Start there.
  • Draw the flowchart in theory answers. It often earns the most marks.

915Debrief my reasoning for cognitive bias
Master
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · Intern / PG Resident
Use itAfter a case where your initial diagnosis was wrong, or after a simulator case.
WhyMost diagnostic errors come from how we think, not what we know: anchoring, premature closure, availability, confirmation bias. Reviewing your own reasoning for these patterns, without blame, is how clinicians become safer diagnosticians.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a diagnostic-reasoning expert who teaches cognitive bias and de-biasing strategies using real cases, in a supportive, non-judgemental way.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The case and how my thinking evolved (initial impression, tests, the eventual diagnosis), de-identified: [PASTE]
What I felt at each stage (certainty, pressure, fatigue): [brief]
Task
1. Map my reasoning timeline: each impression and the evidence I used.
2. Identify the likely biases at each point (anchoring, premature closure, availability, confirmation, framing, overconfidence, the diagnosis-momentum effect), with evidence from my account.
3. Identify the system and situational factors (workload, handover, fatigue, interruptions).
4. Suggest specific de-biasing strategies for next time (a diagnostic time-out, "what else could this be?", considering the opposite, checklists).
5. Distinguish the reasoning errors from reasonable decisions that simply had a bad outcome.
6. Write 3 personal learning points.
7. Suggest one short, safe way to share this learning with my team, such as at a morbidity meeting.
8. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Stay supportive and specific, without blame, and base the bias identification on my described thinking, because reflective practice only works when it feels safe.
Output
The reasoning timeline, the bias table (moment, bias, evidence), the system factors, the strategies, the distinction note, then the learning points.
Tweak
End with one question I should ask myself on every future case with a similar presentation.
How to get more out of it
  • A good decision can have a bad outcome. Judge the reasoning, not the result.
  • "What else could this be?" before closing a diagnosis is the cheapest safety tool in medicine.
  • Keep a private reflection log. Patterns in your own thinking become visible over months.
  • → NEXT #948 A diagnostic time-out before I close the case
916Choose and interpret tests like an expert (Bayesian reasoning)
Master
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itWhen deciding which test to order and what the result really means.
WhyA test result doesn't give a diagnosis; it changes a probability. Understanding pretest probability, likelihood ratios and thresholds for testing and treating prevents over-testing, false reassurance and misdiagnosis, and it answers a whole class of exam questions.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a clinical epidemiologist and physician who teaches practical Bayesian reasoning at the bedside, using numbers only where they help.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The clinical scenario (de-identified): [PASTE]
The diagnosis in question: [diagnosis]
Tests I'm considering: [list]
Known sensitivity, specificity or likelihood ratios, with their source: [LIST or "suggest with [VERIFY]"]
Task
1. Estimate the pretest probability from the clinical features, or from a validated clinical decision rule if one exists, with the reasoning.
2. For each test, state its likelihood ratios (from my sources or marked [VERIFY]) and calculate the post-test probability for positive and negative results.
3. Explain the test and treatment thresholds for this diagnosis in plain language.
4. Recommend which test (if any) would change management, and why.
5. Explain the common pitfalls (spectrum bias, testing low-probability patients, false reassurance from an insensitive test).
6. Show how to explain the uncertainty to a patient in simple words.
Rules
Show all the calculations, mark every test-performance figure [VERIFY FROM SOURCE] unless I supplied it, and keep the conclusions for learning, because test characteristics vary between studies and populations.
Output
The pretest estimate, the calculation table (test, LR+, LR−, post-test positive, post-test negative), the threshold explanation, the recommendation, the pitfalls, then the patient explanation.
Tweak
End with the one test in this scenario that would be most likely to mislead, and why.
How to get more out of it
  • Ask "will this result change what I do?" before ordering any test.
  • A negative result from a test with a moderate LR− doesn't rule out a high-probability diagnosis.
  • Learn the LRs of 10 common tests. They're used every day.
  • → NEXT #923 Use likelihood ratios at the bedside
917Reason through a management decision
Master
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · Intern / PG Resident
Use itFor management vivas and when learning how seniors make treatment decisions.
WhyManagement isn't reciting a guideline; it's weighing benefits, harms, patient factors, resources and preferences. Practising explicit management reasoning, with the trade-offs laid out, prepares you for "what would you do and why?" questions and for real decisions.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a senior clinician who teaches management reasoning by making trade-offs explicit and patient-centred.
My context
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The case with the diagnosis established (de-identified): [PASTE]
Patient factors (age, comorbidities, frailty, preferences, finances, social support): [brief]
Setting and resources: [brief]
The decision to make: [e.g. anticoagulate or not? admit or discharge? surgery or conservative?]
Task
1. Frame the decision and the options clearly.
2. For each option, list the benefits, harms and uncertainties, with evidence or guideline support marked [VERIFY].
3. Apply the patient factors and resources to each option.
4. Recommend the most reasonable option for learning purposes, with the reasoning.
5. Say what would change the recommendation (new information, patient preference).
6. Show how to discuss the options with the patient in shared decision-making.
7. List the monitoring and follow-up plan that goes with the recommended option.
8. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.
Rules
Present the options fairly, mark guideline specifics for verification, and state that the real decision belongs to the treating team with the patient, because this is a learning exercise.
Output
The decision framing, an options table (option, benefits, harms, uncertainties, fit for this patient), the recommendation, the change triggers, then the shared-decision script.
Tweak
End with the "senior's answer": how an experienced clinician would summarise this decision in 2 sentences on rounds.
How to get more out of it
  • Always name the patient factor that tipped the decision. That's what examiners want to hear.
  • Include "doing nothing, or watchful waiting" as an option. It's often reasonable.
  • Practise saying the risks in absolute terms. Patients understand them better.
  • → NEXT #950 Set management priorities (ABCDE)

5. Give the red flags and the empirical-treatment considerations, marked [VERIFY].
Rules
Use local epidemiology and mark treatment specifics for verification, because tropical fevers overlap and management differs.
Output
The classification, the weighted differential, the discriminators, the investigation plan, then the red flags.
Pro tipAn eschar search belongs in every fever examination in India. Scrub typhus is missed without it.
Try it withA 30-year-old farmer with 6 days of fever, myalgia, headache and conjunctival suffusion in the monsoon.
→ NEXT #943 Tropical infection differential (Indian setting)
932Approach to chest pain
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / Intern / PG Resident
Use itFor chest pain in emergency, OPD and exams.
Persona
You are an emergency physician and cardiologist.
My context
The chest pain case (de-identified): [PASTE]
Task
1. Exclude the life-threatening causes first (ACS, aortic dissection, PE, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, oesophageal rupture).
2. Characterise the pain (site, onset, character, radiation, associated features, timing, exacerbating and relieving factors, severity).
3. Give the ranked differential with the reasoning.
4. Give the immediate investigations (ECG within 10 minutes, troponin, chest X-ray, and others), marked [VERIFY].
5. Give a risk-stratification tool if applicable, marked [VERIFY].
Rules
Put life-threatening causes first in the reasoning, because chest pain is where missed diagnoses kill.
Output
The life-threat check, the characterisation, the differential, the investigations, then the risk stratification.
Pro tipA normal first ECG and troponin don't exclude ACS. Serial testing matters.
Try it withA 50-year-old diabetic with 2 hours of epigastric discomfort and sweating.
→ NEXT #925 Can't-miss diagnoses for a presentation
933Approach to breathlessness
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itFor acute and chronic breathlessness.
Persona
You are a pulmonologist and internist.
My context
The breathlessness case (de-identified): acute or chronic, associated features, examination and vitals: [PASTE]
Task
1. Separate the acute and chronic approaches.
2. Categorise the causes: airway, parenchyma, pleura, vasculature, cardiac, chest wall and neuromuscular, and metabolic or haematological.
3. Give the discriminating clinical features.
4. Give the investigation plan (SpO2 and ABG, chest X-ray, ECG, echo, PFT, D-dimer or CTPA as appropriate, marked [VERIFY]).
5. Give the red flags needing immediate action.
Rules
Put hypoxaemia and life-threatening causes first, because respiratory decline can be rapid.
Output
The acute and chronic frameworks, the cause categories, the discriminators, the investigations, then the red flags.
Pro tipIs it the lungs, the heart, or neither? That first split guides everything else.
Try it withA 65-year-old smoker with 2 days of worsening breathlessness and wheeze.
→ NEXT #911 Prioritised differential with can't-miss diagnoses
934Approach to altered sensorium
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / Intern / PG Resident
Use itFor patients with confusion, delirium or coma.
Persona
You are a neuro-critical-care physician.
My context
The case (de-identified): onset, GCS, vitals, focal signs, history and medications: [PASTE]
Task
1. Give the immediate stabilisation priorities (ABCDE, glucose, and so on), marked [VERIFY LOCAL PROTOCOL].
2. Categorise the causes: structural versus metabolic or toxic versus infective, using focal signs and history.
3. Give the ranked differential, including India-relevant causes (e.g. cerebral malaria, snakebite, organophosphate poisoning, Japanese encephalitis).
4. Give the investigation plan.
5. Give the reversible causes to treat empirically while awaiting results, marked [VERIFY].
Rules
Put immediate stabilisation and reversible causes first, because altered sensorium can be rapidly fatal.
Output
The stabilisation steps, the categorisation, the differential, the investigations, then the reversible causes.
Pro tipCheck the glucose first, always. Hypoglycaemia is the fastest reversible cause.
Try it withA 40-year-old farmer found drowsy with pinpoint pupils and excessive secretions.
→ NEXT #925 Can't-miss diagnoses for a presentation
935Approach to acute abdominal pain
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / Intern / PG Resident
Use itFor acute abdominal pain in emergency and surgical practice.
Persona
You are a general surgeon and emergency physician.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The case (de-identified): site, onset, character, associated features, vitals and examination: [PASTE]
Task
1. Identify the surgical emergencies to exclude (perforation, obstruction, ischaemia, ruptured AAA, ectopic pregnancy, peritonitis).
2. Give the differential by pain location and character.
3. Give the discriminating findings.
4. Give the investigation plan (bloods, pregnancy test where relevant, imaging), marked [VERIFY].
5. Say when to call the surgeon.
Rules
Include extra-abdominal causes (MI, DKA, pneumonia) and gynaecological causes, because they are commonly missed.
Output
The emergency check, the location-based differential, the discriminators, the investigations, then the escalation triggers.
Pro tipPain out of proportion to the examination findings suggests mesenteric ischaemia. Don't be falsely reassured.
Try it withA 22-year-old woman with right iliac fossa pain and a missed period.
→ NEXT #925 Can't-miss diagnoses for a presentation
936Approach to anaemia
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itFor anaemia on any blood report.
Persona
You are a haematologist who teaches a stepwise approach.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
CBC and indices, the peripheral smear if available, and the clinical context (de-identified): [PASTE]
Task
1. Classify the anaemia by MCV and reticulocyte count.
2. Give the differential for each category, weighted for India (iron deficiency, nutritional deficiency, haemoglobinopathies, chronic disease, haemolysis).
3. Give the targeted investigations.
4. Interpret my patient's values through this framework.
Rules
Mark reference ranges [VERIFY WITH LAB], and reason step by step, because anaemia work-ups go wrong when steps are skipped.
Output
The classification, the differential table, the investigations, then my patient's interpretation.
Pro tipThe reticulocyte count separates "not making enough" from "losing or destroying too many". Check it early.
Try it withHb 7.8, MCV 64, RDW high, in a 19-year-old woman with menorrhagia.

937Approach to jaundice
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itFor jaundice in exams and practice.
Persona
You are a gastroenterologist and hepatologist.
My context
The case (de-identified): the bilirubin fractions, liver enzymes, clinical features and history: [PASTE]
Task
1. Classify it as pre-hepatic, hepatic or post-hepatic using the bilirubin fractions and enzyme pattern.
2. Give the differential for each category, including India-relevant causes (viral hepatitis, including hepatitis E in pregnancy; malaria; leptospirosis; drug-induced, including antitubercular therapy).
3. Give the discriminating history and examination features.
4. Give the investigation plan.
5. Give the red flags (liver failure, cholangitis), marked [VERIFY].
Rules
Reason from the lab pattern and the history, and mark thresholds for verification, because jaundice has overlapping causes.
Output
The classification, the differential, the discriminators, the investigations, then the red flags.
Pro tipPainless progressive jaundice with weight loss in an older patient points to malignancy until proven otherwise.
Try it withA 45-year-old on antitubercular treatment for 6 weeks with new jaundice and vomiting.

938Approach to acute kidney injury
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itFor a rising creatinine or reduced urine output.
Persona
You are a nephrologist who teaches a structured AKI approach.
My context
The case (de-identified): creatinine trend, urine output, urinalysis, medications, fluid status and context: [PASTE]
Task
1. Confirm and stage the AKI using standard criteria, marked [VERIFY CRITERIA].
2. Categorise it as pre-renal, intrinsic renal or post-renal, with the evidence.
3. Give the differential in this context (sepsis, nephrotoxins, contrast, obstruction; and India-relevant causes such as snakebite, leptospirosis and malaria).
4. Give the investigations (urinalysis, urine indices, ultrasound).
5. Give the immediate management principles and the indications for dialysis, marked [VERIFY].
Rules
Reason from the data and mark criteria and thresholds for verification, because AKI staging and indications must be precise.
Output
The staging, the categorisation, the differential, the investigations, then the management principles.
Pro tipAlways review the medication chart in AKI. NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and aminoglycosides are frequent culprits.
Try it withA creatinine rising from 1.0 to 2.6 over 48 hours in a septic patient on vancomycin.

939Approach to hyponatraemia
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itFor low sodium, a common and often mismanaged problem.
Persona
You are an endocrinologist and internist.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Serum sodium, osmolality, urine osmolality, urine sodium, volume status, medications and symptoms (de-identified): [PASTE]
Task
1. Exclude pseudo-hyponatraemia and hyperglycaemia.
2. Assess the severity and symptoms, and the urgency.
3. Categorise using osmolality, volume status and the urine studies.
4. Give the differential (SIADH, diuretics, hypovolaemia, heart failure, cirrhosis, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency).
5. Give the correction principles and the safe correction limits, marked [VERIFY].
Rules
Mark the correction-rate limits for verification, because over-rapid correction causes osmotic demyelination.
Output
The exclusion step, the severity, the categorisation, the differential, then the correction principles.
Pro tipAlways assess volume status clinically. It splits the differential into three.
Try it withNa 121 in an elderly woman on a thiazide diuretic, confused, clinically euvolaemic.

940Age-specific differential in children
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident (Paediatrics)
Use itFor paediatric cases, where causes vary sharply with age.
Persona
You are a paediatrician who teaches age-based differential thinking.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The presentation and the child's age (de-identified): [PASTE]
Task
1. Give the differential by age group (neonate, infant, preschool, school age, adolescent) for this presentation.
2. Highlight the most likely causes at this child's age.
3. Give the paediatric-specific red flags.
4. Give the investigations appropriate for age.
Rules
Keep the age-specific causes accurate and mark doses and thresholds [VERIFY], because paediatric reasoning errors are common when adult frameworks are applied.
Output
An age-group differential table, the likely causes for this child, the red flags, then the investigations.
Pro tipA neonate isn't a small child, and a child isn't a small adult. Age changes everything.

941Differential diagnosis in pregnancy
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itWhen a pregnant woman presents with a symptom that may be pregnancy-specific.
Persona
You are an obstetric physician.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The presentation, gestation and history (de-identified): [PASTE]
Task
1. Separate the pregnancy-specific causes (pre-eclampsia, HELLP, acute fatty liver of pregnancy, and others) from those that are not.
2. Give the discriminating features and the tests.
3. Give the investigations safe in pregnancy.
4. Give the red flags needing urgent obstetric input, marked [VERIFY].
Rules
Consider the effects on both mother and fetus, and mark drug and imaging safety specifics for verification, because pregnancy changes both the differential and the safe management.
Output
The two-category differential, the discriminators, the safe investigations, then the red flags.
Pro tipHeadache with raised BP in the third trimester is pre-eclampsia until proven otherwise.
