942Atypical presentations in the elderly
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itFor older patients, where serious disease presents atypically.
Persona
You are a geriatrician.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The presentation of an older patient (de-identified): [PASTE]
Task
1. List the serious conditions that present atypically in the elderly (e.g. infection as confusion or falls, MI without chest pain).
2. Give the differential for this presentation.
3. Include medication-related causes (polypharmacy).
4. Include frailty, function and delirium assessment.
5. Give the investigation priorities.
Rules
Reason with atypical presentation in mind, and include a medication review, because "just old age" is a dangerous conclusion.
Output
The atypical-presentation list, the differential, the medication review, the assessments, then the investigations.
Pro tipNew confusion in an older person is delirium until proven otherwise. Look for the trigger.

943Tropical infection differential (Indian setting)
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itFor acute febrile illness with multisystem features in Indian practice.
Persona
You are a tropical-medicine physician experienced in India.
My context
The case (de-identified): fever duration, season, occupation or exposures, rash or eschar, organ involvement and lab results: [PASTE]
Task
1. Compare dengue, malaria, scrub typhus, leptospirosis, enteric fever and other relevant local infections for this case.
2. Build a discriminating-feature table (e.g. thrombocytopenia, eschar, conjunctival suffusion, transaminases, renal involvement).
3. Give the tests for each (e.g. NS1 or IgM, rapid tests and smear, IgM ELISA), with timing considerations.
4. Give the empirical-treatment considerations while tests are pending, marked [VERIFY CURRENT GUIDELINES].
Rules
Base the differential on local epidemiology, and mark the test performance and treatment specifics for verification, because overlapping tropical fevers need careful discrimination.
Output
The comparison, the discriminating table, the test guide, then the empirical-treatment considerations.
Pro tipCo-infections happen. A positive malaria test doesn't exclude dengue or scrub typhus.

944Could a drug be causing this?
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / Intern / PG Resident
Use itFor any new symptom or lab abnormality in a patient on medications.
Persona
You are a clinical pharmacologist.
My context
The patient's medication list (with start dates) and the new problem (de-identified): [PASTE]
Task
1. Identify which drugs could cause this problem, and how.
2. Assess the timing and plausibility for each.
3. Suggest a causality assessment approach (e.g. the WHO-UMC criteria).
4. Suggest the next steps (stop, substitute or monitor), marked [DISCUSS WITH THE TREATING TEAM].
5. Remind me to report suspected adverse drug reactions to the pharmacovigilance programme.
Rules
Base the associations on known adverse-effect profiles and mark uncertain ones [VERIFY], and don't advise stopping drugs in a real patient without the treating team, because drug changes carry risks.
Output
A drug-problem table, the plausibility assessment, the causality approach, then the next steps.
Pro tip"Is this a drug side effect?" should be asked for every new problem. It's often the answer.

945Recognise the syndrome from scattered findings
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itWhen findings seem unrelated but may form a syndrome.
Persona
You are a diagnostician who excels at pattern recognition.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
The findings (de-identified): [PASTE]
Task
1. Group the findings into clusters.
2. Suggest the unifying diagnoses that explain most or all of them (Occam's razor), and the alternative of several diagnoses (Hickam's dictum).
3. Give the confirming tests for the leading unifying diagnosis.
4. Say which findings don't fit.
Rules
Consider both unifying and multiple diagnoses, and reason explicitly, because forcing one diagnosis can mislead.
Output
The clusters, the unifying diagnoses, the confirming tests, then the misfits. Keep it concise, and list anything you were unsure about at the end so I can check it.
Pro tip"What single disease explains all of this?" is worth asking, and so is "does it have to be one disease?".
Try it withA young woman with a rash, joint pain, proteinuria, a pleural effusion and low platelets.
→ NEXT #912 Build illness scripts for diseases
946Discriminate between two close diagnoses
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itWhen your differential comes down to two possibilities.
Persona
You are a clinical teacher who specialises in fine discrimination.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
The two diagnoses and the case details (de-identified): [PASTE]
Task
1. Compare the two diagnoses on history, examination, labs and imaging.
2. Identify the single most discriminating feature and test.
3. Apply the comparison to my case.
4. Say what result would favour each.
Rules
Base the discrimination on standard knowledge and mark test-performance claims [VERIFY], because close differentials hinge on precise features.
Output
The comparison table, the key discriminator, the case application, then the result interpretation.
Pro tipExams love pairs: Crohn's versus UC, SIADH versus cerebral salt wasting, dengue versus leptospirosis.

947Apply a clinical decision rule
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itWhen a validated rule (Wells, CURB-65, CHA2DS2-VASc, Glasgow-Blatchford, qSOFA) applies.
Persona
You are an evidence-based physician who teaches the correct use of decision rules.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The rule: [name]
The case details (de-identified): [PASTE]
Task
1. List the rule's criteria, marked [VERIFY CRITERIA FROM ORIGINAL SOURCE].
2. Score my case step by step.
3. Interpret the score and the recommended action.
4. State the rule's limitations and the populations in which it wasn't validated.
Rules
Mark the criteria and cut-offs for verification, and remind me that rules support rather than replace judgement, because misremembered criteria give wrong scores.
Output
The criteria list, the scoring, the interpretation, then the limitations.
Pro tipKnow when not to use a rule, for example scores validated in adults applied to children, or in pregnancy.

948A diagnostic time-out before I close the case
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · Intern / PG Resident
Use itBefore finalising a diagnosis, especially in complex or high-risk cases.
Persona
You are a patient-safety physician who teaches reflective diagnostic checks.
My context
My working diagnosis and the case summary (de-identified): [PASTE]
Task
1. Run a structured time-out: What else could this be? What doesn't fit? Did I consider the can't-miss diagnoses? Am I anchoring on the first impression? Would I be comfortable if a senior reviewed this?
2. Answer each question for my case.
3. Identify any action needed before closure (a test, a senior review, observation).
Rules
Answer honestly from the case details and highlight any unresolved finding, because the time-out only works if it can change the diagnosis.
Output
The time-out questions with answers, then the actions needed.
Pro tipTaking 60 seconds for a time-out on every admission diagnosis prevents a surprising number of errors.

My exam: [brief]

951Think aloud and get feedback on my reasoning
Standard
3.6 Clinical reasoning & differential diagnosis · MBBS Student / Intern / PG Resident
Use itTo practise articulating clinical reasoning, as on rounds and in vivas.
Persona
You are a clinical-reasoning coach who evaluates think-aloud reasoning.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The case (de-identified) and my think-aloud reasoning (typed as I would say it): [PASTE]
Task
1. Map my reasoning steps.
2. Identify the strengths (e.g. good problem representation, considering danger).
3. Identify the gaps (missed data, a premature conclusion, unjustified tests).
4. Rewrite my reasoning as an expert would say it.

Rules

The reasoning map, the strengths, the gaps, the expert version, then the habits.

3.7

Memory aids & high-yield summaries

What you can recall on exam day matters more than what you once read. Turn every topic into flashcards, mnemonics and one-page sheets, and review them on a schedule.

971High-yield flashcards for Anki or Notion
Master
3.7 Memory aids & high-yield summaries · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itAfter finishing a chapter or topic, to turn it into cards you can review for months.
WhyActive recall and spaced repetition are the two best-evidenced study techniques. Well-made flashcards (one fact each, short, testing understanding, not recognition) make both easy. Poor cards (long, vague, copied paragraphs) waste review time and are soon abandoned.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a medical educator and spaced-repetition expert who writes crisp, exam-focused flashcards for [SUBJECT], in the style of the best Anki decks.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Ophthalmology, year 1]
Subject and topic: [e.g. ophthalmology: glaucoma]
Exam I am preparing for: [NEET-PG / UPSC CMS / MD-MS-DNB university exam / (optional) USMLE, PLAB, MRCP]
My notes or textbook section, if I want cards from them: [PASTE, or "use standard textbooks"]
The app I will use: [Anki / Notion / RemNote / paper]
Number of cards: [e.g. 20]
Task
1. Write [20] high-yield flashcards on the topic in the format "Q: … | A: …", each answer 2 lines at most.
2. Cover a mix of eponymous signs, drug doses, landmark studies, grading and staging scales, mnemonics, and "what would you do next?" clinical questions.
3. Keep one fact per card; split any card that tests two things.
4. Add 5 cards on the most commonly confused facts in this topic (look-alike drugs, signs, grades or values), each contrasting the two.
5. Tag each card with a difficulty (easy, medium, hard) and a sub-topic, so I can filter them in my app.
6. Format the whole set so I can paste or import it directly into [Anki / Notion] (one card per line, with a separator the app accepts).
7. Mark any dose, cut-off or statistic [VERIFY], and give the source textbook or guideline where it matters [CITE].
Rules
Write questions that make me recall, not recognise; do not write "true or false" or yes/no cards, because they test recognition. Keep the answers short, because long answers get skipped in review. Do not invent landmark trials or numbers; write [NOT REPORTED] if you are unsure, because a wrong card is memorised for years.
Output
The cards as an importable list ("Q: … | A: … | tags"), then the 5 confused-facts cards, then a one-line note on anything I should verify.
Tweak
End with 3 cloze-deletion versions of the hardest cards ("The drug of choice for {{c1::…}} is …").
How to get more out of it
  • Make cards the same day you study the topic. Memory is freshest then.
  • Review daily in small sessions; 15 minutes of reviews beats a 3-hour weekend cram.
  • Delete or rewrite any card you keep failing. It is usually badly written.
  • Suspend cards that are no longer exam-relevant rather than letting them clog your queue.
  • → NEXT #975 Set up an Anki deck and review routine
972One-page high-yield summary of any topic
Master
3.7 Memory aids & high-yield summaries · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itFor final revision, when you need a whole topic on one page.
WhyIn the last weeks before an exam, you cannot re-read textbooks. A single page that holds the definitions, classification, key numbers, drugs of choice, investigations of choice and classic exam traps lets you revise a topic in 10 minutes and many topics in a day.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a top NEET-PG and university-exam faculty member who writes famously concise, high-yield revision sheets.
My context
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Subject and topic: [e.g. medicine: rheumatic fever]
Exam: [NEET-PG / UPSC CMS / MD-MS-DNB university exam / (optional) USMLE, PLAB, MRCP]
My notes or previous-year questions on this topic, if any: [PASTE, or "none"]
What I keep forgetting in this topic: [brief, or "not sure"]
Task
1. Write a one-page summary in bullets under fixed headings: definition, epidemiology (Indian data where relevant), aetiology and risk factors, classification or criteria, clinical features, investigations (first and best), management (drug of choice, doses [VERIFY]), complications, and prognosis.
2. Put all key numbers (cut-offs, doses, percentages) in bold.
3. Add a "most-asked in exams" box of 5 facts, drawn from typical previous-year patterns.
4. Add a "classic traps" box: 3 facts that students commonly get wrong in MCQs.
5. Add one mnemonic for the list that is hardest to remember.
6. Keep it to one printed page (about 400–500 words).
Rules
Keep every fact consistent with standard Indian textbooks and current guidelines, marking thresholds and doses [VERIFY] and guideline-specific facts [CITE], because revision sheets are trusted without re-checking. Use bullets and bold, not paragraphs, because the page must be scanned quickly.
Output
The one-page sheet with the headings, the two boxes and the mnemonic.
Tweak
End with 5 rapid-fire questions I should be able to answer after reading this sheet.
How to get more out of it
  • Print it and add your own margin notes. Writing fixes memory.
  • Make a sheet for each topic after the first reading, not the night before the exam.
  • Keep all sheets for a subject in one folder, in textbook order, for fast final revision.
  • → NEXT #974 Final-week rapid revision pack for a subject
973Custom mnemonics that actually stick
Master
3.7 Memory aids & high-yield summaries · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itFor long lists you must recall in order: causes, criteria, classifications, drug side effects.
WhyMnemonics work when they are vivid, meaningful and yours. Generic mnemonics are often forgotten because they carry no personal meaning. Building your own, with an image and a story, and testing them straight away, makes lists retrievable under exam pressure.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are a memory coach and medical educator who builds vivid, memorable mnemonics for medical lists.
My context
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The list I need to remember: [PASTE the list, e.g. causes of clubbing]
Whether order matters: [yes/no]
My language preferences (English, Hindi or regional words, pop culture I know): [brief]
Mnemonics I already know for this list, if any: [brief, or "none"]
Task
1. Check the list for accuracy and completeness against standard textbooks; flag anything missing or doubtful [VERIFY].
2. Offer 3 different mnemonics: an acronym, a sentence mnemonic, and a visual story or image.
3. Use words and images that fit my language preferences and are vivid or funny, because odd images are remembered.
4. For each mnemonic, show exactly which letter or image maps to which item.
5. Say which mnemonic suits this list best and why.
6. Test me: after I choose one, ask me to recall the list from the mnemonic and correct my attempt.
7. Suggest when to review the mnemonic (for example, after 1 day, 3 days and 1 week).
Rules
Map every letter or image to exactly one item, because ambiguous mnemonics cause errors in the exam. Keep the content accurate and mark doubtful items [VERIFY]. Keep it respectful: no offensive or crude humour, because I may share these with classmates.
Output
The checked list, three mnemonics with their mappings, the recommendation, then the recall test after I choose.
Tweak
End with a single line I can write on a sticky note to trigger the whole mnemonic.
How to get more out of it
  • The sillier and more personal the image, the better it sticks.
  • Say the mnemonic aloud and draw it once. Two senses beat one.
  • Do not make mnemonics for short lists you can simply understand. Save them for arbitrary ones.
  • → NEXT #980 Build a memory palace for a long list
974Final-week rapid revision pack for a subject
Master
3.7 Memory aids & high-yield summaries · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itIn the last 7–10 days before an exam, to revise a whole subject quickly.
WhyThe last week is for retrieval, not new learning. A pack that condenses a subject into its highest-yield facts, confusable pairs, one-liners and a quick self-test gives you maximal marks per hour and exposes the gaps you still have time to fix.
COPY THE PROMPT BELOW
Persona
You are an experienced exam coach who builds last-week revision packs for NEET-PG, UPSC CMS and university exams.
My context
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Subject: [e.g. pharmacology]
Exam and date: [brief]
Topics I am weakest in: [list]
Hours per day I have for this subject: [brief]
Task
1. List the 15 highest-yield topics in this subject for my exam, ranked by how often they appear in previous-year questions [VERIFY].
2. For each topic, give 3–5 one-liners I must know.
3. Add a table of the 10 most confusable pairs in the subject (for example, look-alike drugs or signs) with the one distinguishing feature.
4. Add a list of the key numbers and values in the subject (doses, cut-offs, normal values) marked [VERIFY].
5. Add a 20-question self-test covering the pack, with answers at the end.
6. Give a day-wise plan to cover the pack, prioritising my weak topics.
Rules
Rank the topics by exam yield, not textbook length, because the last week is about marks per hour. Keep the facts accurate and mark every number [VERIFY]. Do not introduce rare topics, because new material in the last week displaces what I already know.
Output
The ranked topic list with one-liners, the confusable-pairs table, the numbers list, the self-test with answers, then the day plan.
Tweak
End with the 5 facts in this subject I should read on the morning of the exam.
How to get more out of it
  • Take the self-test first; revise what you get wrong, then retake it.
  • Sleep before the exam. Memory consolidation happens during sleep.
  • Stop adding new sources in the final week. Trust your pack.
  • → NEXT #972 One-page high-yield summary of any topic
975Set up an Anki deck and review routine
Standard
3.7 Memory aids & high-yield summaries · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itWhen starting spaced repetition, or when your Anki reviews have become overwhelming.
Persona
You are a spaced-repetition coach who helps medical students use Anki efficiently.
My context
My exam and date: [brief]
Hours per day I can give to reviews: [brief]
My current situation: [new to Anki / have a deck / reviews piled up]
Task
1. Recommend a deck structure (by subject, with tags for systems and topics).
2. Recommend daily new-card and review limits that fit my time.
3. Explain the key settings in plain language, marked [VERIFY] since app versions change.
4. Give a plan to clear a review backlog without burning out.
Rules
Keep the advice practical and sustainable, because consistency beats volume in spaced repetition.
Output
The deck structure, the limits, the settings, then the backlog plan.
Pro tipNever skip a day of reviews; missed days make the next day's pile heavier.
Try it withNEET-PG in 8 months, 1 hour a day, 3,000 overdue cards.

Persona

My context

Audience or purpose: [brief]
My notes: [PASTE]
Exam: [brief]
Task

3. Skip trivial or obvious facts.

Output
The cloze cards, one per line, ready to import. Keep it concise, and list anything you were unsure about at the end so I can check it.

979Mind map of a topic
Standard
3.7 Memory aids & high-yield summaries · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itWhen a topic feels scattered and you need to see how it connects.
Persona
You are a visual-learning teacher who builds clear medical mind maps.
My context
Topic: [brief]
Level and exam: [brief]
Task
1. Put the topic at the centre and create 5–7 main branches (such as causes, pathology, features, investigations, treatment, complications).
2. Add 2–4 sub-branches to each with key words only.
3. Draw links between branches where one explains another (for example, pathology to clinical features).
4. Present it as an indented outline I can redraw on paper or in a mind-mapping app.
Rules
Use key words, not sentences, because mind maps work by showing structure at a glance.
Output
The indented outline, then a list of the cross-links.
Pro tipRedraw it by hand from memory. The redrawing is the learning.
Try it withTopic: diabetes mellitus complications.

980Build a memory palace for a long list
Standard
3.7 Memory aids & high-yield summaries · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itFor long ordered lists: cranial nerve nuclei, drug classes, staging systems.
Persona
You are a memory coach who teaches the method of loci to medical students.
My context
The list: [PASTE]
A familiar place I know well (home, hostel, hospital route): [brief]
Task
1. Choose a route through my place with one location per item.
2. Place a vivid image for each item at each location, linking the image to the item.
3. Walk me through the route once.
4. Test me by asking me to walk it back and name each item.
Rules
Keep the images vivid and clearly linked to each item, and check the list's accuracy [VERIFY], because the palace preserves errors as faithfully as facts.
Output
The route with the locations and images, then the recall test.
Pro tipReuse the same palace for one subject only, to avoid mixing lists.
Try it withThe 12 cranial nerves, placed along the route from your hostel room to the canteen.

My context
Concept: [e.g. the coagulation cascade / the brachial plexus / the renin-angiotensin system]
Exam: [brief]
Task

1. Group the questions by sub-topic and count them.
2. Identify the facts that are repeatedly tested.
3. Turn those facts into a one-page memory sheet.
4. Suggest 5 likely future questions on the same facts.
Rules
Base the patterns only on the pasted questions and say how many you analysed, because patterns from a few questions can mislead.
Output
The count table, the repeated facts, the memory sheet, then the likely questions.
Pro tipRepeated facts are repeated for a reason. Learn them first.

990Link a topic across subjects
Standard
3.7 Memory aids & high-yield summaries · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itFor integrated questions that join anatomy, physiology, pathology, pharmacology and medicine.
Persona
You are a teacher of integrated medical education who links topics across subjects.
My context
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Topic: [e.g. the thyroid gland]
Exam: [brief]
Task
1. Link the topic across subjects: anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, pathology, microbiology, pharmacology, medicine and surgery, as relevant.
2. Give 2 high-yield facts per subject.
3. Show how one subject explains another (for example, how the physiology explains the drug action).
4. Write 3 integrated MCQs that cross subjects, with answers.
Rules
Keep the facts accurate and mark numbers [VERIFY], because integrated questions punish half-remembered links.
Output
A table (subject, facts, link to the next subject), then the integrated MCQs.
Pro tipIntegrated links make each fact easier to recall, because it is stored in more than one place.

991Turn my mistakes into cards
Standard
3.7 Memory aids & high-yield summaries · MBBS Student / PG Resident
Use itAfter a mock test or MCQ session, to stop repeating the same mistakes.
Persona
You are an exam coach who turns errors into targeted revision.
My context
Questions I got wrong, with my answer and the correct answer: [PASTE]
Exam: [brief]
Task
1. For each mistake, identify the missing fact or the misconception.
2. Write one flashcard per mistake that targets exactly that gap.
3. Group the mistakes by pattern (knowledge gap, misreading, confusable facts).
4. Suggest one habit to reduce the commonest pattern.
Rules
Target the specific gap, not the whole topic, and mark facts [VERIFY], because error cards work only when they fix the exact misconception.
Output
The error table (question, gap, card), the pattern groups, then the habit.
Pro tipYour own mistakes make the highest-yield cards you will ever write.

Tools · Volume 3
Which AI tool for which job.
JobBest toolWhy
Learning a topic from your own books and notesNotebookLM, Claude, ChatGPT (upload)Explanations grounded in your sources
Tutoring, active recall and self-testingChatGPT Study mode, Claude, GeminiSocratic questioning and instant feedback
Custom exam tutor from your notesCustom GPTs, Claude Projects, Gemini GemsAnswers only from your uploaded material
Flashcards and spaced repetitionAnki, QuizletProven spaced-repetition scheduling
Audio revision on the moveNotebookLM Audio OverviewTurns chapters into listenable discussions
Visual notes and mind mapsCanva, Napkin AI, ChatGPT imagesDiagrams and summary sheets
Checking facts and recent guidelinesPerplexity, Consensus, the guideline itselfCited sources you can verify
Studying with AI, safely
  • Verify every fact, number and drug dose against a standard textbook or current guideline.
  • Use AI to test yourself, not to avoid thinking. Answer first, then check.
  • Never use AI during an exam or assessment where it isn't allowed.
  • Clinical reasoning prompts are for learning, not for decisions about real patients.

One last thing.

These prompts will not pass your exam for you. They will make every hour of study count: more recall, more practice and more feedback. The doctors who do best will be the ones who use AI to think harder, not less.

Test yourself. Check everything. Walk into the exam hall ready.

This resource is for educational purposes. It does not replace standard textbooks, current clinical guidelines, your university curriculum or your teachers. AI-generated content may contain errors: verify all facts independently. Clinical reasoning prompts are learning aids and are not a substitute for clinical judgement or supervision in patient care.
